This specific French edition was produced to compile and explain his scattered papers for a wider audience.</note>

# FOREWORD

The volume reproducing in its entirety Manuscript A from the Institute <note>The Institut de France in Paris, which holds several of Leonardo's notebooks</note>—the first attempt at a truly faithful, complete, and definitive edition of Leonardo da Vinci's writings—has received the most benevolent and encouraging reception. It has already given rise to remarkable writings containing new insights into Leonardo's genius and works. Foremost among these are a general and in-depth study by Mr. Ch. Lévêque, of the Institute; another study focusing specifically on the philosophical genius of the great artist by Mr. G. Séailles; an article by Mr. Ch. Clément in the *Débats*; and two other recent articles, one from the *Times* by Mr. Wallis, and the other from the *Nuova Antologia* of Rome by Mr. L. Ferri. It can be said, in truth, that all competent judges who have expressed an opinion regarding this volume and this undertaking have now admitted its full interest and utility¹.

However, Mr. J.-P. Richter—the author of a fine and important work recently published in England according to the old method (giving an overview of all Leonardo's writings by means of a large number of extracts classified in an order other than that of the original texts)²—has made an exception. He attributed, especially in a German Review³, a gravity to a few errors of transcription and translation (which my will alone was not enough to avoid) that they are very far from having. This was immediately and generally recognized. In an undertaking as arduous as deciphering and explaining everything that appears in unpublished manuscripts such as these, it would truly be asking too much to claim there were absolutely no faults of interpretation or printing. I stated as much in a study I published in the *Gazette des Beaux-Arts* (on the character of Leonardo da Vinci's writings, and on the...

conclusions that it authorizes), when exact and complete facsimiles everywhere accompany transcriptions and translations whose only pretension is to allow everyone to read them, the inconvenience of errors committed would only be truly serious for those who neglect to make use of these facsimiles¹. I have nonetheless applied myself to gathering in the Errata, which will be found at the end of this second volume, the imperfections that were rightly pointed out to me in Volume A, as well as others that an attentive revision allowed me to discover myself. The care with which Mr. Richter applied himself to highlighting all the words regarding which I happened to be mistaken has facilitated this task for me; but this care, having been pushed a bit far in writings that will endure, obliges me to show, for my legitimate defense, by a few examples found in notes placed at the bottom of the Errata at the end of this volume, that even men of great knowledge or very special competence might not have escaped faults or inaccuracies just as regrettable as mine may have appeared. As for the value of the method we have inaugurated², one can say it is beyond discussion, since a scholar of such authority as Mr. G. Govi has joined it, recommending its use to Italy³, and since in England the idea of bringing to light in their entirety all the writings found there is beginning to prevail⁴.

The second volume of the complete edition of the twelve manuscripts of the Institute will appear to present even more importance, and be better suited to satisfy curiosity than the first, for it includes both the one which, as much by the development of certain subjects as by the importance and variety of the drawings, passes for the principal one, Manuscript B, and the one which, among those known, is perhaps the most finished, Notebook D.

Manuscript B contains 84 folios today; Manuscript D, 10. The second volume of the complete publication will therefore comprise, in total, 94 folios, 188 facsimiles, instead of the 126 comprised in the first, or: 62 more facsimiles⁵.

In order not to lose sight of all the interest these precious notebooks must offer to artists and scholars, one would do well to keep in mind the considerations

<margin>
1. *The Writings of Leonardo da Vinci* (excerpt from the *Gazette des Beaux-Arts* of March, April, June 1881, p. 63, by Charles Ravaisson-Mollien, published by Quantin). In some respects, this study was also criticized by Mr. de Geymüller, in the *Chronique des Arts* of June 11, 1881, with the greatest courtesy (see in the Errata note 1 of folio 1 recto of Manuscript A), and by Mr. Richter in *The Literary Works of L. da V.*, perhaps without enough impartiality. These criticisms are far, I believe, from being all indisputably well-founded. I hasten to recognize that on points of detail I was mistaken, or may have been mistaken. Thus, was I wrong to suggest interrogatively that Leonardo spoke in January 1511 of Benedetto da Maiano, a time at which it turns out the latter was dead; thus it is very possible that the technical remarks of Mr. de Geymüller on the architecture shown in the sheet of 1473 (and although certain lines of the landscape could, in my opinion, indicate perspective at least as well as "cultivated fields") should make one regard this sheet as representing a site in Italy and not the Righi <note>A mountain in Switzerland; the author is debating the location of a specific Leonardo landscape drawing</note> (see page 40 of the said Study). Thus again, I undoubtedly went astray regarding the person, though not the horses, of the Cyprus sheet (p. 41, and in *Le Temps* of February 27, 1881). But I see no reason to renounce what I said about the nature of Leonardo's genius as it appears in his writings, nor most at least of the conclusions I drew from it. The disagreement that arose between Messrs. Govi and Richter regarding this hypothesis of a journey to the Orient, of which so much has been said, proves that I was not wrong to estimate that it was wise not to yet consider the question resolved for or against. I also persist in believing that the famous letter to Ludovico Sforza <note>original: "Louis le More"</note> is not in Leonardo's hand (a recent analysis of the *Codex Atlanticus* <note>original: "l'Atlantique"</note> has strengthened me in this conviction), and that, consequently, it is admissible, until proven otherwise, that it may not have been originally written by him or for him. As for the facsimiles, I am still persuaded that the best ones to adopt for the complete publication were those very ones we adopted, that is to say, as produced by photography, unmodified under any pretext, and not straightened (see at the end of the offprint, the *Study* in question, and the facsimiles of the *Literary Works of L. da V.*), etc., etc.

4. See: *The Times* of August 9, 1883.
5. The small Notebook D interrupts the alphabetical order, but it could take its place in this volume, whereas Manuscript C could not. Moreover, the former completes, from certain points of view in the sense the publication was understood, Manuscripts A and B. Manuscript C, on Light and Shadow, will follow well after the treatise on Optics in Manuscript D, in the next volume.

### FOREWORD.

to which the publication of Manuscript A led—which, as I have said, was intended to appear before the other manuscripts of the Institute—to clearly demonstrate the true nature of the various manifestations of their author's genius throughout the course of his other writings¹.

Manuscript B, like the preceding one, treats a variety of subjects, among which one will notice passages relating to spirits, Morals, the Arts of drawing, Music, bizarre inventions, Water, and many others, which denote the profound study that Leonardo made—even though he was a "disciple of Experience" <note>original: "disciple de l'Expérience." Leonardo famously called himself "ostantado di lettere" (a man without letters) but a "discepolo della sperienza" (disciple of experience), prioritizing observation over book-learning.</note>—of Antiquity, Geometry, and Mechanics; finally, it is with remarkable consistency that he discusses Architecture, Building, Roadworks, and engineering works (various constructions, Churches, Palaces, Public ways, Sluice gates, Kitchens, Chimneys, etc.). This includes not only construction from the artistic point of view—the buildings and roads of Milan—but also the careful arrangement of their smallest details. He also covers warfare on land and water (weapons, soldiers, combat, fortifications), not only studying what it had been in all times and among all peoples, but through a deep search for means that could serve to perfect its practice. It was likely in this latter order of studies, and not, as has been believed, through a petty whim, that Leonardo da Vinci applied himself with great perseverance to combining a mechanism that could allow man to fly by the flapping of wings—a mechanism of which the final pages of Manuscript B contain a most curious overview².

Leonardo da Vinci's research on flight occupied him in the most serious manner for a very long time; considerable portions of several of his manuscripts are filled with the notes he took in this regard. The great inventor attached, it seems to me, only secondary importance to the difference in physical constitution between man and birds, and did not consider the difficulty of finding a point of support—given the physiological organization of man—to be insurmountable³. Man can swim and navigate; why could he not fly? he perhaps asked himself.

He who had imagined a process (which has been used in our own day) for walking on water (Codex Atlanticus, folio 7 recto; Gerli, *Drawings of L. d. V.* plate XXXII, z) saw things from a high vantage point; considering at the same time—with that habit of generalizing everything on which I have had occasion to insist several times—all those diverse animals that fly under the most varied conditions, from the eagle to the bat, the dragonfly, and the gnat, and whose limbs are but modifications of those which for others serve to swim or walk, he probably believed that the solution to the problem was more likely to be found in determining certain relationships between weight, body volume, <term>wingspan</term> <note>original: "envergure"</note>, strength, the movement of wings or membranes, and air resistance. Was Leonardo pursuing only a chimera here? I believe that could not be proven. Since the era in which he lived, man has momentarily flown several times⁵; why then, if serious accidents have delayed further experiments, should there not come an hour when science definitively takes possession of the air, as it has taken possession of land and sea? And who knows if the disclosure of Leonardo's writings might not

### FOREWORD.

...not assist in the noble works of this time to give a new impetus to this art of rising, to which all of humanity has aspired? I will return elsewhere to this interesting point in more detail¹.

One of the passages of Manuscript B relating to aeronautics (folio 83 verso) was recently pointed out by Mr. Govi to the Academy of Sciences, as containing a proposal for a screw propeller <note>original: "propulseur à hélice"</note> and as an interesting parallel to other passages in the *Atlanticus* <note>The *Codex Atlanticus* is the largest collection of Leonardo da Vinci's drawings and writings, currently held in the Biblioteca Ambrosiana in Milan.</note> regarding the parachute².

Manuscript B had already been cited several times previously for the scientific importance of some of its texts: notably by Venturi for fortifications, pearl fishing in India, and Greek fire; by Delécluze for the description of a steam cannon <note>original: "canon à vapeur"; Leonardo called this invention the "Architronito."</note> attributed by Leonardo to Archimedes; by Libri and Mr. Govi for a passage concerning whether, through compressed air, spirits can exist without bodies in this world; by Mr. Courajod for an interesting drawing regarding interlacings; and by Mr. de Geymüller for church plans related to Bramante's designs for the construction of St. Peter's in Rome. Several other pages have recently appeared, in whole or in part, in the work of Mr. Richter.

Manuscript B must be compared particularly, and in several respects, to the *Atlanticus*; I will attempt to show this soon while accounting for the mission I recently fulfilled in Milan. Although much smaller, it has the advantage of a pagination which, while not by Leonardo himself, is very old and matches the sequence of subjects³. On the first page, one finds a few lines that will seem worthy of the attention of those seeking to clarify the question of whether Leonardo traveled to the East; these are strange characters <note>likely referring to Leonardo's experiments with non-Western scripts or cryptic ciphers</note>, which should be compared with those found—though they are quite different—in another of the Institute's autograph notebooks and among several pages of the *Atlanticus* (for example, folios 4 recto and verso, 19 recto, 298 verso). In the same vein, many other passages in the rest of Manuscript B will be noted where, concerning matters of war, there is mention of Eastern lands. This manuscript is also important for the author's biography, because it can likely be assigned to a precise period of his life: the end of his time in the service of Ludovico the Moor <note>Ludovico Sforza (1452–1508), the Duke of Milan and a major patron of the Renaissance.</note>, since we see him naming Milan, the Duke, and the Duchess, regarding works he seems to plan for the city and the princes. In one instance, he mentions a "Marchesino" (folio 4 recto), who might be, if I am not mistaken, Lord Marchesino Stange, Ludovico's secretary, to whom the latter wrote a letter on June 30, 1497, published by Mr. Richter⁴.

***

1. "Of the many problems posed to the world today, there is perhaps none greater than that of aerial navigation. Past failures must not be seen as precursors to future defeats, for it is only in these last few years that the subject of artificial flight has been taken up with a truly scientific spirit. — As societies for the advancement of aeronautics have been established in England, America, France, and other countries, there are reasons to believe that our knowledge of this most difficult department of science will continue to grow until the complicated problem is solved." J.-B. Pettigrew, *Animal Locomotion (International Scientific Series)*.
2. On this occasion, I pointed out to the same Academy another passage of Manuscript B, interesting for a different reason, concerning telephones. (*Proceedings of the Academy of Sciences*, August 29 and September 19, 1852. — See the notes for folios 6 recto and 83 verso.)
3. The author's very clear intention for this manuscript, as with Manuscript A and several others, was that the pages should follow—at least as drafts—the very order in which they are found. It is true that sometimes this intention is expressly indicated by references, numbers, or this instruction: "Turn the page" <note>original Italian: "volta carta"</note>; but I believe no conclusion can be drawn to the contrary from the absence of this elsewhere. Thus, in Manuscript D, where the pagination is in Leonardo's own hand and where it can hardly be contested that everything follows a sequence as in a treatise, we see the scholar writing: "turn the page," whereas he does not write these words at the bottom of the other pages. Leonardo usually makes these references when a sentence is not finished.
4. *Leonardo*, London, 1880, p. 18. — It was not until 1494 that Ludovico Sforza took the title of Duke, says Mr. de Geymüller in *The Literary Works of Leonardo da Vinci*, Vol. I, p. 26, no. 751. Before 1494, "Duke and Duchess of Milan" would refer to Gian Galeazzo and Isabella of Aragon.

<meta>This page continues the preface, specifically discussing the relationship between Leonardo's various notebooks (Manuscripts A, B, and D) and his projected "Treatise on Painting."</meta>

# FOREWORD.

Likewise, it will be possible to determine approximately the date at which Leonardo must have written Manuscript D; it was likely when the *Treatise on Painting* was on the verge of being completed. As for this latter manuscript <note>Manuscript D</note>, much less substantial than the B collection, but which has the advantage over it of not having lost any leaves^1 and of bearing an original pagination, it will suffice to say, to make its value understood, that it is from this work that Venturi drew the passage relating to the camera obscura <note>original: "chambre obscure"; an early optical device that led to the camera</note> (Manuscript D, folio 8. — Venturi, *Essay*, etc., p. 23).

Of all Leonardo's manuscripts, the one bearing the letter D may appear the most scientific. Is this a reason to think that—as one would only wrongly believe of Manuscript A, as I stated in the Study cited above—notebook D cannot have any interest or utility for art? The opposite is perhaps true. This notebook, which appears to be the fair copy of some of the long-sought drafts on optics and perspective^2, of which Manuscript A provides examples, gives in a form that seems almost definitive in the author's mind a part of the *Treatise on Painting*^3. It may be through a profound knowledge of the nature of the eye that Leonardo da Vinci wished to begin, in order to establish, according to his way of seeing, the bases of the chapters on perspective, which were to form a part of this *Treatise*; also, although Manuscript D is primarily related only to optics proper—to the study of the eye in all living beings—it discusses both perspective and painting. Leonardo distinguishes, parenthetically, the painting in use among the painters of his time (which was entirely conventional, according to him) from the true painting, to be founded on the experimental knowledge of the laws and phenomena of perception.

As for Manuscript B, it contains several passages relating to the proportions of man and on the composition of colors, which were written with the *Treatise on Painting* in view. To show all the interest that it, too, offers to artists, there is no need to recall further the considerations that lead one to think of it what has been recognized as true regarding Manuscript A. It will be enough to announce that many of the figures explaining the texts can count, for their elegance, their finesse, and their energy, among the most beautiful sketches of the great master. One of them may serve as an example: that of a warrior on horseback (folio 46 verso), to be compared with certain sketches of the statue of Francesco Sforza, and the riders of the Battle of Anghiari^4.

For Manuscripts B and D, especially for the first, even more attention and more requested advice have not been able to preserve me absolutely from all errors. Far from desiring that they pass unnoticed, I hasten to give warning of them. Indications of these will be found in the errata following those of Manuscript A. Those which are serious are, moreover, if I am not mistaken, very rare; I point out here, in this regard, the leaves: 3 verso, 4 recto, 7 recto, 9 verso, 12 recto, 13 recto, 15 recto, 18 verso, 20 verso, 23 recto, 35 recto, 36 recto, 40 verso, 54 verso and 63 verso. I have, moreover, done everything in my power so that in all respects the second volume would be superior, and increasingly superior, to the first. I hope that those who can imagine the fatigue I have had to brave and overcome to reach this goal will grant me some benevolent indulgence.

---

1. See the general preface at the beginning of Volume A (Manuscript B).
2. "In ancient times, Perspective was synonymous with Optics." <note>original Italian: "Anticamente Prospettiva era sinonimo d'Ottica."</note> (Govi, *Leonardo as Scientist and Man of Letters — Essay on the works of Leonardo da Vinci*, p. 13).
3. This is perhaps the occasion to point out to those who do not yet know it, an important edition of the *Treatise on Painting* which appeared a short time ago in Germany: *Leonardo da Vinci, the Book of Painting according to the Vatican Codex (Urbinas) 1270, edited, translated and explained by Heinrich Ludwig in three volumes; Vienna, 1882, Wilhelm Braumüller.* <note>original German title: "das Buch von der Malerei..."</note>
4. See: *Leonardo da Vinci and the statue of Francesco Sforza*, by L. Courajod, 1879, published by Champion.

# FOREWORD.

It will be noted that from the perspective of the beauty of the work, progress has been made by Mr. Quantin <note>Albert Quantin (1850–1933), a famous French printer and publisher known for high-quality art books</note>, specifically the direct printing of photographic transfers replacing the previous method of pasting, and that these transfers are even closer to perfection than those of Manuscript A.

To the transcription of the texts, I have thought it useful to add a transcription of the letters that accompany a great number of figures, in cases where these letters would be difficult to find in the facsimile.

For Manuscript D, I hesitated on the manner of transcribing the figures and the commentaries that accompany them in the margin; but, all things considered, it seemed to me that the best course of action would be to reproduce, in general, first everything that is written on the right in the margin, provided that I warn the reader here that they must always take into account the position—which is easy to find—that the figures or texts printed first in small characters occupy laterally on the facsimiles in relation to the main texts.

Finally, for each of the manuscripts B and D, I have compiled an alphabetical table of contents, perhaps even more complete than that of Manuscript A, in which the corrections noted in the Errata have been taken into account, and which it would be well to compare with the latter.

The pagination of Manuscript B has not been transcribed as it was for Manuscripts A and D, because it did not appear to me to be in Leonardo's own hand <term>autograph: a manuscript or signature written by the author themselves</term>. The same applies to a certain number of words written in the ordinary direction <note>Leonardo famously wrote in "mirror script," from right to left; "ordinary direction" refers to standard left-to-right writing</note> on various pages, which are transcriptions by several hands in the Spanish and Italian languages.

# FOREWORD.

It will be noted that from the perspective of the beauty of the work, progress has been made by Mr. Quantin <note>Albert Quantin (1850–1933), a famous French printer and publisher known for high-quality art books</note>, specifically the direct printing of photographic transfers replacing the previous method of pasting, and that these transfers are even closer to perfection than those of Manuscript A.

To the transcription of the texts, I have thought it useful to add a transcription of the letters that accompany a great number of figures, in cases where these letters would be difficult to find in the facsimile.

For Manuscript D, I hesitated on the manner of transcribing the figures and the commentaries that accompany them in the margin; but, all things considered, it seemed to me that the best course of action would be to reproduce, in general, first everything that is written on the right in the margin, provided that I warn the reader here that they must always take into account the position—which is easy to find—that the figures or texts printed first in small characters occupy laterally on the facsimiles in relation to the main texts.

The same applies to a certain number of words written in the ordinary direction <note>Leonardo da Vinci famously wrote in "mirror script," from right to left; "ordinary direction" refers to standard left-to-right writing added by later collectors or librarians.</note>

# PROPORTIONS — PAINTING — MORALS — FORCE — MOVEMENT.

— The foot, from the tip to the heel, fits 2 times from the heel to the knee, that is to say, where the leg bone meets that of the thigh.

— The hand, up to where it meets the arm bone, fits 4 times from the tip of the longest finger to the shoulder joint.

— Note: How <term>aqua vitae<note>original: "eau-de-vie" - literally "water of life," a high-proof distilled spirit used as a solvent in alchemy and art.</note></term> gathers within itself all the colors and scents of flowers; and if you wish to make azure, put cornflowers <note>original: "bleuets [?]"</note> into it, and then poppies <note>original: "coquelicots [?]"</note>.

— For the figure of Fame, one must paint the entire person covered in tongues instead of feathers, in the shape of a bird. <note>This refers to the classical personification of Fama (Renommée), whose many tongues represent the spreading of rumors and news.</note>

— *If... If your body were in proportion to your virtue, you would have no desires in this world.*

— *You believe in fame and reputation...*

— *You grow — in reputation — like bread — in the hand — of children.* <note>Likely a metaphor for how quickly or easily a reputation can be "consumed" or broken down, or perhaps how it swells like rising dough.</note>

— Water that descends by one inch per hour...

— Definition of force and movement in animals. I say that the said movement is caused by several points of support.

— Force is created by the deflation of muscles and the shortening of muscles that retract, as well as by nerves that tighten as much as the sensation <note>original: "sentiment"</note> requires, which passes through the empty cords. <note>Leonardo and his contemporaries often theorized that nerves were hollow tubes through which "animal spirits" or sensations traveled to trigger movement.</note>

### ACCOUNTS — FABRICS FOR AN APPARATUS — EXPLOSIVE BOMB.

— On the 28th of April, I had from Marchesino 103 pounds and [furthermore?] 12 <note>The "pound" here refers to the *lira*, a unit of currency in Renaissance Milan.</note> ¹.

This powder is surrounded by a bit of <term>tow<note>original: "étoupe" — coarse, broken fibers of flax or hemp used for stuffing or as tinder.</note></term> soaked in secondary turpentine, and the rest is wrapped in hemp turpentine moistened with turpentine, linseed oil, and pitch; and let the wrappings be sparse so that the flames have air, for otherwise you would accomplish nothing.

<header>WATER — SPIRITS — MOTION AND PROPORTION — MECHANICS.</header>

— Water that descends by one inch <note>original: "once"; a historical unit of measure</note> per mile will have a motion of 1/4 brasse <note>original: "brasse"; a unit of length roughly equal to the reach of a man's arms, about 6 feet</note> for one beat, that is to say, one musical beat. That which descends by 2 inches per mile *will descend* and have a motion of 1/2 brasse per beat, and likewise that which descends by 4 inches will have a motion of one brasse per beat.

— There can be no voice [sound] where there is no motion or percussion of air; there can be no percussion of air where there is no instrument; there can be no *incorporeal* incorporeal instrument; since this is the case, a spirit can have neither voice, nor form, nor strength, and if it takes on a body, it will not be able to *enter* penetrate or enter where the doors are closed — 4 —

— 4 — and if someone were to say that by gathered and tightened [compressed] air, the spirit takes on bodies of diverse forms, and that by this instrument it speaks and moves with force, to this part I say [I reply] that where there are neither nerves nor bones, there can be no force exerted in any movement made by imagined spirits. — Flee the precepts of those speculators whose reasonings are not confirmed by experience¹.

### ON MOTION AND PROPORTION

— If you want to know where and in what part of the path the object projected by a violent cause [acts most?], you shall make a mound of fresh earth; with a crossbow you shall shoot an arrow into it from various distances, and where the same arrow sinks in the deepest, there is the distance that produces the most force.

Suppose this case: the arrow, marked for 400 brasses, shoot it first from 25, then from 50. Move back until 400, shooting every 25 [brasses], and thus you will see in what part of the flight the arrow has the most force, whether at 1/3, or 1/4, or 1/5 of the way.

— If you want to see an experiment in proportion, if a stone is thrown by the small *bricole* <note>a "bricole" is a type of small medieval catapult or traction trebuchet</note> to 20 brasses with a counterweight of ten, see if a counterweight of 20 will throw it twice as far, more or less, and let what you throw be fresh earth wrapped in paper. Let the earth be fresh so that it does not bounce after the impact; let it be wrapped in paper so that it does not stick to the *bricole*.

— To raise and place a beam through a window with ease.

**OF MOTION AND PROPORTION**

If you wish to know where, or in what part of its path, an object propelled by a violent cause <note>meaning an external force, like a shot or a throw</note> [acts with the most power], you shall make a mass of fresh earth and, with a crossbow, shoot an arrow into it from various distances; and where the same arrow sticks deepest, that distance is where it is strongest. Let us suppose the case that the arrow is marked for a range of 400 *braccia*; make the first shot at a distance of 25, then at 50, and so on, moving back 25 *braccia* at a time until you reach 400, shooting every 25. Thus, you will see in what part of its course the arrow is most powerful: whether at 1/3, 1/4, or 1/5 of the way. If you wish to see an experiment in proportion: if a stone is thrown 20 *braccia* by a small <term>briccola: a type of medieval catapult or counterweight engine</term> with a counterweight of ten, see if a counterweight of 20 will throw it twice as far or not. And let that which you throw be fresh earth wrapped in fresh paper—the earth so that it does not bounce after the impact, and wrapped in paper so that it does not stick to the *briccola*.

How to raise and place a beam through a window with ease.

# OPTICS

## THE NATURE OF MIRRORS.

— If you place the line *a b* in front of a convex mirror <note>A mirror that curves outward, like the back of a spoon.</note>, the lines of the resemblances [images] positioned in this way—directing themselves toward its center—*a b* will decrease in size just as *c d* is; and if you place the line *h m* in front of the cavity of the convex mirror <note>The author likely refers here to the concave side, or the interior curve, of the mirror.</note>, the species <term>species: an archaic term for the visual form or "likeness" of an object traveling through the air</term> go toward this mirror along lines originating from its center, so that the line *h m* will increase in size just as *e f* is; and if the object placed in front of the cavity of the mirror is located at the midpoint of its center *g*, such as the line *n p*, this line will be carried onto the mirror at the location *e f* upside down; indeed, as the species are constrained to travel in straight lines, *n* is carried along its line to *f*, and likewise *p* is transported to *e*.

<vocab>optics, mirror, convex, center, species, lines, resemblances, image</vocab>

<summary>This page explains the geometric principles of reflection in curved mirrors, demonstrating how images are magnified, diminished, or inverted depending on their position relative to the mirror's center.</summary>
<keywords>optics, catoptrics, convex mirrors, concave mirrors, image inversion, geometry of light, visual species</keywords>

### [Printed Commentary]

->THE NATURE OF MIRRORS<-

— If you place the line *a. b.* in front of a convex mirror, because the lines of the resemblances placed before it direct themselves toward its center, *a. b.* will decrease to the size of *c. d.*; and if you place the line *h. m.* in front of the convex mirror, the species go to that mirror along lines divided from its center, and the line *h. m.* will increase to the size of *e. f.* And if the object placed in front of the mirror is beyond its center *g*, like the line *n. p.*, said line will be carried [carried] to the mirror at the location *e. f.* upside down; because, as the species are constrained to travel in straight lines, *n.* is carried by its line to *f*, and likewise *p.* transfers itself to *e.*

<note>Leonardo uses "spechio cholmo" (heaped/convex mirror) to describe the geometry of how light rays converge or diverge relative to a central point, a fundamental principle of optics.</note>

<summary>Leonardo explains the geometric rules of reflection for curved mirrors, detailing how images (species) are magnified, reduced, or inverted based on their distance from the mirror's center. The text demonstrates his belief that light and images must travel in perfectly straight lines.</summary>
<keywords>optics, convex mirrors, reflection, geometry of light, visual species, image inversion, catoptrics</keywords>

This <insert>the device illustrated here</insert> <note>original: "la pièce ici figurée"</note> is attached to the middle of a piece of plank, or a length of chain, or a thick rope, which is joined to a piece of stone heavier than the plank, so that the stone drags behind the plank. And this plank shall be 12 fathoms <term>fathoms: "brasses," a measurement of the reach of outstretched arms, roughly 6 feet</term> long, and its flat surface is full of nails.

# WAR MACHINES

### THE RHOMPHAIA
<note>original: "rohmphea" — while historically a Thracian polearm, Leonardo uses the term here to describe a massive, mobile spiked barrier or projectile beam.</note>

This rhomphaia can be pulled with docked-tail horses <note>original: "cortaldi" — horses with docked tails, often used for heavy labor; however, Leonardo also used this term to refer to short-barreled cannons or bombards</note> just as the ancients pulled with other instruments. This device is attached in the middle of a piece of plank, or a piece of chain, or a thick rope, which is joined to a piece of heavy stone—heavier than the beam itself—so that it pulls from behind the beam. The front edge of this beam is full of spontoons <term>spontoons: long spikes or half-pikes</term> one cubit <term>cubit: an ancient unit of length, approximately 18-22 inches</term> long. This beam shall be called 12 braccia <term>braccia: "arms," a Florentine unit of measurement; 12 braccia is roughly 23 feet or 7 meters</term> long, and its flat surface is full of nails.

---

### THE RHOMPHAIA

— This rhomphaia can be pulled with docked-tail horses <unclear>short cannons?</unclear> just as the ancients pulled with other instruments. This is attached in the middle of a piece of plank, or a piece of chain, or a thick rope, which is joined to a piece of stone heavier than the beam, so that it pulls the beam from behind. The front edge of the beam is full of spontoons one cubit long, and this beam shall be 12 braccia long, and its flat surface is full of nails.

# MOVEMENT — MATTERS OF WAR.

### ON MOVEMENT.

#### BOW:

— If you make a crossbow or a bow that is drawn—both the bow itself and the arrow—and then released by a crossbow mechanism, the arrow will undoubtedly travel a great distance. Let the arrows be made almost entirely of iron so that they are heavy.

— Rhomphaia <note>original: "Rhomphée" — likely referring back to the heavy spiked beam described on the previous page.</note>.

— For walls and ramparts.

— This crossbow, in order to have a great "rise" <note>likely referring to the tension or the arc of the draw</note>, drives its arrow with great force. Let the thin parts be made with a better temper than the thick parts; take the example of the center of an anvil.

— Catapult.

— Scorpions.

— If you load these 4 crossbows one by one and release them at the same time, you will see a good trial. But ensure that each one is 12 braccia <term>braccia: an Italian unit of length, roughly 23 inches</term> or more, and if they are one braccia wide and half a braccia thick, you can give them a great rise—that is to say, 6 braccia.

#### SCORPIONS.

— The scorpion is a machine that can throw stones, darts, and arrows; and if it is made large, it will be suitable for breaking the engines of the enemy.

Other authors are of the opinion that the scorpion is a poisoned arrow which, if it touches the blood even slightly, brings immediate death. And it is said that such a weapon was found among the Scythians <note>ancient nomadic people of Central Eurasia</note>, others say by those of Candia <note>modern-day Crete</note>; the mixture is made of human blood and serpent venom. One should only use this weapon against traitors, because it originates from them.

# MOVEMENT — WEAPONS AND MACHINES OF WAR.

### On MOVEMENT:

— This arrow, if it is made of iron and feathered, will travel fast.


### CATAPULT:

— The catapult, according to what Nonius¹ and Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman author of Natural History</note> say, is an instrument invented by this Ticlete <margin>this famous Tiglath?²</margin>, which launched a dart of 3 cubits <term>cubit: an ancient unit of length based on the forearm, roughly 18 inches</term>, with a three-sided iron head, launched by means of wooden arms released from the tension of twisted sinews <note>referring to torsion springs made of hair or animal gut</note>.

— A piece of steel as well, returning to its natural state <note>referring to the potential energy of a bent spring</note>, will be able to forcefully drive a dart placed in its path.

---

1. Nonius Marcellus <note>a 4th-century Roman grammarian</note>.
2. Tiglath-Pileser <note>original: "Tiglath Phalassar"</note>, conqueror and King of Nineveh after Nebuchadnezzar.

# ENGINES OF WAR.

### SLING [Ballista] :

— Driven deep into the ground with their branches and pins. Trample the earth placed over them layer by layer, but only after a wide ditch has been made.

### MUSKETS.

<note>The term "mousquets" here likely refers to early mechanical bolt-throwers or large crossbows rather than handheld firearms.</note>

— The arrow *a b* remains attached to the string and the arrow *b c* is the one that flies into the distance.
— An arrow that cannot be shot if the plant <gloss>stem?</gloss> <gloss>shaft?</gloss> is not fully grown.
— Poison arrow; and its iron head is triangular and hollowed out.

### RHOMPHAEA.

— The rhomphaea is an instrument that projects long, flaming pieces of wood; according to Aulus Gellius <note>A 2nd-century Roman author known for "Attic Nights"</note>, it was in use among the people of Thrace, and among other nations it was called the "flaming one."

### BOW.

— The bow, it is said, was discovered by those of Arcadia, though some say <gloss>by</gloss> Apollo; those of Candia <note>Modern-day Crete</note> call it Scythian, as if from Scythia. It is heavily used among the Eastern peoples; they make the arrows for these bows out of reeds, and in their battles there are sometimes so many in the air that the darkened daylight appears as night. For this reason, they hold clouds and rain in hatred, and no less the winds, because they divert the course of their arrows; these causes often bring about truces and peace between them.

# WEAPONS OF WAR.

### CALTROPS OR TRIBULI.

— <term>Caltrops: or *murex* / *tribuli*; spiked metal devices scattered on the ground</term> are to be employed on the battlefield, sown in areas where one suspects an enemy assault, and also thrown among the enemy when they are pursuing their victory <note>to hinder a pursuing force during their retreat</note>.

### SCALPRUM.

— The <term>scalprum: a sharp knife or chisel-like tool</term> was a sharp iron instrument used to wound and to control elephants. <note>Titus</note> Livy states in the seventh book of the Carthaginian War <note>referring to the Second Punic War</note> that many more elephants were killed by *the Carthaginians* (those who guided them) than by the enemy. Indeed, when these beasts fell into a frenzy against their own side, their handler would strike the sharp scalprum with a great blow between the ears, where the neck joins the nape of the neck; this was the swiftest death that could be given to such a large beast.

### VERUTUM.

— The <term>verutum: a short javelin used by Roman light infantry</term>, according to what I find in a comedy by Plautus <note>a Roman playwright, c. 254–184 BC</note>, is a lance with a long handle and a sharp iron tip for throwing.

### SOLIFERREUM.

— The <term>soliferreum: a heavy javelin forged entirely from iron</term> is a type of weapon made completely of iron, which the soldiers threw during the initial assaults. <note>Titus</note> Livy makes mention of it in the fourth book of the Macedonian War.

### SLING.

— The sling is made of a double cord, somewhat wide at its bend, in which a stone is placed; it is then swung twice with the arm. One of the cords is released, and the stone flies through the air with a whistle, as if launched from a <term>ballista: a large ancient engine for throwing stones</term>. Flavius¹ says that it was discovered among the inhabitants of the Balearic Islands, and that it is they who know how to use it with excellence; he notes that mothers would not allow their children to touch any food other than that which had been knocked down *by* them from a target with a stone released from the sling. However, Pliny says that this same sling was an invention of the Syrophoenician people.

### GLANDES.

— <term>Glandes: literally "acorns," referring to almond-shaped lead bullets</term> are lead balls thrown with crossbows and slings.

<note>Sketch of a chisel-like instrument.</note>

<note>Sketch of a person's arm and a sling in motion.</note>

<header>WAR ENGINES.</header>

### AUCTEURS.

— The *aucteur* <note>original: "aucteur"; likely a corruption of the Latin "cultellus" or "culter" for a knife or cleaver</note>, according to what Celidonius¹ says, is a scythe-like weapon with a cutting edge on only one side and the length of a fathom <note>term: brasse (fathom); a measurement of length based on outstretched arms, roughly 5 to 6 feet</note>. It has a handle forked in the manner of a swallow's tail; it is not carried in a sheath, but naked, attached to the belt.

### DANISH AXES.

— The Danish axes <note>original: "danoises"</note> are somewhat long small axes; it is said they were very much in use among the Danish peoples. But what must be considered in iron instruments for war is that those quenched <insert>tempered</insert> in oil will have a delicate edge, and those quenched in water will be raw <insert>harsh</insert> and brittle; those extinguished in goat's blood will have the greatest hardness. Oil, white lead, and pitch preserve iron from all rust.

### SCYTHES.

— The scythe <note>original: "faux"</note> is an iron tool in a lunar shape <insert>crescent-shaped</insert> and a staff is joined to one of the horns <insert>one of the crescents</insert>. This weapon was very much in use among those of Thrace <note>an ancient region in Southeast Europe</note>, and no less in naval combat than on land; later it passed to the use of farmers and peasants <insert>country folk</insert>.

### SCYTHES.

— Among the Romans, scythes of an unheard-of size were used on ships; when they were pulled skillfully with ropes, they cut the ropes of the yardarms <note>term: antennes (lateen yards); the spars that hold the sails</note> as if they had been razors, making the sails fall at the same time as the yards, and that which should have given aid to the enemies became a great hindrance to them.

### FRAGILIQUE.

— The *fragilique* <note>an early form of incendiary or chemical grenade</note> is a ball of half a foot, full of small tubes made of paper and coated with pitch, sulfur, and <unclear>corsican?</unclear>, such that as soon as one has smelled it, one falls into a faint; in the center of this ball, there is gunpowder <note>original: "poudre de bombarde"</note>, which, when lit, sets fire to all the tubes, and when it is thrown among the troops with a sling <unclear>...</unclear> the fire first takes to a plug and the sparks go scattering over a space of 100 fathoms.....<unclear>...</unclear>

# WAR ENGINES.

### CHARIOT ARMED WITH SCYTHES.

— These chariots armed with scythes were of various kinds, and they often caused no less harm, certainly, to friends than to enemies; indeed, the captains of armies, believing that by using them they could throw the enemy's troops into confusion, instead created fear and devastation among their own. Against these chariots, one must make use of archers, slingers, and spearmen, hurling all sorts of darts, spears, stones, fire, the sound of drums, and shouting. Those who act in this manner should keep themselves dispersed so that the scythes do not find them. In this way, the horses will be terrified and will turn back uncontrolled among their own side, despite the efforts of their drivers, and cause them great obstruction and harm. The Romans used iron caltrops <note>original: "tribules"; iron multi-pointed devices designed to always have one spike facing upward to injure horses' hooves</note> against them, which hindered the horses; these, having fallen to the ground from exhaustion, left the chariots motionless.

### ROMPHAEAS.

— The romphaeas <note>term: romphile/romphaea; a long-handled polearm or powerful shock weapon used by Thracian and Macedonian infantry</note> were spears of 3 cubits <note>term: coudée (cubit); an ancient measurement based on the length of the forearm, approximately 18 inches</note> in length, covered in iron points, and they were thrown into the midst of the enemy with a cord attached to a stick used as a sling; they were a great hindrance to the enemy.

### ROMPHAEAS.

The *rocaces* <note>original: "rocaces"; an obscure term likely referring to a type of pike or heavy javelin</note> and the romphaeas were used by the people of Macedonia against the Tartars [?], who are accustomed to running as long as their lives last [all their lives] between the ranks [?] and, bypassing the spears, they kill the striker [the one who was about to strike them].

->**SCYTHED CHARIOT**<-

These scythed chariots were of various kinds. They often did no less damage to friends than to enemies, because the captains of the armies, believing that they could disrupt the enemy ranks with these, instead created fear and damage among their own men. Against these, it is necessary to use archers, slingers <note>original: "fondatori"</note>, and spear-throwers, and to hurl every manner of darts, lances, stones, and fire; [also] the noise of drums and shouts. Such operators should be spread out so that the scythes do not find them. Because of this, the horses will be frightened, and being unbridled <note>meaning out of control</note>, they will turn back among their own people despite their drivers, becoming a great hindrance and damage to themselves. The Romans used against these the <term>caltrops</term> <note>original: "triboli"; spiked metal devices scattered on the ground to maim horses' hooves</note> sown of iron, which impeded the horses; having fallen to the ground from the pain, they left the chariots motionless.

The *rhomphaia* were shafts of 3 cubits <note>a cubit is an ancient unit of length, roughly the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger</note> which were full of iron points and were thrown among the enemies with a cord attached to a stick, used like a sling; and these were a great hindrance to the enemies.

**SCYTHED CHARIOT**
— these scythed chariots. were of various kinds. and often did no less damage to friends than to enemies and these that the captains of the armies believing with these to disrupt. the ranks of the enemies with these created fear and damage among their own. against these. it is necessary. to use. archers. slingers. and throwers and to hurl every manner of darts lances. stones. fires. noises of drums shouts and such operators should stay spread out so the scythes do not find them and because of this the horses will be frightened. which unbridled. will turn among their own despite their governors [drivers] and will be a great hindrance and damage to their very selves the romans used against these the caltrops sown of iron which impeded the horses and fallen to the ground from the pain left the chariots without motion.

**RHOMPHAIA**
— *rhomphaia* were shafts of 3 cubits. which were full of iron points and were thrown among enemies with a cord attached to a stick used as a sling and these were a great hindrance to enemies.

**RHOMPHAIA**
— *rochace* — *rhomphaia*. and *rochace*. were used. by those of macedonia against the tartars. [?] who are accustomed as long as life lasts to run skewered and pierced by lances until they kill the wounder.

# — ARCHITECTURE —
# — CROSSING RIVERS / GLASS BELLS —

— The logic of an arch is one-third of the diameter of [its curvature]; [following the remark of] the German in the cathedral <note>original: "l'allemand dans la cathédrale"; this likely refers to Heinrich von Gmünd or another Northern master mason who consulted on the construction of the Milan Cathedral, with whom Leonardo had famous disagreements regarding structural integrity</note>.

— Build a barrel vault <note>original: "voûte en tonneaux"; a cylindrical vault shaped like a half-cylinder</note> and do not let it push the columns outward.

### FOR CROSSING A RIVER.

— When you wish to cross a river with an army, you must make use of [attachments] joined to the saddle; and because horses cannot swim well due to the splashing waves, you shall fix a paddle <note>original: "rame"</note> to the neck—behind the neck—so that it [the horse] can operate as needed <note>meaning to swim with greater ease and stability</note>.

### FOR MAKING A GLASS BELL.

— You shall make the furnace in the [ordinary] manner, that is, like a mortar <note>original: "à bombardes"; referring to a short, large-caliber cannon, suggesting the furnace shape</note>; and when the glass is melted, pour it into the heated mold (placed within the hearth).

# WEAPONS, GUNNERY, AND MILITARY STRUCTURES.

— A spear <term>lance<gloss>a pole weapon with a pointed metal head</gloss></term> to be used in the midst of enemies; designed so that every time the enemy enters the small fork, it must happen that the spear strikes him.

— This spear, every time the front part strikes, it collapses into itself. And this collapsing part ignites the interior and communicates the fire to a liquid mixture contained within the spear. The liquid, set aflame by the impact, scorches the armor and enters through the joints of the cuirass <note>a piece of plate armor covering the torso</note>; the fire follows it and burns whatever it finds.

— If you wish to shoot an arrow into a cap <note>original: "bonnet"</note> that is behind a palace, such that you cannot see this cap, do as follows: Set as a sighting point for your crossbow, with its arrow, some mark located at the summit of this palace. The arrow will pass over the palace and then fall behind it; from then on, what you must do is place the cap at the spot where the arrow struck the ground. Return then to the first place from which you shot the arrow, and aim it at the first sighting point on the summit of the palace; upon releasing the arrow, it will follow the same path as before and strike the cap. However, remain firmly in your original position, using the same crossbow.

— You shall set fire to these bombards <term>bombardes<gloss>early, large-caliber cannons used in sieges</gloss></term> at the same time, and they will produce a good result <note>original: "bon fruit," literally "good fruit," meaning a powerful or effective outcome</note>.

— Two bastions <term>bastions<gloss>projecting parts of a fortification designed for defensive fire</gloss></term> of which one can defend the other with its artillery, and let the diameter be 40 braces <term>brasses<gloss>a unit of length based on the reach of a man's arms, roughly 1.6 to 1.8 meters</gloss></term>.

— You shall make the ditch at least 3 braces deep, so that the infantry <term>fantassins<gloss>soldiers who fight on foot</gloss></term> who emerge from the bastion to skirmish <note>original: "escarmoucher," to engage in a minor or preliminary fight</note> can, if they are pursued, save themselves by jumping into the said ditch.

# GEOMETRY — ARCHITECTURE

— Here we show how to make a square and from it an octagon <note>original: "octogone"</note>.

— Here we show the rapid way to make a square and to divide it into 8 equal parts. First make the line *d e*, then place the compass at point *d* and make the line *h m*; then draw the line *s p* over the 2 intersections, place the compass in the middle of the cross at point *c*, make a circle, and where the intersection of this circle with the arms of the cross occurs, there will be the angles of your square. Next, take the measurement of *b c* and place it at *a b*, and place this same [measurement] at *d r*; do the same for each face [side] and you will have divided the square into 8 <note>The author is describing a method of "squaring the circle" or inscribed geometry common in medieval and Renaissance drafting</note>.

— Here we mark on the given line *a b* how to make a square and an octagon.

— If you want to quickly divide a circle into 8 equal parts, you will first make the line *a b*, then put one of the points of the compass at point *a* and make the line *M n*, then put the other point at *b* and make the line *o p*. Then, on the intersections made by the two oblique curved lines, you will draw the line *c d*, and 4 equal angles will be made at the center *s*, on which you will fix one point of the compass, and you will make your circle which will remain divided into 4 equal parts. Then you will take the midpoint [*m*] of one of these parts, and with this measurement you will divide the three others, that is to say *f o n*, and from 4 faces, 8 will have been made.

— If you keep a family in a house, make the dwellings in such a way that at night, neither they nor any strangers you might lodge are masters of the exit of the house; so that they cannot enter the dwelling where you live and sleep, close the entrance *m*, and you will have closed the whole house <note>This reflects the security concerns of the period, where domestic architecture was designed to control movement and ensure the safety of the head of the household</note>.

Then on the intersections made by the 2 oblique curved lines you will draw the line c . d . and 4 right angles will be made in the center s . upon which you will fix one point of the compasses and you will make your circle, which will remain divided into 4 equal parts. Then take the midpoint of one of these parts and with that measurement divide the other three, that is f . o . n . p . and from 4 sides, 8 will be made.
— If you keep a household <note>original: "famiglia"</note> in the house, make their dwellings in such a way that they are not [in control] of the exit of the house at night, nor any strangers you might lodge; and so that they cannot enter the dwelling where you live or sleep. If the door m . is locked, the whole house is locked.

# GEOMETRY

— How to construct an equilateral triangle <note>A triangle where all three sides are of equal length.</note> upon a given line *a c*.

— Here is shown how one can construct a pentagon <note>A five-sided polygon.</note> upon a given line *a d*.

— To find <unclear>the length of</unclear> the sides of the pentagon, move away from the circle by 1/7th of those sides.

— If you wish to construct a pentagon upon a given line, you shall proceed in the manner illustrated above upon the given line *a d*. Place one point of the compass at point *a* and with the other you shall draw the line *b c*; then move the said point of the compass, placing it at *d*, and with the other draw the line *e f*. Then, to find the midpoint of line *a d*, you shall draw the line *h m* through the intersections *p r*. This being done, divide half of the line *a d* into 4 equal parts as seen in *a s* and one.... (These parts may be made by opening the compass at random, provided that they are equal.) Take one of these parts and place it at the top of the line *p s*, as it appears in *p g*; then draw a line from *g* to *a*, and where the intersection of the line *p s* occurs, there lies the center of the circle, which will have within it the capacity to receive$^1$ <note>original: "recievere"</note> upon its circumference five sides equal to the first given line *a d*.

— If you wish, upon a given line, to construct an equilateral triangle, *place*—let us say the said line is *a c*—place the fixed point of the compass at point *a*, and with the other point you shall draw the line *b c*; then put the point at point *c* and draw the line *a b*, then put the point on point *b* and draw the line *a c*; finally, draw straight lines to each of the 3 points, and you will have an equilateral triangle.

---

1. The letter *r* in the word *recievere* <note>To receive or contain.</note> in the manuscript text presents a rare form, which makes it resemble a *y*, and of which an example has already been seen in Manuscript A (folio 3, verso *alturita*).

If you wished to make a pentagon upon a given line, you shall do it in the form figured above. Upon the given line *a. d.*, place the point of the compass <note>original: "sesto" — a common Renaissance term for a pair of compasses.</note> at point *a.* and with the other you shall make the line *b. c.* Then swap the said point of the compass and here placing it in *d.* and with the other make the line *e. f.* Then to find the middle of the line *a. d.* you shall draw the line *h. m.* through the intersections *p. r.* This being done, divide half of the line *a. d.* into 4 equal parts as appears in *a. s.* and one of these parts can be made by opening the compasses at random provided that the parts are equal; and one of these parts place at the top of the line *p. s.* as appears in *p. g.* Then draw a line from *g.* to *a.* and where it intersects on the line *p. s.*, there shall be the center of the circle, which will have in itself the capacity to receive upon its line five sides similar to the first given line *a. d.*

# GEOMETRY — SOLDERING FOR A ROOF

— Given the line *a b*, you shall make an equilateral triangle *a d b*, and you shall draw a line through the middle of its base that descends from the top angle; you shall divide it into 5 equal parts. Place one of the points [of the compass] on the fourth part [division], at point *e*, and make your circle [so that] it touches the ends of the given line, and you will see that this line will fit 5 times into the said circle. <note>This is a geometric method for inscribing a regular pentagon within a circle based on a pre-determined side length.</note>

— The reason is this: If *d c* is the space between the center and the sides that divide the circle into 6 parts <note>The radius of a circle is equal to the side of an inscribed hexagon.</note>; take 1/5 part of the line as from *d* to *e*; on the said *e*, place your compass point, and you will make a circle that removes 1/6 part of the first. Therefore, it remains divided into 5.

— You shall make the lead sheets as thin as you can, because being enclosed between the two layers [?], they do not need a very great thickness. <note>The original French "sols" usually means "grounds" or "floors," but here likely refers to layers of bedding material or masonry.</note>

— Of the irons *m n*, one must have two, so that when one cools its lead, you can pull the furnace [?] for the other and no time is lost.

->METHOD FOR SOLDERING TOGETHER A LAYER [?] OF LEAD ON AN OPEN ROOF.<-

— You shall do it thus: when you have finished the final vault of your building, you shall place over it a layer of bricks, which should be quite level [flat]; then, you shall have an iron a quarter of a <term>braccio: an Italian unit of measurement (literally "arm"), approximately 23 inches or 58 cm</term> wide having 4 sharp edges as high as half a knife blade, as seen in *m n*, and you will place it under the joints of the lead sheets. Then strike the said sheets with a wooden mallet, so that the sharp edges of the iron penetrate them [?]; then have a bottomless furnace [?] which is a quarter [of a braccio] wide, the same height, and as long as the iron underneath *m n*. Fill the said furnace [?] with glowing coals and melt the lead joints together; do this everywhere, then cover with lime, linseed oil, and bricks. . . . [?] a finger's depth of lowering at the sides [?] $^1$.

1. *The writings of L. de V. (Extract from the Gazette des Beaux-Arts, 1881) p. 46.*

# — FOLIO 14 (recto). —

<note>This page features a facsimile reproduction of a folio from Leonardo da Vinci's manuscripts, containing mirror-script text and several drawings, accompanied below by a printed scholarly transcription.</note>

---

<note>Translation of Leonardo da Vinci's handwritten notes, following the scholarly transcription of the original Italian.</note>

<margin>
<note>Geometric diagram involving a circle and triangle in the top left corner.</note>
</margin>
— Let the given line be **a. b.** You shall make an equilateral triangle **a. d. b.** and draw a line upwards through the middle of its base, which descends from the upper angle. Divide this line into 5 equal parts and place one of the points of the compass <note>original: "sesto"</note> upon the fourth part at point **e.** Then make your circle so that it touches the ends of the given line, and you will see that said line will fit exactly 5 times into said circle.

— The reason is this: if this **d. c.** is the space found between the center and the faces that divide the circle into 6 parts, take away 1/5 part of the line as from **d. e.** upwards, and make your compass point there. You will make a circle that is 1/6 part smaller than the first; therefore, it remains divided into 5.

<margin>
<note>Botanical study of flowers, likely violets, located in the center-right of the facsimile.</note>
</margin>

<margin>
<note>Mechanical sketches showing a mallet and a rectangular soldering tool or mold labeled 'm' and 'n'.</note>
</margin>
— You shall make the lead plates as thin as you can, because being enclosed between the two floors <note>original: "soli," likely referring to layers of a floor or ceiling</note> they have no need for excessive thickness. — Of the irons **m. n.** one should have 2, so that when one cools its lead, you can pull the brazier <note>original: "focolare"</note> to the other so that no time is lost.

->**METHOD OF SOLDERING TOGETHER A SINGLE SHEET OF LEAD OVER AN OPEN SURFACE.**<-

— You shall do it thus: when you have made the final floor of your building, make above it a single layer of bricks that is very level. Then, have an iron tool 1/3 of a <term>braccio<gloss>An Italian unit of measurement, roughly the length of an arm or 23 inches.</gloss></term> wide, which has 4 sharp edges as high as half the spine of a knife, as appears in **m. n.** Place this under the joints of the lead plates. Then strike the top of said plates with the wooden mallet <note>original: "mazo dilegnio"</note> so that the edges of the iron are driven into them. Then have a bottomless brazier 1/4 wide and of similar height, and as long as the iron below, **m. n.** Fill said brazier with glowing coals and cause the joints of the lead to melt together. Do this everywhere. Then cover with lime, linseed oil, and <unclear>quick-setting brick</unclear>, and give it a slope of one finger's depth at the sides.

# — LAUNDRY — DRYING ROOM — STATICS —

— A kind of wash-house. **D** shall be the well, **a** shall be the place for the lye <note>Traditional laundry used "lessive," a cleaning solution made by soaking wood ashes in boiling water</note>, **b** where the linens are kept, and **c** where the water and ashes are boiled. At the foot of the tubs, there will be a channel from which the water will exit so that the wash-tub remains clean; likewise, there will be a channel leading from the well to above the tubs.

— **C** shall be a drying room <note>original: "étuve"</note> which shall be heated by the kitchen chimney, using a copper pavilion <note>original: "tabernacle" or "pavillon"</note> two fathoms <term>fathom: translated from "brasse," a historical unit of measurement based on the span of a man's outstretched arms, approximately 6 feet</term> high and one wide. In this same location, a stone shall be placed on top in the summer so that the drying room can still be used. **B** will be a place for storing salt, and alongside section **a**, there will be an opening to enter the chimney in order to apply heat to the salted meat <note>original: "remettre le feu à la viande salée," referring to the curing and smoking process</note> and similar items. In its ceiling, many smoke ducts shall be constructed, having various outlets on the four sides of the chimney; thus, if a north wind should cause trouble, the smoke can find an exit on the opposite side. The smoke is distributed through these numerous ducts to produce good salted meat; it perfectly cures tongues, sausages, and similar things. But take care that when you push the small door **a**, a window opens opposite it to light the small chamber; this is achieved by a rod joined to the door and the window in this manner.

— **P** shall be the same in **a** as in **r**.

— I find by experience that the wood **c d** will place less of a load on point **d** (which is half the base of the triangle **a d c**). That is to say: if the beam is 6 fathoms long and weighs 6 pounds, and half of the base **a b** is one fathom, I say that the rod will impart 5 fathoms <note>Leonardo is using the length of the lever arm to describe the proportional distribution of weight</note> of its weight to point **d**, and one pound of force is supported at point **c**.

# ARCHITECTURE AND FORTIFICATIONS

— A latch <note>original: "Loquet"; the transcriber notes a degree of uncertainty in the reading</note> that holds the door.

— A type of fortress with double ditches <note>original: "fossés," defensive trenches or moats</note>. — There must be 300 braccia <note>A "braccio" (plural braccia) is an Italian unit of measurement, roughly 23 inches or 58 centimeters, literally meaning "an arm's length."</note> between each point where light is received through the slits of the upper roads. At each arch, there must be a round spiral staircase <note>original: "escalier à limaçon rond"</note>, because people tend to urinate and relieve themselves in the corners of square landings. At the first vault, let there be a door through which one enters the public latrines and urinals, and by the aforementioned staircase, one may descend from the high road to the low road. Let the high roads begin outside the city gates, and once they reach these gates, let them have a combined height of 6 braccia. Let the said site be established near the sea or another large body of water, so that the filth of the city, carried away by the water, may be transported far away.

### FIRE BOX — CENTER OF GRAVITY. ###

— This is [designed for] a slow-burning fire <note>original: "long feu"; literally "long fire," referring to a fire maintained over a long duration, often used for portable heating or as a delayed ignition source</note>

— This box should be made of iron; let there be within it a piece of coal <note>original: "charbon"; likely charcoal, which smolders rather than flames</note>, or a wick, or any other [combustible] thing [?]. GEOMETRY.

— How one can construct an octagon on a given line *a m*.

— If you wish to construct an octagon quickly upon a given line, you shall do it in this manner: Let us say that *a m* is the given line; place one point of the compass on point *a*, and you shall swing the other around it, making the line *s t*, then place the other point on *m*, and you shall make the line *v x*. Between the two intersections, you shall draw the line *p r*, then divide the half-line *a p* into three parts, and place one of the parts thus made above the upper intersection, which shall create the center of the circle. This circle will be capable of containing 8 of the given lines upon its circular line <term>circumference; the outer boundary of the circle</term>.

— How one must find the center of a circle started upon an oblique <insert>curved</insert> line *s f*.

— To find the center of a small portion of a circle, it is necessary for all lines originating between equal angles, either that their meeting-point bears a resemblance <note>original: "ressemblance"; the author is likely discussing geometric symmetry or proportionality</note> to the place from which they depart, or that they converge toward the cause of their origin. <note>This passage is notably obscure in the original manuscript, likely referring to the convergence of radii at a central point.</note> (1).

— If you divide a pyramid into many equal parts, as is seen here previously, you will find that as many times as *a b* goes into *d e*, so many times *b e* goes into *c e*. And furthermore, *a b* will go as many times into *b c* as *d e* goes into *e c*.

# TREE PRUNING AND ARCHITECTURE

— If you want the tree to make its branch **n** as thick as **m**, keep the small shoots of branch **m** pruned back, while leaving the shoots on **n**, and it [**n**] will grow to be like **m**.

— If you want a spear <note>original: "lance"; likely referring to a long wooden shaft or pike</note> that does not warp, take it from tree **b**, which, due to its thinness, will be almost exactly the required thickness for the spear.

— From tree **c**, you will only get one good spear that will never bend; it must be taken from the side that faces North. All the others will warp because of the humors <term>sap or moisture; based on the ancient theory of the four humors</term> which always move with the sun.

— If you remove a ring of bark from tree **d**, it will dry out above the ring, while everything below it will remain alive. If you make the said ring during a bad moon <note>referring to lunar cycles in traditional agriculture</note>, and then prune the plant at the base during a good moon, the part from the good moon will be preserved and the rest will rot.

— If you want a beam or any other straight piece of wood not to warp, saw the wood lengthwise into two parts, turn the two parts head-to-foot <note>reversing the grain direction of one half relative to the other</note>, fasten them well together, and they will never warp.

— For this building, it would also be good to raise it according to the line **a b c d**.

# — FOLIO 17 (verso). —

<note>This page contains a facsimile of Leonardo da Vinci's Folio 17 verso from a manuscript, followed by a printed transcription of the handwritten notes. The folio features architectural studies of centrally planned churches and botanical/technical notes on timber and plant growth.</note>

### [Translation of Leonardo’s Notes]

<note>Leonardo's mirror script translated into English. These notes relate to the small diagrams at the top right of the folio.</note>

If you want tree **a** to make its branch **n** as thick as **m**, keep the branches of branch **m** pruned back, while leaving the branches on **n**, and it will grow as large as **m**.

If you want a spear <note>original: "lancia"; a long wooden shaft for a weapon or tool</note> that does not warp, take it from tree **b**, which, because of its thinness, will serve almost exactly for the thickness of the spear.

In tree **c**, you will find only one good spear that will never bend, and that one shall be taken from the side that faces North <note>original: "tramontana"; the North wind or direction</note>; all the others will warp because of the humors <term>omori: the internal fluids or sap of the plant, thought to be influenced by solar heat</term> which always move with the sun.

If you remove a ring of bark from tree **d**, it will wither from the ring upward, and from there downward it will remain alive; and if you make the said ring during a "bad moon" <note>referring to traditional lunar gardening cycles</note> and then cut the plant at the foot during a "good moon," the part from the good moon will be preserved and the rest will be ruined.

If you want a beam or any other straight timber not to warp, saw the wood lengthwise into two parts and turn the said parts head-to-foot <note>reversing the grain of one half against the other to cancel out tension</note>; fasten them well together and they will never warp.

<note>The following line appears below the second architectural drawing.</note>

This building would also be well-suited to be constructed from the line **a. b. c. d.** upward.

---

### [Printed Commentary Translation]

— If you want tree **a** to make its branch **n** as thick as **m**, keep the branches of branch **m** pruned, leaving the branches on **n**, and it will grow like **m**.
— If you want a spear that does not warp, take it from tree **b**, which by its thinness will serve almost for the thickness of the spear.
— In tree **c**, you will not get but one good spear that never bends, and that will be taken from that part which faces North, and all the others will warp by the humors that always move with the sun.
— If you lift a ring of bark from tree **d**, from the ring up it will dry and from there down it will remain alive; and if you make the said ring in a bad moon and then cut the plant at the foot in a good moon, that of the good moon will maintain itself and the rest will spoil.
— If you want a beam or other straightness not to warp, saw the wood lengthwise in two parts and turn the said parts head to foot; fasten them well together and never will they warp.
— This building would still be well to make it from the line **a. b. c. d.** upward.

| :--- | :--- |
| *edifitio* | building / edifice |

# FORTRESSES — CHURCH ROOFS — CENTER OF GRAVITY.

— The guarding of fortresses must be carried out night by night. Let no one know who falls to him as a companion; let them be drawn by lot every evening at the very moment [of the watch?]. In times of suspicion <note>meaning times of war or unrest</note>, let them be called three times per hour, and in times of peace, let the "secrets" <note>likely referring to silent patrols or password checks</note> be conducted without calling out, 3 or 4 times a night, at regular intervals.

— The center of any suspended weight establishes itself directly under its support.

— For any church, it is not good for the roofs to be visible; the top must be flattened, and the water should descend through channels to conduits made in the border <note>Leonardo preferred the aesthetic of hidden roofs, common in High Renaissance "all'antica" architecture</note>.

— A fortress that commands <note>original: "bat," meaning to have a line of fire over</note> the ditches and the rampart beyond the ditches.

— 14 fathoms <term>fathom: a unit of length (braccia), roughly the span of a man's arms</term> — 14 fathoms — b A <insert>1</insert>.

— Gate — Gate — Portcullis <note>original: "Herse"</note> <insert>2</insert>.

— The fortress should have 3 gates, and when one employs only two, it remains not always closed <note>Leonardo is describing a "lock" system for security</note>; that is to say, it is necessary that when you enter [pass] the first portcullis, the two front gates can be closed. And when you enter [pass] the middle one, the portcullis and the front gate are closed; and when you enter the last one, the middle gate and the portcullis are likewise closed.

— Let **A** be a ditch [or perhaps a mound], over which a bridge [drawbridge] is lowered, which descends at **b A**. Build it inside the tower, so that whoever is inside does not find their path interrupted while on a short-tailed horse <note>original: "cour-taud," a docked horse</note>, as might happen to one who was here on the right hand—that is to say, in front of the Castle of Milan <note>The Sforza Castle in Milan, where Leonardo worked</note>.

# ARCHITECTURE (STRENGTH OF ARCHES, CELLARS AND GARDENS).

— Reasoning....

— For what reason this arch is strong.

— I say that it is impossible for a body larger than another to enter into a smaller one. If this is so, the line *g c h* is much larger than *g h*; therefore, the larger will not enter into the smaller *g h*, unless *g h* breaks. It is clear that one can realize that wanting to break a beam by pulling <note>The original French "tirant" suggests tension or stretching</note> it would be hardly feasible; it will therefore be admitted for the said reasons that *g h* cannot break because the angle *g f h* will be pulled, and that the angle *g c h* and the semicircle above can never pass through the chord or base *g h*.

— And likewise *b d f* as well as *a m e* cannot undergo any change if the beam *c m* does not break. Since it is scarcely possible—indeed, almost impossible—for the arch to break, added to the practice of chaining and tripling the pieces of wood that go into the curve *g a b c d e h*, it will be entirely secure, [especially] by adding two oblique supports <term>buttresses: structural reinforcements built against a wall to support or resist lateral forces</term>, as seen in figure *r s t*.

— Garden <margin>This word is read in the right-hand part of the figure at the bottom of page 1.</margin>

— The earth that is removed from the cellars must be raised alongside, until it creates a garden that is at the height of the hall; but ensure that between the ground of the garden and the wall of the house there is a gap, so that the moisture does not spoil the main walls.

<keywords>architecture, structural engineering, arches, geometry, buttresses, cellar excavation, garden design, moisture prevention</keywords>
