# — FOLIO 19 (verso). —

<note>This page features a facsimile of Leonardo da Vinci's original manuscript at the top, followed by a printed transcription. Leonardo wrote in "mirror script," from right to left, which required a mirror to read easily. The translation below follows the standardized transcription provided on the page.</note>

— reasoning
— For what reason this arch is strong:
— I say that it is impossible for a larger body to enter a smaller one. Since the line *g-c-h* is much larger than *g-h*, the larger will not enter the smaller *g-h* unless it breaks. It is clear that one can see that wanting to break a beam by pulling <note>Leonardo uses the logic of tension; a beam is much harder to snap by pulling it from its ends than by bending it</note> is hardly feasible. Therefore, you will admit by the stated reasons that *g-h* cannot break to pull the angle *g-f-h*, and the angle <note>original: "langolo" refers here to the curved segment</note> *g-c-h* and the semicircle above can never pass through the chord <term>chord: the straight line connecting the ends of an arc</term> or base *g-h*.

— Likewise, *b-d-f* and *a-m-e* cannot undergo any change <note>meaning structural shifting or deformation</note> if the beam *c-m* does not break. Since it is hardly possible—indeed, almost impossible—for the arch to break when the chaining <term>catenary reinforcement: a method of binding structural elements together to resist outward pressure</term> and the tripling of the planks that go into the curve *g-a-b-c-d-e-h* are added, it will be entirely secure by adding to it two transverse supports <term>struts: diagonal braces used to reinforce a frame</term>, as appears in figure *r-s-t*.

— garden <margin>The word "garden" appears here as a label for the architectural sketch</margin>

— The earth that is excavated from the cellars <note>original: "chanove," referring to storage vaults or basements</note> must be raised up alongside so high that it creates a garden that is level with the hall <note>the "sala" or main reception room of a villa</note>. But ensure that between the soil of the garden and the wall of the house there is a gap, so that the moisture does not spoil the main walls <term>load-bearing walls: the primary walls that support the weight of the roof and upper floors</term>.

<note>Vocabulary from the original Italian: arch (archo), beam (traue), reinforcement/chaining (lancatenatura), to triple/reinforce (rinterzare), garden/orchard (orto), cellars (chanove), main/master walls (maesstri).</note>

<summary>Leonardo explains the structural physics of arches, arguing they are secure because the curved top cannot physically pass through the narrower straight base without the materials breaking. He also provides a clever landscaping tip: use soil from basement excavations to create elevated gardens, but leave a gap to prevent dampness from seeping into the house walls.</summary>
<keywords>structural engineering, geometry, arches, tension, residential architecture, garden design, moisture prevention, cellar excavation</keywords>

# LANCES AND MASTS — A KIND OF CLOCK — WATER LIGHTS.

->— 40 long lances originating from a center.<-

->— To erect a mast <note>original: "antenne"; specifically a nautical yard or mast</note> [of a ship] with ease.<-

# ARCHITECTURE — MECHANICS

— The transmission from *m* to *s n* occurs because if *g* touched *h*, the casing would touch the wall and the lever *m* could not remain inside; I conclude that the angle (of the casing) under *g* touches the two faces [sides] of *g* that are turned toward it, and there will be no displacement unless the casing appears [?] slightly flared <note>original: "embrasée". In this context, it likely refers to an architectural splay or a widening of the opening.</note>.

— Arrange it so that the lever *m* is "female" <note>A mechanical term for a hollow or receiving part.</note> with its "son" <note>Likely referring to a smaller internal component or pin.</note> inside the body; when the other "female" *n* has moved as far away from its companion as the thickness of the "female" *m*, you detach the entire instrument and pull out the "female" lever *m*. Then you remove the "female" *n* and place *m* into the space created between *n* and *s*, and then you return *n* to its place, and you use the "female" lever as you please — *a* is a piece of iron located between the mold [?] and the iron, so that *b* heats up better, and when you perform this operation [this task], disassemble [?].

<note>Leonardo frequently used gendered language ("female" and "male") to describe how mechanical parts fit together, a practice still common in engineering today.</note>

<column-break/>

### TECHNICAL VOCABULARY
*   **Transmission:** The transfer of motion or force between parts.
*   **Lever:** A rigid bar used to transmit motion.
*   **Casing:** The outer frame or box (original: "caisse").
*   **Instrument:** The mechanical device or tool as a whole.
*   **Iron:** The metal component or tool (original: "fer").
*   **Operation:** The specific mechanical task or function (original: "office").

# BRIDGES — TRANSMISSION OF NEWS

— Bridge — Water¹ — a b c d.

— This bridge cannot be broken, provided that the main beams <note>original: "poutres maîtresses"</note> marked a, b, c, and d are strong and well-fastened together.

— This bridge could have two levels of passage, one above the other.

— One can build, across a distance of one hundred thousand <note>likely referring to a unit of distance like cubits or paces</note>, one hundred houses in which there are one hundred guards; these men, by means of underground corridors, will make a piece of news heard within a quarter of an hour.

# BOMBARDS

— Never create gun ports <note>original: "bombardières"; openings in a wall through which cannons are fired.</note>, nor any other holes in the lower parts of fortresses, so that the enemy, by positioning their bombards directly opposite, cannot easily create larger breaches in the walls. Thus, let there be no holes in any castle walls; the defenses of the battlements <note>original: "créneaux"; the notched parapets atop a wall used for protection while firing.</note> are quite sufficient. Towers should only be pierced at the bottom as much as is necessary to allow for passage, at night, along the castle walls and its moats.

— A large bombard <note>A heavy, early form of cannon used primarily in sieges.</note> which is loaded from the rear, and a single man screws and unscrews it.

— Wedge¹.

— The handle **b** is a worm screw <note>A mechanical arrangement where a screw meshes with a gear to provide precise movement or mechanical advantage.</note>, which turns the tail of the balance by means of the pinion <note>original: "roccha"; a small gear or cogwheel.</note>, which must be as long as the screw that enters the barrel <note>original: "trompe"; the main body or muzzle of the gun.</note>, and the pivot **a n** is joined to a bronze ring that encircles the tail. But ensure that this ring is positioned further toward the side of the bombard, so that the tail is somewhat in balance <note>In equilibrium.</note>. And let the breech <note>original: "culasse"; the back part of the firearm behind the bore.</note> weigh only 4 pounds more than the muzzle, so that when the breech, in recoiling, is in section **c**, this tail remains straight, allows for loading, and then is easily raised; so that by turning the worm screw in the pinion, it is pushed toward the barrel and screwed in, after which a wedge is placed behind, between the breech and the rampart. And this [bombard] is suitable for a galley <note>A low-built, Mediterranean ship propelled by oars and sails, common in naval warfare.</note>.

— Foundation of the castle (rolling tower <note>original: "tour roulante"; a mobile siege engine used to protect attackers and ladders while approaching defensive walls.</note>) illustrated below.

# LIGHTING OF A COURTYARD

-> Lighting of a courtyard. <-

— If the courtyard has its walls from **r** to **m** and from **f** to **n**, it will be illuminated by the portion of the sky **c d**; and if the walls are as high as from **r** to **s** and from **f** to **t**, it will only see and receive light from the part of the sky **a b**. <note>Leonardo is demonstrating a geometric principle of optics: as the height of the surrounding structures increases, the "aperture" of available sky decreases, thereby reducing the intensity of light at the bottom of the courtyard.</note>

# TO RAISE WATER.

— If you want to raise water for one mile and have it remain on the mountain, proceed as it is illustrated above. And if you want a stream of water as thick as your leg, make the pipe as thick as your thigh. If it rises one mile, make it descend two miles, and the force of the water between **b** [and] **c** will be such that it will pull along the water located at **d** and **e** and will turn the wheel of the pump-syringes <note>original: "schizzaroli"; these are mechanical devices that use a piston to project or move fluid.</note>. And know that no air can enter the reservoir through the pump-syringes; indeed, every time the piston <term>âme: literally the "soul" of the device, referring here to the inner piston or plunger</term> of the syringe moves back, the valve <term>animelle: a small leather flap or valve that allows fluid to move in only one direction</term> at the bottom of the reservoir closes, and even if it has not been tightly sealed, it cannot admit air because it is located 2 braccia <term>braccia: an Italian Renaissance unit of measurement, roughly 23 inches or 58 cm</term> underwater, so that it cannot admit air without first admitting those 2 braccia of water. And when you wish to first fill the pipe, gather a small pool of water using irrigation channels <term>roggie: small man-made canals or trenches</term>, and block the pipes at their base with earth—that is, at **c** and **e**; then, release the pool into the pipe. When the wheel is half a braccia deep in the water, seal the box tightly, and then unblock the pipe at its base at **c** at the same time, and make the wheel 4 braccia in size.

---

1. *Schizzare* means: to squirt, to gush; *schizzatoio*: a syringe, pump, or instrument for projecting air or water.
2. Compare *Treatise on the Motion and Measurement of Water* <note>original: "Trattato del moto e misura dell'eau"</note>, Book IX, Chapter VII, p. 442, plate 35, fig. 198.

It details specific mechanical components like pistons and valves used to prevent air from entering the system and breaking the vacuum.</summary>

— If you wish to make water rise for one mile and have it remain at the top of the mountain, proceed as it is illustrated above. And if you want the stream of water to be as thick as your leg, make the pipe <term>condocto: a conduit or channel</term> as thick as your thigh. # ON MOTION (ACQUIRED SPEED)

### ON THE NATURE OF MOTION

— If a wheel, whose motion has become increasingly violent <note>In this context, "violent" refers to high-velocity or forceful motion driven by an external power source</note>, continues to turn many times on its own after its motor <note>The "motor" refers to the primary mover or source of energy, whether human, animal, or mechanical</note> lets go, it appears clear that if this motor persists in turning in addition to the aforementioned speed of motion, this persistence can take place with little force.

— And I conclude that in wishing to maintain this motion, the motor will always experience little fatigue, and all the more so because by its nature it will fix itself <insert>in the continuation of the action begun</insert> <note>This describes the principle of inertia: an object in motion tends to stay in motion unless acted upon by an external force</note>.

— A method by which a single man will be able to saw any large beam into planks. But ensure that the teeth of the saw are turned toward the counterweight.

— In what manner one ought to experiment with a rule *concerning weights* <note>original: "de ponderibus" — a reference to the medieval and Renaissance science of weights, often associated with the works of Jordanus de Nemore</note>.

<summary>The author explores the concept of momentum (acquired speed) and how it reduces the effort required to maintain motion, proposing a counterweighted saw as a practical application of these mechanical laws.</summary>
<keywords>mechanics, momentum, inertia, labor-saving devices, saw technology, science of weights, physics</keywords>

### ON THE NATURE OF MOTION

If a wheel, having become forceful in its motion, is then abandoned by its motor, it will turn many times by itself; therefore, if that motor persists in turning atop the aforementioned velocity of motion, it appears that this persistence is achieved with little force.

And I conclude that in wishing to maintain this motion, the motor will always experience little fatigue, and all the more so as it will settle into its natural course.

# WEIGHT AND FORCE

->— If it is possible to set this up [?]. <-

— Experience [shows?] that a weight placed upon an arch is not supported <note>original: "chargé" — literally "charged" or "loaded"</note> by its columns, but rather the greater the weight placed upon the arches, the less the arch and the weight press upon the columns [?]¹. The experiment is this [shows the following]: If a man has been placed upon a <term>scale</term> <note>original: "peson" — a type of spring balance or weighing instrument</note>, in the middle of the interior of a well, and you then have him spread his hands and feet against the walls of this well, you will see that he weighs much less upon the scale. Give him a weight upon his shoulders, and you will see by experience that the more weight you give him, the more strength he will find in opening [spreading] his arms and legs; and the more he supports himself against the walls, the more weight will be missing from the scale.

---

1 Libri, *History of the Mathematical Sciences in Italy*, III, 46. <note>A reference to Guglielmo Libri's 19th-century work on the history of science.</note>

# — FOLIO 27 (recto) —

## Manuscript Facsimile

<note>Leonardo's mirror script transcribed normally left-to-right. Original 15th-century Italian spelling and abbreviations (e.g., tildes for nasals, crossed 'p' for 'per') are preserved.</note>

<margin>
if possible, fix it <note>original: "se possibile fiqsi" — likely "ficcarsi," meaning to fix, insert, or set up.</note>
</margin>

<note>Drawing of a hoisting machine or crane mechanism with a central vertical screw/mast. This reflects Leonardo's interest in mechanical advantage.</note>

<note>Drawings of architectural vaulting and a geometric polyhedron, illustrating the intersection of geometry and structural engineering.</note>

Experience shows that a weight placed upon an arch does not load itself onto its columns; rather, the greater the weight placed upon the arches, the less the arch and the weight press upon the columns. The experiment is this: if a man is placed upon <term>scales</term> <note>original: "stadere" — a type of steelyard or balance scale</note> in the middle of the shaft of a well, and you then have him spread his hands and feet against the walls of said well, you will see that he weighs much less on the scale. Give him a weight upon his shoulders, and you will see by experience that the more weight you give him, the more force he will exert in spreading his arms and legs, and the more he will brace himself against the walls, and the more the weight will be missing from the scales.

# GEOMETRY (DIVISION OF THE CIRCLE)

— This, with a single opening of the compass, remains divided into 3, 5, 6, and 30, in 22 <note>The transcription is uncertain here; likely referring to specific points or segments.</note> in 2 <note>Unclear reading in the original manuscript.</note> in a d, a m, a c, c m, n s.

— If you wish, with a single opening of the compass, to find a way to divide a circle into 5 equal parts, and into 3, and into 30, you shall do thus: place the point of your compass at point **a**, and make the line **b c**, then place the other point at **c** and make the line **a d**, then draw the line **b** to the intersection **n**, and where this line that is being traced touches the circle, at **m**, there is the finished measure. That is to say, that in **a m** is the fifth part of the circle, in **a c** the sixth part, in **c m** the thirtieth part, and in **a d** the third.

— The reason for this is that if you divide the circle into thirty parts, **a c** contains 5 of them, which is 1/6 of 30; **a m** contains 6 of them, which is the fifth of 30; **a d** contains 10, which is 1/3 of 30; and **c m** contains one, which is 1/30.

->FLAMMÉE AND OTHER SIMILAR ENGINES OF WAR.<-

## Flammée.

— The *flammée* <note>A term for an incendiary "flame-ball" or fire-pot</note> is a ball composed in this manner: Let these things be boiled together, that is to say, willow charcoal, saltpeter, brandy <note>original: "eau-de-vie"; likely referring to distilled alcohol or spirits used as a fuel</note>, incandescent sulfur, pitch, camphor, and a thread of Ethiopian wool. Let this thread be plunged <insert>?</insert> into this composition, wound into the shape of a ball, and [furnished with] sharp spikes; it is thrown at [launched upon] ships, as if by a sling. This is called Greek fire <note>original: "feu grec [grégeois]"</note>; it is an admirable thing which burns everything, even under water. Callinicus <note>original: "Callimaque [Callinicus?]"; Callinicus of Heliopolis is the historical architect credited with inventing Greek fire in the 7th century</note>, an architect, was the first who taught this to the Romans <note>The author likely refers to the Byzantine Romans (Eastern Roman Empire)</note>, by whom it was afterwards much employed, and especially by the Emperor Leo, when the Eastern peoples came against Constantinople with an infinite number of ships, which were all burned by this material¹.

---

## Philocrothe — Arzila — Crusida — Lampade — Astula.

— The *philocrote*, the *arzila*, the *crusida*, the *flammée*, and the *lampade*, although presenting differences, are of almost the same substance, and their fire is similar to that spoken of above—that is to say, [to that] of the *flammée*—except that one adds to the said composition liquid varnish, petroleum oil, turpentine, and strong vinegar. These things are dried in the sun after having been pressed together; then, they are wound around . . . . . . . . . of hemp and reduced to a round shape. Next, they are thrown with a cord; some drive the point of a dart into them, launching it after having moistened the dart; some drive very sharp nails into them. A hole being left in the said ball or mass to set it on fire, [care is taken that] all the rest [is] covered with colophony <note>A form of resin obtained from pines</note> and sulfur. Our ancestors used this mixture, joined and bound to the tip of a spear <term>haste: a long thrusting spear or pike</term>, to defend themselves and resist the impetuous attack of enemy ships. Lucan <note>A Roman poet (39–65 AD)</note> says that Caesar, having made this fire, threw it with *lampades* <note>incendiary torches or lamps</note> among the ships of the Cherusci peoples of Germany; he burned not only the said ships, but the buildings constructed on the seashores were consumed by a similar conflagration.

---

1. Venturi, *Essay*, etc., p. 30. <note>Referring to Giambattista Venturi, an 18th-19th century physicist and historian</note>

The **flammea** <note>A "flaming" incendiary ball</note> is a ball composed in this form: let these things be boiled together, namely willow charcoal, saltpeter, <term>aqua vite</term> <note>literally "water of life," referring to high-proof distilled alcohol</note>, sulfur, incense, and pitch with camphor and a thread of Ethiopian wool. This thread alone, soaked in the said composition, is wound into the shape of a ball with sharp spikes. It is thrown at ships with a cord in the manner of a sling. This is called **Greek fire** and it is a marvelous thing, for it burns everything even under water. Callimachus <note>Leonardo likely means Callinicus of Heliopolis, the 7th-century architect credited with inventing Greek fire</note>, the architect, was the first who taught it to the Romans <note>The Byzantines, who called themselves Romans</note>, by whom it was afterwards much used, and especially by the Emperor Leo when the Oriental peoples came against Constantinople with an infinite number of ships, all of which were burned by this material.

# BOMBARDS

— This bombard, called a *courtaud* <note>A "short" or "curtal" cannon, known for its wide bore and loud report</note>, makes more noise than any other; the longest one makes the least noise.

->— Ascatola [Box-bombard?] — Lightning-bombard —<-

— A <term>canicule</term> <note>original: "canicule"; likely referring to a small tube or fuse-channel</note> made of double cardboard or lead, so that the fire may be set to the powder in the middle. But the <term>tail</term> <note>original: "queue"; the breech or powder chamber</note> is made of fine copper, and the <term>workmanship</term> <note>original: "le rempart ou le travail"; referring to the structural integrity of the breech</note> must be in all points perfect.

The **lightning-bombard** is a bombard that has the void of its breech in a spherical shape, at the center of which arrives a thin iron tube finely bored; this iron must be full of fine powder. This is done for two reasons: first, so that having reached the center of the ball <note>the spherical powder chamber</note>, the fire passing through the tube ignites all the rest of the powder packed in that ball at the same time; secondly, so that the touch-hole of the bombard does not wear out. And the said round cavity will not resist the vehemence of the powder unless it is made of fine copper; the rest can be made of 4 parts tin to 100 parts copper <note>A specific bronze alloy for the barrel</note>. This is the best machine that can be made.

Let it be posed for whoever wants a true experiment: whether the bombard exerts more force by pushing backward than by pushing the shot forward. Let a piece of lead be made as a barrier behind, and a work of lead as a target in front. Between the rear barrier and the bombard, let an iron ball be placed similar to the one fired forward at the target, and let each be made of iron. The ball that has most pressed its obstacle is the one that was pushed by the greatest violence.

<note>Leonardo is here exploring the laws of action and reaction, attempting to measure the "recoil" force against the "muzzle" force using lead deformation as a gauge.</note>

# ENGINES FOR WAR.

## — Bombite — <note>A specific type of incendiary projectile or small explosive device.</note>

## — Clotombrot — <note>Likely a corruption of a Greek or Latin technical term, referring here to a "pestilential" or chemical-gas shell.</note>

— If you set the fire at the right time and make a bed *underneath* for me, you will perform wonders; and so that the smoke is not smelled, mix in sweet-smelling perfumes. Let this ball be made of chopped tow <note>coarse flax or hemp fibers</note>, sulfur, and pitch, so that when it burns, the enemy does not recognize the invention. <note>The perfumes act as a masking agent to hide the chemical nature of the weapon until it is too late.</note>

— The *clotombrot* is a ball thrown by a *trabiculo* <note>original: "trabiculo"; a small ballista or catapult</note>, that is to say, by a ballista which is one fathom <note>original: "brasse"; a unit of length based on the reach of outstretched arms, roughly 6 feet</note> high and which is full of the tails of small tubes <note>likely small cartridges or fuses</note>, all of which must fit into a small space at the same time; it is used by throwing it into a bastion <note>a projecting part of a fortification</note>, and there is no way to prevent its pestilential action. <note>The "pestilential action" refers to the suffocating or poisonous fumes released by the device.</note> Otherwise, it would be unwise to use it, for it would harm you as much as your enemies. And if you throw 6 or 8 of these balls among your enemies, you will certainly be the victor. This is therefore good to throw into the midst of them; light a wick inside, and it will eventually set fire to the center of all the tubes.

## — This is for ships:

When ships are hindered <note>perhaps referring to being becalmed or locked in close-quarters boarding</note>, have wicks ready to hold behind the enemy, and at that moment, throw balls full of lit wicks behind the enemies—that is to say, onto the ship. The enemies, intent on protecting themselves from the fire, will abandon their defenses.

<note>Translator's note on vocabulary: The author uses a mix of traditional siege terminology and experimental chemical warfare concepts.</note>

# BOMBARDS <note>term: bombarde; an early type of large-caliber cannon used for siege warfare.</note>

— For one who wishes to test which [cannon] is the best, it will be necessary to raise them upright [placing them vertically]; two judges must stand in the middle, and by first setting fire to one, they shall note how much time passes after the explosion before the ball returns to the ground; one shall do the same for the other, and the one that is the slowest [to return] shall hold the honor <note>The longer the "hang time" of the projectile, the greater the muzzle velocity and power of the cannon.</note>. But ensure that the tubes are of equal length, that the breeches <note>term: queues; the rear part of the firearm where the charge is placed</note> are at the discretion of the artificer, that the balls are of the same weight, and that the powder comes from the same barrel.

— Arch-thunder <note>original: "Architonnerre"; a steam-powered cannon design attributed to Archimedes and studied by Leonardo.</note>

— This machine is loaded at the breech with copper, and the hole [the hollowed part] is made of iron; and it is good if, after you have well-packed the powder, you pierce it with an arrow and fill said hole with fine powder.

— This one is of lesser power, because it breathes <note>likely meaning it leaks air or pressure</note> a little and because the powder cannot be packed as well in the cardboard as in the copper, and furthermore the cartridge "swims" <note>fits loosely</note> a bit in its breech.

— This one falls into the same error as the first one above, but it is quicker to load than any other; it does not require the wedge and its iron casing.

— The one below is the most useful and the strongest, because it is made of a single piece and is loaded by the mouth [muzzle-loaded], but make its hole <note>the vent or touch-hole</note> out of iron.

# WICKER BOAT — BLOWGUN.

— If you wish to be able to cross a river at your pleasure with your army while remaining dry, you should do as follows: Construct a boat made of willow branches; then, give it double sides <note>referring to a double-bottomed or compartmentalized hull</note> so that they can be opened from underneath, and fill this body with gravel. When you are in the desired location, open the bottom of the gravel reservoir so that it falls to the riverbed; once this is done, close the reservoir and return to the bank to reload. You must have many of these machines, but the main body of the boat must be wrapped on the exterior with ox-hide so that it does not sink <insert>*sink to the bottom*</insert> <note>Leonardo is describing a method for building a ford or a submerged causeway by systematically dumping ballast from skin-covered wicker coracles</note>.

— To make a blowgun <note>original: "sarbacane"; here referring to a sophisticated pneumatic or mechanical tube weapon rather than a simple toy</note> that shoots with marvelous force, you shall do as follows: Draw a steel wire through a draw-plate using a <term>winch [argano]<gloss>a mechanical device for pulling or lifting heavy loads; likely a wire-drawing bench</gloss></term>¹, the thickness of a finger; then temper it, and hammer over it two plates of fine copper, which you will also draw through the plate. Then, half by half, solder them together with silver; next, wrap thick copper wires over the top and flatten them with the hammer, but first solder them, repeating this 3 or 4 times [?] in the same manner. Make the <insert>*blowgun*</insert> 12 <term>braccia<gloss>an Italian unit of measurement, roughly 23 inches or 58 cm</gloss></term> long <note>approximately 23 feet or 7 meters</note>, and ensure it shoots a steel arrow of 1/3 of a *braccia*.

1. See the use of the instrument called a *winch* [argano], folio 35 recto, last figure.

# Manuscript Facsimile

<note>Sketch showing a method for fording a river using a woven willow boat filled with gravel that can be dumped from the bottom.</note>

If you wish to be able to ford a river with your army at your will, you shall do as follows: make a boat of willow wicker; then, make it with double sides so that they can be opened from underneath, and fill that body with gravel. When you are in the place where you want [to cross], open the bottom of the hopper <note>original: "bottino"; here referring to a discharge compartment or reservoir</note> containing the gravel so that it falls to the bottom. Once this is done, close the hopper and return to the bank to reload. You should have many of these, but the main body of the boat itself must be wrapped on the outside with ox-hides so that it does not sink <insert>to the bottom</insert> <note>Leonardo is describing a portable engineering solution: using hide-covered coracles to systematically dump gravel and build a submerged causeway or ford for troops.</note>.

---

<note>Sketch of a horizontal tube representing a "cierbottana" (blowgun or airgun).</note>

To make a <term>blowgun [cierbottana]<gloss>a tube for launching projectiles; Leonardo’s design suggests a high-pressure metal version rather than a simple wooden pipe</gloss></term> that shoots with marvelous force, you shall do as follows: draw a steel wire through a <term>draw-plate [filiera]<gloss>a tool with holes of decreasing size used to shape metal wire</gloss></term> using a large <term>winch [argano]<gloss>a mechanical device for pulling or lifting heavy loads</gloss></term>, [making it] as thick as a finger. Then, temper it and hammer onto it two plates of <unclear>...</unclear> <note>likely copper or brass</note> which you will also draw through the plate. Solder them together, half by half, with silver; then wrap thick wires of <unclear>...</unclear> over it and flatten them with the hammer, but first solder them, and do this 3 or 4 times <unclear>in a similar</unclear> manner. Make it 2 <term>braccia<gloss>an Italian unit of length, approximately 23 inches or 58 cm</gloss></term> long, and have it shoot a steel arrow 1/3 of a <term>braccio</term> long.

# THE ARCHITONNERRE, AN INVENTION OF ARCHIMEDES (STEAM CANNON)¹.

->— a b c d² — Ensure that the iron rod c n is fixed in the middle of the tablet attached beneath it, so that the water may fall all at once around this board.<-

->— Sight. — Architonnerre <note>original: "Architonnerre"; literally "Arch-thunder," a name Leonardo gave to this steam-powered cannon</note>³. —<-

— The Architonnerre is a machine made of fine copper, an invention of Archimedes; and it throws iron balls with great noise and fury. It is used in this manner: the third part of the instrument consists of a large quantity of charcoal fire; when the metal has been well heated by them, tighten the screw d, which is above the water vessel a b c; and by tightening the screw from above, the vessel will open at the bottom. The water, having fallen, will descend into the heated part of the instrument, and there it will suddenly transform into a smoke <gloss>steam</gloss> which will appear marvelous, especially to see the fury and to hear the roar [of the machine]. This [machine] used to hurl a ball weighing one talent <note>An ancient unit of weight, roughly 60 to 75 pounds</note>. . . [?]

# FORTIFICATIONS OF THE CASTLE OF MILAN

— The moats of the castle of Milan, inside the <term>guirlande: an outer defensive wall or "garland" encircling the main fortress</term>, are 30 <term>brasses: an ancient unit of measurement, roughly 6 feet</term> wide; its ramparts are 16 brasses high and 40 wide, and that constitutes the garland.

The exterior walls are 8 brasses thick and 40 high, and the walls of the interior of the castle are 60 brasses, which pleases me in every respect; except that I would wish to see that the <term>bombardières: embrasures or openings through which cannons (bombards) are fired</term> located in the walls of the garland do not project <note>original: "ne fassent pas saillie?"</note> into the interior secret passage—that is to say, at point **S**—and furthermore, that one must descend <insert>go down</insert> through each one <note>referring to a change in floor level for security</note>, as appears at **m f**. This is because good bombardiers always aim at the embrasures of fortresses, and if they were to break through a single embrasure in the said garland, they could, in the manner of cats <note>referring to "cats," a medieval siege engine or a stealthy climbing maneuver</note>, enter through the said breach and make themselves masters of all the towers, all the walls, and secret corridors of the garland. 

Now, if the embrasures were designed like **m f**, should it happen that a bombard breaks one of the said embrasures and the enemies enter the interior, they would not be able to pass any further; moreover, they could be repelled and driven out by someone positioned directly above them. The corridor **f** must be continued through all the walls, from three-quarters of the way down and through the top, so that it has no exit, neither onto the walls nor into the towers, except for the one by which one enters, which shall have its beginning inside the fortress. The said secret way **f** must have no vent or opening to the outside; it must receive light from the side of the fortress through thick <term>arbalestrières: narrow slits for crossbowmen</term>.

<summary>Leonardo analyzes the defensive architecture of the Sforza Castle in Milan, proposing a redesigned internal corridor system to prevent invaders from seizing the entire perimeter if a single cannon embrasure is breached.</summary>
<keywords>Milan, Sforza Castle, fortifications, military engineering, ballistics, defensive architecture, Leonardo da Vinci</keywords>

# THE MOAT OF THE CASTLE OF MILAN FROM THE INSIDE

->The moat of the castle of Milan from the inside<-

<note>Drawing of the fortifications of the Castello Sforzesco in Milan, showing the 'ghirlanda' (outer wall), the main castle walls, and internal defense systems including gunports (bombardiere) and secret passages.</note>

The moats of the castle of Milan, inside the <term>ghirlanda: an outer defensive wall or "garland" encircling the main fortress</term>, are 30 <term>braccia: a Renaissance unit of measurement, approximately 23 inches or 58 cm</term> wide. Its embankment is 16 braccia high and 40 wide, and this is the ghirlanda.

The outer walls are 8 braccia thick and 40 high, and the inner walls of the castle are 60 braccia, all of which pleases me; except that I would wish to see that the <term>bombardiere: gunports or embrasures for cannons</term> which are in the walls of the ghirlanda did not open into the internal secret passage—that is, at **S**. Instead, one should descend into each one, as appears at **m f**. This is because good bombardiers <note>artillerymen</note> always aim at the gunports of fortresses, and if they were to break through even a single gunport in the said ghirlanda, they could then, by way of "cats" <note>likely referring to *gatti*, a type of mobile siege gallery or perhaps a metaphor for stealthy climbing</note>, enter through the said breach and make themselves masters of all the towers, walls, and secret hollows of the said ghirlanda. 

Therefore, if the gunports are made like **m f**, and it should happen that a bombard <note>a large early caliber cannon</note> breaks one of these gunports and the enemies enter inside, they cannot pass any further; rather, they would be beaten back and driven out by the <term>piombatore: a "murder hole" or machicolation used to drop projectiles or boiling liquids</term> from above. And the passage **f** should be continued through all the walls, from three-quarters of the way down, and from there upward it should have no exit, neither in the walls nor in the towers, except for the one where one enters, which shall begin in the <term>rocca: the central keep or strongest part of the fortress</term>. And the said secret way must not have any opening to the outside; rather, it should take its light from the side facing the keep through frequent <term>balestriere: narrow slits for crossbowmen</term>.

<summary>Leonardo analyzes the defensive vulnerabilities of the Castello Sforzesco, proposing a redesigned system of gunports and secret passages to ensure that a single breach in the outer wall does not compromise the entire fortress.</summary>
<keywords>Milan, Castello Sforzesco, military architecture, fortifications, ghirlanda, gunports, siege defense, braccia, engineering</keywords>

# ARCHITECTURE. — INCENDIARY BALL.

— This ball must be 2 and $\frac{1}{2}$ <term>braccia: a Renaissance unit of measurement, roughly 23 inches or 58 cm</term> high, and full of tubes which throw one-pound balls; these [smaller balls] must be coated with pitch inside the tubes so that they do not fall out. # THE LOCKS OF MILAN. — CANALS OF THE TICINO.

->Lock Basin. <note>original: "Conque"</note> — System of canals for the city.<-

— It is necessary to often utilize a river that flows <note>has a current</note>, so that it does not corrupt the city air; and also, this will provide a facility for washing the city frequently, when the sluice gate <note>original: "support"; likely referring to a water-gate or dam</note> beneath the said city is raised. With rakes and scrapers, one will carry away the filth that has accumulated there, which, by mixing with the water, would make it turbid. And this must be done once every year.

— Let the floor of the cellars be 3 braccia <note>a "brasse" or braccio was a Renaissance unit of measurement, roughly 23 inches or 58 cm</note> higher than the surface of the water in the canals, and let it slope toward the canals, so that if any flood should occur, all the water may then drain away at once, leaving the cellars clean.

— *The Ticino* <margin>The following words accompany the figure on the left of the manuscript page, written from bottom to top.</margin> — A larger canal, so that one can, if necessary, divert the entire river through it when the flow is too great, and close the other entrances, so that no water remains in any other canal.

<note>Main text blocks on the right side of the page:</note>

One should often have a river that flows, so that the air of the city is not corrupted <note>Leonardo believed stagnant water caused "bad air" or disease</note>; and furthermore, it will be a convenience for washing the city frequently when the sluice <term>sostegnio</term> <note>a support or dam used to hold back water</note> under the said city is raised; and with rakes and scrapers, the mud that has multiplied in those [canals] shall be removed, which will mix with the water, making it turbid; and this should be done once every year.

Let the floor of the cellars <term>canove</term> <note>storage rooms or wine cellars</note> be 3 <term>braccia</term> <note>a Florentine unit of measure, approximately 23 inches or 58 cm</note> higher than the surface of the water of the canals, and let them slope toward the canals, so that if any flood should occur, the water may depart together with the rest and leave the cellars clean.

Ticino — <note>The Ticino river, a major tributary of the Po in Northern Italy</note>
main canal, so that one can, in case of need, send the entire river through this—that is, when it is too swollen—and close the other entrances, and so that this [overflow] does not exit into any other canal.

# A WELL-CONDITIONED STABLE¹.

->— m K p s R — f [?] — 4 — a b².<-

->— 3 4 5 6 —<-

— To make a very polished [clean] stable.

— How a stable ought to be composed. You shall first divide its width into 3 parts, and its length is free [at your discretion]. And let the three said divisions be equal, each with a width of 6 <term>braccia</term> <note>A "braccio" (plural "braccia") was a Renaissance unit of measurement, roughly 23 inches or 58 cm.</note>, and 10 high. The middle part shall serve the stable masters, and the 2 side parts for the horses, of which each horse must take 3 <term>braccia</term> in width and 6 <term>braccia</term> in length, being half a <term>braccio</term> higher in the front than in the back.

— The manger must be 2 <term>braccia</term> above the ground, *the rack shall have* . . the beginning of the rack shall be at 3 <term>braccia</term> and its highest part at 4 <term>braccia</term>.

Now, wishing to keep what I promise—that is, to ensure that the said place, contrary to what is universally the case, be very polished [clean] and neat—as for the upper part of the stable, which is to say where the hay is kept, the said place must have at its outer head a window 6 high and 6 wide; from which the hay is easily led onto the said floor, as can be seen in the instrument³ <note>Leonardo refers here to a mechanical device or drawing of a hoist/delivery system.</note>. It must be placed in a space 6 <term>braccia</term> wide and of the same length as the stable, as appears at K p. Of the 2 other parts that flank the first one in the middle, let each be divided into 2 parts; let the two sides for the hay be 4 <term>braccia</term> wide, for the sole office *of those who administer* . . and for the passage of those charged with the administration of the stable; let the 2 other parts bordering the walls be 2 <term>braccia</term> wide, as appears at S R, and let their office be to give hay to the mangers through conduits that are narrow at their start and wide over the mangers, so that the hay does not get stuck on the way. Let them be well-plastered and very polished, [as they are seen] figured where it is marked 4 f s. As for providing drink, let the mangers [troughs] be of stone, such that they can be uncovered, just as one uncovers chests by lifting their lids.

# NAVAL WARFARE AND ARCHITECTURE <note>original: "GUERRE NAVALE ET ARCHITECTURE"</note>

— Short-cannons <term>courtauds: short, thick-walled cannons used for heavy impact at close range</term> are effective against large ships.

— Serpentines <term>serpentines: long, thin-barreled cannons designed for range rather than power</term> are good for light galleys, in order to be able to attack the enemy from a distance; it [the serpentine] should fire a 4-pound lead ball, and its barrel must be as long as 40 of those small balls.

— A building must always be detached around its entire perimeter if one wishes to show its true form. <note>Leonardo often intersperses architectural theory with military notes; here he argues for the aesthetic and structural independence of a monument.</note>

— This half-pike <term>esponton: a type of polearm or boarding pike</term> will stop the machine along with the ship, if the impact is great.

— This fire-boat <term>zepata: likely a derivation of 'zapata' or 'zopata,' referring here to a small, low-profile fire-ship or incendiary device</term> is also good for setting fire to bridges at night, but give it a black sail <note>to ensure stealth and camouflage in the darkness</note>.

— <margin>The letter 'm' indicates the prow of the vessel on the accompanying drawing.</margin> This fire-boat is good for setting fire to ships that could withstand a collision, during the siege of a port, or to other ships within the harbor. It should be made thus: first, place wood one fathom <term>brasse: a measurement of roughly 6 feet, based on the reach of a man's arms</term> out of the water, then tow <term>étoupe: coarse flax or hemp fibers used for caulking and as tinder</term>, then bombard powder <note>early gunpowder</note>, then small sticks of wood, then others gradually larger and larger; next, place the iron wires with the linen-fire at the top, and when you have the wind to your liking, direct the rudder. When the fire reaches the ship, the bent wires will ignite the powder, and it will do what is required.

***

1. The top of this page from Manuscript B was reproduced in facsimile by Mr. de Geymüller. *The Projects, etc.*, plate 43, fig. 4 (see above, folio 24 recto, note 1). See also: *The Writings of Leonardo da Vinci*, by Charles Ravaisson-Mollien (p. 39, extract from the *Gazette des Beaux-Arts*).
2. This letter indicates, on the figure to the right, the prow of the vessel.

# WEAPONS FOR THE OFFENSIVE. — GEOMETRY.

### NAMES OF OFFENSIVE WEAPONS:

— Acinaces <note>original: "acinace"; a short Persian saber</note>, dagger <note>original: "daga/dague"</note>, sword <note>original: "ensis"</note>, gladius <note>the standard Roman short sword</note>, sword <note>original: "spada/épée"</note>, harpe <note>a curved sword or sickle-shaped blade</note>, lingula <note>a small tongue-shaped blade</note>, machaira <note>original: "machæra"; a Greek cutting sword</note>, stragulum <note>original: "stragule"; a type of javelin or covering</note>, dolones <note>original: "doloni"; secret daggers hidden in canes</note>, sica <note>original: "sicca"; a curved thracian dagger</note>, pugio <note>a Roman dagger</note>, clunaculum <note>original: "clunade"; a sacrificial dagger worn at the haunch</note>, secespita <note>a long bronze sacrificial knife</note>, mucro <note>the sharp point of a sword</note>, aclides <note>a small javelin attached to a strap</note>, missile <note>original: "telum"</note>, verutum <note>a short light javelin</note>, clubs <note>original: "fusti"</note>, staffs <note>original: "baculi"</note>, spears <note>original: "haste"</note>, shafts <note>original: "hastili"</note>, pikes <note>original: "concti/conti"</note>, lance <note>original: "lancea"</note>, pilum <note>the heavy Roman javelin</note>, gaesum <note>a heavy Gallic javelin</note>, ruma <note>a dart</note>, rumex <note>a type of spear</note>, sparum <note>a rustic hunting spear</note>, javelin <note>original: "iaculo"</note>, sarissa <note>the long Macedonian pike</note>, gabina, shields <note>original: "clipei"</note>, axe <note>original: "securis"</note>, tragula <note>a barbed javelin thrown with a strap</note>, mace <note>original: "clava"</note>, cateja <note>original: "chategia"; a projectile weapon or boomerang-like club</note>, dolabra <note>a pickaxe or entrenching tool</note>; the double-axe <note>original: "la bipenne"</note> <margin>See, for the meaning of the preceding words, folios 41 recto to 44 recto.</margin>.

— This [method], using a single compass setting, divides the circle **b c** into 3 equal **b c** parts, into 6 **a c** parts, into 8 **f c** parts, and into 24 **a f** parts.

If you wish to divide a circle into 8 equal parts without decreasing the opening of the compass, you know that from 6 to 8 there is one-third of 6; therefore, the opening of the compass with which you made the circle being a sixth part of that circle, you will divide this sixth part into 4, and 3/4 of this sixth [of the] circle will be the eighth part of the whole [the entire circle]. If you wish to divide this sixth part into 4 parts, you shall do thus: Having made your circle, without changing the opening of the compass, place one of its points at point **a**, and, moving the other point, you will make the line **b c**, then, fixing the point at **c**, make with the other the line **a d**, place the line. . . , then, place the point of the compass at **b**, and make the line **d e a**, and make the line **d e f**; from **a** to **f** is found 1/4 of the line **a c**. Therefore, for the reasons stated above, if **a c**, divided into 4 similar [parts]. . . , contains within it 4 twenty-fourths [of the circle], similarly . . . . . .

But, to better understand the reasons above, if your circle had been divided into 24 parts, **a c**, which is the sixth part of this circle, contains six... 4, which says [since] 4 times 6 [makes] 24, [and] **f c** [which] contains 3, [is the eighth of the circle], since 8 times 3 similarly makes 24. Therefore, you have here three differences [different modes] of dividing a circle, without opening or closing the compass; as **a f** is a 24th of the circle, **f c** is 1/8 of the circle, and **a c** is 1/6, exactly <margin>See above, folio 27 verso. The constructions offered in Manuscript A for the division of the circle were only approximations; this one is exact.</margin>. But I remind you well that you should perform the proof with careful attention to [regarding] the straight line **b c**, omitted above; it is this line which guides [directs the drawing] of the line **d f**, that is to say, where it has its intersection with the line **d a**, at point **e** [by means of point **e**, where it meets the line **d a**].

<note>Geometric diagram showing a circle divided by various arcs and lines to demonstrate fractional divisions (1/3, 1/6, 1/8, 1/24) using a fixed compass opening.</note>

— This single opening of the compass <note>original: "seste"</note> divides the circle into 3 equal parts **b. c.**, and into 6 [parts] **a. c.**, and into 8 [parts] **f. c.**, and into 24 [parts] **a. f.**

If you wish to divide a circle into 8 equal parts without closing the compass, you know that from 6 to 8 is one-third of 6. Therefore, since the opening of the compass with which you made the circle is 1/6 part of that circle, you will divide said sixth part into 4, and 3/4 of this sixth of a circle will be the eighth part of the whole. To divide this sixth part into 4 parts, do as follows: Having your circle, without moving the compass from its opening, place one of its points on point **a**, and moving the other point, make line **b**. Fix the point at **c**, and with the other make line **a. d.** Put down the line, then place the point of the compass at **b** and make line **d. e. a.** Then draw the line **d. e. f.**, and from **a** to **f** is 1/4 of the line **a. c.** Therefore, by the reasons stated above, if **a. c.** is divided into 4, it holds within it the four twenty-fourths; likewise.

But to better prove the reasons above, if your circle were divided into 24 parts, **a. c.**—which is the sixth part of that circle—contains within it six [parts of] 4, for 4 times 6 is 24. **f. c.** contains within it 3 [parts], for 8 times 3 likewise makes 24. Thus you have here 3 different types of divisions in one circle without opening or closing the compass: where **a. f.** is one twenty-fourth of the circle, **f. c.** is 1/8 of the circle, and **a. c.** is exactly 1/6. But I remind you well: perform the test with care on line **b. c.** mentioned above, which was forgotten earlier; it is the one that guides line **d. f.**, that is, where it intersects line **a** at point **e**.

# THE SHAPING OF IRON. — ENGINES FOR WAR.

— n¹. — At the opening of the iron forge <note>original: "mine [forge?]"; the translator suggests this refers to the furnace or forge rather than a mineral mine</note>, there are bellows made of a single piece—that is to say, without leather—and when they are raised, the air enters through their small window *n*, and when they are lowered, the air escapes through the pipes.

— Bellows for a galley <note>a Mediterranean warship propelled by oars</note>, half a cubit <note>original: "brasse"; a traditional unit of measurement roughly equal to the reach of a man's arms</term> long and one-eighth thick. — A lance-like weapon for a galley, with three cutting edges and two musket tubes <note>original: "escopettes"; an early form of carbine or short-barreled firearm</note>.

# OFFENSIVE WEAPONS.

### NAMES OF WEAPONS.

— **Acinaces.** — Acinaces <note>original: "Acinace"; a short, straight sword or dagger</note> is the name of this knife; and it was so named among the Scythians and the Medes, according to what Acron <note>Helenius Acron, a Roman grammarian</note> says.

— **Dagger.** — This one among the Ligurians <note>an ancient people of north-western Italy and south-eastern France</note> was called a *daga* <note>original: "Daga"</note>.

— **Sword.** — **Gladius.** — The *ensis* <note>Latin poetic term for sword</note> and the *gladius* <note>the standard Roman short sword</note> are types of weapons and are the same thing, as Quintilian maintains in the tenth book of his *Institutes* <note>original: "Institutions"; referring to *Institutio Oratoria*</note>, which does not [?]. The *gladius*, according to Pliny in the sixth book of *Natural History* <note>original: "Naturale Istoria"</note>, was invented by the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note>, and as Varro maintains, when the *gaesum* <note>original: "gæsum"; a heavy iron javelin used by the Gauls</note> was abolished, it was put in its place. It has been called an *aclis* <note>original: "aclide"; a small javelin or spiked club</note>, because it is used for slaughter <note>original: "clade"; Latin for destruction or carnage</note> and the death of enemies.

— **Spada [Sword].** — The *spada*, the *ensis*, and the *gladius* are names of weapons universally known, and especially among the ancients.

— **Harpe.** — The *harpe*, according to what Lucan says in the ninth [book], is a sickle-shaped sword <note>original: "épée en serpe"</note> with which Perseus killed the Gorgon <note>Medusa</note>.

— Names of weapons . . .

— The *arcie* <note>likely referring to early projectile weapons like arquebuses or crossbows</note> were called *manubalistes* <note>original: "manubalistes"; a hand-held ballista or crossbow</note>.

# OFFENSIVE WEAPONS.

— Stragula. — Lingula.

— Lingula <note>original: "Lingula"; literally "little tongue," a small blade shaped like a tongue</note>, and according to what Naevius <note>Gnaeus Naevius (c. 270–201 BC), an early Roman epic poet and playwright</note> says in one of his tragedies: *ceisonia* <note>original: "ceisonia"; a rare philological term likely referring to a cutting instrument</note>, is what a small knife in the shape of a bird's tongue is, or used to be, called.

— Machaera.

— Machaera <note>original: "Machæra"; a Greek or Roman sword or large knife, typically with a single edge</note> is a type of long weapon with a pointed section; Caesar <note>Julius Caesar</note> mentions it in the second [book] of his *Commentaries* <note>referring to the "Commentaries on the Gallic War"</note>.

— Stragula.

Stragula <note>original: "Stragule"; this is likely a manuscript variant or error for "tragula," a type of light javelin or barbed spear used by the Gauls and mentioned by Caesar</note> is a weapon for throwing and for manual use [with the hand]; Caesar also mentions these in the second [book] of the *Commentaries*.

— Dolones.

The *dolones* <note>original: "doloni"; from the Greek "dolon," meaning a stiletto or a dagger hidden inside a staff or cane</note> are a type of weapon mentioned by Plutarch in his *Life of Gracchus* <note>referring to the Life of Tiberius Gracchus, where hidden blades were used during the civil unrest in Rome</note>.

— Dolones.

— Some others have held the opinion that *dolones* are whips, within the shaft <note>original: "verge"; the handle or rod</note> of which daggers are hidden.

— Sica.

— The *sica* <note>original: "sica"</note> is a small knife which was used by ancient assassins [among the ancients, by assassins], called *sicarii* <note>original: "sicaires"; the term became synonymous with hired killers or "dagger-men"</note> because of the name of this knife, according to Quintilian <note>Marcus Fabius Quintilianus, a celebrated Roman rhetorician</note> in the ninth [book] of the *Institutes* <note>referring to the "Institutio Oratoria"</note>.

# OFFENSIVE WEAPONS.

-> OFFENSIVE WEAPONS. <-

---

— Dagger. <note>original: "Pugio"</note>

The dagger, according to Pompeius Festus <note>A 2nd-century Roman grammarian</note>, is a short knife with two points.

— Dagger. <note>original: "Pugio"</note>

Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a prolific Roman scholar</note> says that a long staff tipped with iron was also called a dagger.

— Sacrificial Knife. <note>original: "Clunade" / "Clunaculum"</note>

*Cluna*... The sacrificial knife is a bloodthirsty knife <insert>for cutting into the living flesh</insert>.

— Secespita. <note>A long, bronze or iron sacrificial knife used in Roman rituals</note>

The secespita is a long knife with a round handle; it is made from a single piece of ivory, decorated with gold and silver, which the pontiffs and the flamens <note>high-ranking priests of ancient Rome</note> used at sacrifices. Some say it was an axe, and others the *manara* <note>likely a reference to a sacrificial hand-knife</note> knife.

— Sword Point. <note>original: "Mucro"</note>

The *mucro* refers to the sword <note>original: "ensis"</note> and the blade <note>original: "gladius"</note>, according to *Plisci*... Priscian <note>A 6th-century Latin grammarian</note>, in the second book of the grammatical art.

— Aclides. <note>A type of ancient throwing weapon or spiked club</note>

Aclides, according to Servius <note>A 4th-century commentator on Virgil</note>, are certain weapons so ancient that they have been forgotten in warfare. Nevertheless, one reads that they were pieces of wood, some of which were half a cubit <note>roughly 9 inches</note> long and some round; inside were fixed sharp [sharpened] and prominent [protruding] iron points, which were thrown [launched] among the enemies with a cord or with leather straps, and whoever received the blow quickly met [had a quick encounter with] the one who had created [caused] it.

**Sacrificial Knife** <note>original: "clunade," likely referring to the Roman "clunaculum"</note>

*Cluna*, *clunade*: it is a bloodthirsty knife <note>used for slaughtering sacrificial animals</note>.

<note>Label for axes</note>
**Secespita** <note>A long, bronze or iron sacrificial knife used in Roman rituals</note>

The *secespita* is a long knife with a round handle made of a single piece of ivory and decorated with gold and silver; these were used by the high priests <note>original: "pontefici"</note> and the flamens <note>priests devoted to a particular deity</note> at sacrifices. Some say it is the axe <note>original: "lascura"</note> and others the cleaver-knife <note>original: "lamanara acoltello"</note>.

<note>Label for a thin pointed blade</note>
**Sword Point** <note>original: "mvcronē"</note>

*Mucro*, *ensis*, and *gladio* <note>three Latin terms for sword or its point</note> are the same according to Priscian <note>a 6th-century Latin grammarian</note> in the second book of the *Art of Grammar*.

<note>Label for spiked throwing clubs</note>
**Aclides** <note>An ancient Roman throwing weapon</note>

*Aclides*, as Servius <note>a 4th-century commentator on Virgil</note> maintains, are certain weapons so ancient that they are no longer mentioned in war. Nevertheless, one reads that these were pieces of wood, some a half-cubit <note>about 9 inches</note> long and some round, and fixed inside were sharp and protruding iron points; these were thrown among enemies with a cord or with leather thongs, and whoever received its blow quickly met his Creator <note>i.e., it was a lethal weapon</note>.

### OFFENSIVE WEAPONS.

— Telum <note>original: "Telum," a general Latin term for a missile or projectile weapon</note>.

The ancients generally called all things that, in war, were suited to be thrown by hand *telum*, such as darts, wooden shafts, arrows, spears, lances, stakes, and stones.

— Verutum <note>a short throwing spear or javelin used by Roman light infantry</note>.

The *verutum*, according to Nonius Marcellus <note>a 4th-century Roman grammarian and lexicographer</note>, is a small and very narrow weapon.

— Fusti <note>clubs or cudgels</note>.

The *fusti* are those first weapons used by the human race <insert>mankind</insert>, today called by the common folk <note>original: "vilains," referring to peasants or country-dwellers</note>: stakes; and their points were slightly charred <note>fire-hardening was a primitive method used to strengthen wooden tips before the widespread use of metal</note>.

— Baculus <note>a staff or walking stick</note>.

The *baculus* is a staff without a hook [?], with which unfortunate slaves were beaten.

— Spear <note>original: "Haste," from the Latin *hasta*</note>.

It is said that the spear was invented by the Lacedaemonians <note>the Spartans, famous for their hoplite warfare</note>; they are excellent and perfect when made of ash or hazel, but better still of rowan <note>mountain ash</note>, because this wood is more supple and flexible.

— Astili <note>small spear shafts or light javelins</note>.

The *astili* are small lances which are thrown skillfully by hand.

— Conti <note>original: "concti," referring to the *contus*, a long, heavy cavalry pike</note>.

The *conti* are very long and strong lances, without iron heads but with a sharpened point, *of which Lucan <note>a 1st-century Roman poet</note> makes mention*.

— Lance <note>original: "Lancea"</note>.

The *lancea*, of which Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, the Roman naturalist</note> says it was invented by the Aetolians <note>a people from central Greece</note>; Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a Roman scholar</note> says that "lance" is a Spanish word.

# OFFENSIVE WEAPONS.

— The *pilum* <note>a heavy Roman javelin</note>, the Roman spear, the *gaesum* <note>original: "gæsum"</note> of the Gauls, the *sarissa* <note>original: "larissa [sarissa]"</note> of the Macedonians.

The *pilum* was a spear used by the Romans, in the same manner as the *gaesum* among the Gauls and the *sarissa* among the Macedonians. And these spears were sawn along their length into two equal parts; then, their ends were swapped <insert>one of these parts was placed in the opposite direction of the other</insert>, they were joined together with fish glue, and at every half-cubit <note>approximately 9 inches or 22 centimeters</note>, they were bound with sinew. Authors say that these spears were so perfect that when they were suspended by a cord like a balance scale, they did not bend. And if someone, having first pulled it back, then thrust it forward with violence, no armor was found strong enough to offer resistance to it. They were very much in use among the Britons.

->— *Gaesum*.<-

The *gaesum* is a weapon used among the peoples of Gaul, and they are no less useful <insert>it is no less useful</insert> for throwing than for employing in another manner.

->— *Ruma*. — *Rumex*. — *Telum*. — Gallic *sparum*.<-

The *ruma*, the *pilum*, the *rumex*, and the *telum* <note>general Latin terms for missiles or darts</note> are consistent with one another, and similar to the Gallic *sparum* <note>a curved hunting spear or lance</note>.

->— Javelin (*jaculum*)<-

The javelin, it is said, was invented by Aetolus, son of Mars; and of this Hermes <insert>Trismegistus</insert>, Varro, and Pompeius Festus bear witness, saying that javelins are rustic, rural, and of vile and low condition, which are called <gloss>scattering? from: fit to be thrown in all directions?</gloss>.

<header>WEAPONS OF WAR.</header>

### — Cross

The cross was found among the Germans, and it is said that this weapon is in the first rank of deadly weapons, given that if it is thrown with or without a cord among the enemy troops, it never falls there in vain. In effect, it travels through [cleaves] the air by the sharp edge, and if it does not gather [catch] the enemy with a single point, it finds him with two; and if it does not meet him at all, by fixing itself in the ground, it is no less harmful to the enemies by striking the horses and the infantry. One carries, when going into combat, 4 or 6 of them around the belt.

---

### — <note>The title for this section is missing in the original manuscript, but describes a type of caltrop or spiked projectile</note>

This system was very much used among the Hebrews, the Syrians, and the peoples neighboring [them]. They threw them with cords and long ties among the enemies when they found themselves defeated and put to flight by them, so that those [enemies], being brought down [? overthrown], would cease [?] their pursuit; and they also sowed them along their [own] path [?].

---

### — Telico <note>Likely a corruption of the Latin *telum* (missile/dart) or a specific regional term for a primitive projectile</note>

These were in use among the first men; they were made of cane [reed], that is to say, having taken a piece of cane with 2 knots, one split one [knot] through the middle, and it served the purpose of the feather of the arrow; the other was made into a point and filled with earth in order to give it weight, and these weapons were launched with a cord.

### Manuscript Facsimile Transcription

<note>Leonardo's mirror writing transcribed into standard left-to-right Italian script.</note>

<note>Sketch of a cross-shaped projectile weapon.</note>
<margin>Cross</margin>

The **cross** <note>original: "cruce"</note> was found among the **Germans** <note>original: "tedesci"</note>, and they say this weapon is among the foremost of **deadly weapons** <note>original: "armi mortali"</note>. This is because, when it is thrown with a cord as is the custom into the enemy ranks, it never falls in vain; it cleaves through the air with its edge, and if it does not strike the enemy with one point, it finds him with two. And if it does not find the enemy, it fixes itself in the ground, where it is nonetheless harmful to the foes; for being a blow to the horses and the infantry, one carries 4 or 6 of these around the waist when going into battle.

---

<note>Sketch of a long projectile or cord-based weapon.</note>

This method was much used among the **Hebrews** and **Syrians** and neighboring peoples; these they threw with cords and long bindings among the enemies when they were being overtaken and put to flight, so that those [enemies] would be hindered in their pursuit; and they also scattered them from where they departed.

---

<note>Sketch of a projectile made from cane, weighted and feathered.</note>
<margin>Telico <note>Likely derived from the Latin "telum," meaning a dart or missile.</note></margin>

These were in use among the first men; they were made of **cane** <note>reeds</note>, that is, taking a piece of cane with two nodes. One [node] they split through the middle and made it serve as the feather of the arrow; the other they sharpened and filled with earth so that it would have weight, and these were launched with a cord.

### Printed Transcription

— **Cross**
The cross was found among the Germans, and they say this weapon is in the principal rank of deadly weapons. Because this being thrown with a cord according to custom among the ranks, it never falls in vain; and this which runs through the air by its edge, if it does not catch the enemy with a single point, it finds him with two; and if it does not find the enemy, it sticks itself in the ground where it is no less a harm to the enemies. For being a strike for the horses and infantry, 4 or 6 of these are carried around the belt when going to battle.

— This method was much used among the Hebrews and Syrians and neighboring peoples, and these they threw with cords and long bindings among the enemies when they were overcome by them and put to flight, so that those [pursuers] would end their course [be stopped]; and they also sowed them from where they departed.

— **Telico**
These were in use among the first men and were made of cane; that is, taking a piece of cane with 2 nodes, one they split through the middle and it made the use of the feather of the arrow; the other they pointed and filled with earth so that it would be weighted, and these were drawn with a cord.

# WEAPONS FOR WAR.

— **Sirile.** — The *sirile* <note>a specialized long spear or pike</note> is a very long spear; it was found among the Numidians <note>ancient North African people known for their light cavalry</note>. They were accustomed to using it often to strike down enemies and they sat on horseback without a saddle or stirrups, armed only with a doublet <insert>?</insert> filled with cotton, onto which the hooks of the long *siriles* were attached; [the enemies] being caught off guard were easily struck down.

— **Cariffe.** — The *cariffe* is a wide spear that attacks from a great distance. And if it happened that the flaming ball <note>likely an incendiary projectile attached to the weapon</note> was caught, the soldier would recover it by striking with the sharpened iron found at the top of the spear, and having it again, would scourge the unfortunate soldiers.

— **Miricide** — The *miricide* is a spear of 3 fathoms <note>original: "brasses," a measurement of roughly 6 feet</note>, and when it is extended, of 5 and 1/3 fathoms; it is used among soldiers in the manner that peasants <note>original: "vilains," referring to common laborers or serfs</note> thresh wheat <note>describing a flail-like motion</note>.

— **Malcoli.** — **Malcoli.** — The *malcoli* <note>original: "malleoli," Latin for "little hammers," referring to incendiary fire-arrows</note>, according to Ammianus Marcellinus <note>a 4th-century Roman soldier and historian</note>, are a type of darts and arrows. Their shaft is made of cane [reed], and where the cane ends, a distaff <note>a tool used in spinning wool</note> is joined; upon the distaff is the iron for piercing. In the cavity of said distaff, one must put tow <note>coarse flax or hemp fiber</note> *and pitch . . .* soaked in pitch, set it on fire, and throw it slowly, so that the force of the air does not extinguish it. Some say that in this cavity an indestructible . . . inextinguishable fuel <note>original: "nourriture," literally "food" for the fire</note> is made, which is created with colophony <note>pine resin</note>, sulfur, and saltpeter, things which must be liquefied with laurel oil—some say petroleum oil—duck fat, marrow of <unclear>meat</unclear>, ferula <note>giant fennel</note>, sulfur, colophony, camphor, <unclear>rasa</unclear>, and tow. This composition was called among the ancients "incendiary," that is to say, a thing fit for burning. The tow also, [with] the fat and the petroleum...

# MOUNTED SOLDIERS ARMED WITH HANDGUNS. — ORDER OF BATTLE.

— Scorpion. — Viper. <note>Likely names for specific types of artillery or crossbow engines</note> — 1 2¹ — This crossbow has 2 iron wires, [arranged] so that one catches an iron ring at the top or upper extremity on one side, and the other on the other side, as shown in 1 and 2.

— This one is a mounted handgunner <term>escopettier: a soldier armed with an escopette, an early form of portable firearm</term>, which is an extremely useful invention. These handgunners must <insert>should</insert> carry with them a pouch full of single-layer cardboard tubes <term>cartouches: early cartridges containing a pre-measured charge of powder</term> filled with powder, so that by inserting them frequently [into the weapon], one may overcome the excessive number of enemies; and the said handgunners must hold themselves in squadrons, like the crossbowmen, so that when one part [of them] fires, the other loads; but first, ensure that the horses have been accustomed to such noises. Or else, plug their ears.

->— m r t n — c a b d —<-

### ORDER [of battle] FOR MOUNTED CROSSBOWMEN IN OPEN FIELD.
**M n** are the crossbowmen who... <unclear>illegible</unclear> turn to the left, retreating backward while reloading. **R t** are those who move forward with loaded crossbows, and these 4 files constitute a single route. **A b** are 4 files of crossbowmen who return with their crossbows discharged to reload them again; **c d** are those who, with their crossbows loaded, meet the enemy, and this order of eight lines is used in the open field. Let it be arranged so that those who have fired return through the middle, so that if they should ever be turned by the enemy, the loaded crossbowmen, staying on the outside [on the flanks], may strike a greater terror into the said enemies.

### TYPE OF CROSSBOW.
The crossbow should not exceed 2 *braccia* <note>original: "brasses", approximately 4 feet or 1.2 meters</note>, and when drawn to the nut <note>the rotating catch that holds the string</note>, it should not exceed 1/3 of its length; let it be wide, thin, and made of steel welded between 2 plates of soft iron.

### ORDER FOR MOUNTED HANDGUNNERS. 
But ensure they have a large supply of thin, single-layer cardboard tubes filled with powder, with the ball inside, so they only have to insert them and apply fire; being thus prepared, they have no need to retreat like the crossbowmen trained to reload.

### ORDER OF MOUNTED CROSSBOWMEN IN OPEN FIELD

**m. n.** are the crossbowmen who, as they <unclear>turn</unclear> to the left, pull back to reload. **r. t.** are those who go forward with loaded crossbows; and these 4 files are for one path. **a. b.** are 4 rows of crossbowmen who return with empty crossbows to reload them anew. **c. d.** are those who, with loaded crossbows, encounter the enemy. And this same [order applies to the handgunners].

### NATURE OF THE CROSSBOW

The crossbow should not exceed 2 braccia <term>braccia: an Italian unit of measurement, roughly 23 inches or the length of an arm</term>, and the string should not exceed 1/2 of its width when being mounted on the nut <term>nut (noce): the rotating cylindrical component that holds the bowstring in place until the trigger is pulled</term>. It should be wide and thin, and made of steel welded in the middle of two plates of soft iron.

### ORDER OF MOUNTED HANDGUNNERS

Make sure <note>original: "maffa," a shorthand used by Leonardo for 'make sure' or 'ensure'</note> that they have a large supply of thin, single-layer paper tubes <note>early cartridges</note> filled with powder with the ball <term>balotta: a small lead bullet</term> inside, so that they have nothing to do but insert [it] and give fire. Being so quick, they have no need to return to the rear to reload like the crossbowmen.

# DEFENSE OF A FORTIFIED TOWER AT SEA.

-> — Main route — Route along the ditches — Gate. — <-

-> — Manner of closing the gate. — <-

-> — Castellan <note>The governor or warden of a castle</note> — Mercenaries <note>original: "Provisionati" - soldiers serving for pay or provisions</note> — <-

Because someone wishing to capture a tower situated in the sea will arrange for one of his loyal followers to confer with the castellan, and when he [signals?], the guards will pull up the rope ladder given to him by the enemies to the battlements, and the walls will fill with soldiers; to prevent this, divide the tower into eight spiral staircases <term>spiral staircases: "escaliers à limaçon," literally snail-shell stairs</term>, and divide the defenses and the living quarters at the base into eight sections for the soldiers. And if the mercenary <note>The paid soldier</note> wished to be alone, the others would not be able to stand with him upon the walls; and the defensive area shall be so small that only four people can be held there. The castellan, who lives above everyone else, can drive them out using the machicolations <term>machicolations: floor openings through which stones or boiling liquids could be dropped on attackers</term>, and close them off with portcullises <term>original: "sarrasines" - a type of sliding defensive grating</term>, and then release smoke <note>possibly "powder"</note> at the start of the spiral staircases; and by no means should any foreign soldier live with the castellan, but only his own family.

(1) See folios 50 recto and 59 verso.

# DEFENSE OF A FORTIFIED CASTLE.

— To block off a valley¹.

— Let the illustrated arches be staggered within the thickness of the wall—that is, they should not all share the same base [let them not all have their foundation] on a single pillar, but rather on several. This is so that if the cannons <term>bombardes: early, large-caliber cannons used for throwing stone balls</term> break one of these pillars, the arches will not collapse [will not fall into ruin].

— Solid. — Solid.

— Let the walls be solid and without battlements, and let the passageway for traveling from one fortified tower to another [?] be located within the wall that goes underground.

— Chamber of the castellan <term>castellan: the governor or warden of a castle</term>. — Here, the castellan drives out the mercenaries <note>original: "provisionati" — soldiers serving for pay or provisions</note> from every location [from everywhere].

— a² — Let **a** be a portcullis <term>sarrasine: a sliding defensive gate, literally "the Saracen"</term>, which is solely under the power of the castellan.

# SHORT CANNONS FOR SHIPS

— These <term>short cannons (courtauds)</term> <note>original: "courtauds" — a type of short-barreled, large-bore artillery piece, often used for close-range naval engagements.</note> must be placed upon strong ships; and these two short cannons shall have, connected by a strong chain or a new rope that has been wetted, a scythe twelve <term>fathoms (brasses)</term> <note>original: "brasses" — a unit of length based on the reach of a man's arms, roughly 6 feet.</note> long, one foot wide at its middle, and one finger thick at the back of its blade; the fire must be given [ignited] at the same moment.

On the use of the naval scythe.
</margin>

<note>The "wetted rope" mentioned would prevent the friction of the launch or the heat of the discharge from immediately severing the line connecting the two projectiles.</note>

# ENGINEERS. — INFLAMMABLE BALL. — FIRE ARROW. — ORGAN VIOLA. — CLOCK.

-> — Names of engineers: <-

Callias of Rhodes, Epimachus the Athenian, Diogine the Rhodian philosopher <note>likely Diognetus, the architect who defended Rhodes</note>, Calcedonius of Thrace, Febar of Tyre <margin>See folio 51 recto</margin>, Callimachus the architect, master of fires <margin>See above: folio 30, verso</margin> <note>likely Callinicus, the 7th-century inventor of Greek Fire</note>.

---

— Prepared fire ball. Take tow <note>coarse, broken fibers of flax or hemp</note> soaked with pitch, turpentine, and linseed oil; then, twist it around so that you make a ball; over this, place hemp dyed in double-distilled turpentine, and when you have made the ball, make 4 or 6 holes in it as thick as your arm, fill them with loose hemp dyed in double-distilled turpentine and <term>bombard powder</term> <note>early gunpowder used for large cannons</note>, then place the ball in the bombard <margin>Below the preceding text is a figure, which must be that of the inflammable ball.</margin>.
