— This is a dart to be shot by a large <term>belly-crossbow</term> <note>original: "arbalète à panse"; a powerful crossbow braced against the stomach to span</note>; and the 2 horns have their fire contained in linen; when the point sinks in, the horns squeeze together and set fire to the powder and the pitched tow. This weapon is good for ships, wooden bastions, and other similar instruments. But no one will achieve a good result in burning if the fire does not ignite after the impact, because if you try to light the fire before, the violence of the wind extinguishes it on its way.

---

— f a b <margin>f is read under the vertical piece at the top of the apparatus, a b below f.</margin> — This is the method of movement for the bow of the <term>organ viola</term> <note>original: "viole organiste"; a mechanical stringed instrument invented by Leonardo da Vinci using a friction wheel</note> <margin>See Amoretti, *Historical Memoirs*, pages 32-33</margin>. If you make the notches of the two-stroke wheel smaller than each other by a certain number of teeth, and so that they do not meet together, as seen in a b, the bow will have a smooth movement; otherwise, it will move in jerks. If you do it my way, the <term>pinion</term> <note>original: "rochetta"</note> f will always move in a steady manner.

---

— 4 — Springs for the clock, such that when one has finished its course, the other begins. And during the turn made by the first, the second remains immobile. The first is fixed by a screw onto the second, and when it is fully fixed, the second spring takes up the same movement, and so do they all.

<note>Mechanical drawing (middle left) of a vertical series of conical pulleys or stacked gears.</note>

To make a worked fire ball: take tow <note>coarse flax or hemp fibers</note> soaked with pitch, turpentine, and linseed oil; go about winding it around so that it forms a ball. Over this, place hemp dipped in double-distilled turpentine. Once you have made the ball, make 4 or 6 holes in it as thick as your arm; fill those with loose hemp dipped in double-distilled turpentine and <term>bombard powder</term> <note>early gunpowder for cannons</note>, and place this in the bombard.

<note>Mechanical drawing (middle right) of an incendiary dart (dardo) designed for a ballista, showing mechanical prongs at the tip.</note>

This is a dart to be shot from a large <term>belly-crossbow</term> <note>original: "balestra a pancha"; a powerful crossbow braced against the abdomen to span</note>. The two horns have their fire contained in linen cloth; when the point strikes and fixes itself, the horns squeeze together and ignite the powder and the pitched tow. This is effective for ships, wooden bastions, and other similar structures. No one will succeed in burning anything if the fire does not ignite *after* the impact, because if you try to light the fire beforehand, the fury of the wind will extinguish it during its flight.

**f a b** — This is the method of motion for the bow of the viola organista. If you make the notches of the wheel in two stages, so that one set of teeth is smaller than the other and they do not clash together (as shown in **a** and **b**), the bow will have a single, equal movement. Otherwise, it will move in jolts. If you make the <term>rocchetto</term> <note>a small gear or bobbin</note> **f** in my way, it will always move smoothly.

4 springs for the clock: when one has finished its course, the other begins. In the turning that the first one makes, the second stays still; the first is fixed by a screw onto the second, and when it is entirely wound, the second spring takes up the same motion, and so they all do in sequence.

---

— Names of engineers: Callias of Rhodes, Epimachus the Athenian, Diogenes the Philosopher, Rodanus of Chalcedon in Thrace, Febar of Tyre, Callimachus the architect, master of fires.

— Worked fire ball: take tow soaked with pitch, turpentine, and linseed oil; wind it around to make a ball; over it place hemp dipped in double-distilled turpentine. Make 4 or 6 holes as thick as your arm and fill them with loose hemp dipped in double-distilled turpentine and gunpowder; put this in the cannon.

— This is a dart for a large belly-crossbow. The two horns hold fire in linen; when the point hits, the horns compress and ignite the powder and tow. Good for ships and wooden defenses. Fire must ignite after the blow, or the wind kills the flame in transit.

— **f a b** — The motion of the viola organista bow. Use two-stage wheel notches so teeth don't clash; this ensures smooth motion without jolting. My design for gear **f** ensures constant speed.

— 4 clock springs: as one ends, the next starts. The first screws into the second so that motion is handed off continuously through the whole set.

A way to measure heights and widths and distances without moving your feet: place a <term>perfect square</term><note>quadro perfetto: a geometric instrument used for surveying, likely a quadrant or a square frame with sights</note> on the ground as appears above; then place your eye above the angle **m** and look toward the foot of the tower of which you wish to know the distance; and as many times as **b a** goes into **a c**, so many times **m n** goes into **n f**. And if you should wish to know, without moving yourself or your square, the true height of the tower, you shall do thus: place your eye at angle **n** and look at the summit of the tower **p**, and as many times as **b c** goes into **c n**, so many times **p f** goes into **f n**. And you, knowing by the first measurement the true distance that is between **f n**, you will be able to know how much the tower goes inside; that is, if **b a** goes 3 times into **a m**, so likewise **m n** goes 3 into **n f**; and if **m n** is distant one <term>braccio</term><note>braccio: an Italian unit of length, literally a 'arm', roughly 23 inches or 58 cm</note>, **n f** will be 3 <term>braccia</term>. And knowing this, you can then know if **b c** goes 2 times into **c n**, so **p f** goes 2 into **f n**. Now you know by the first reasoning that **f n** is 3 <term>braccia</term>, and if **p f** goes 2 times into these 3 <term>braccia</term>, it comes to be exactly one and 1/2 <term>braccia</term>, and it is a just and good rule.

## FOLIO 59 (recto)

This also is of great utility.

This shall be a small wheel made of fig wood on the inside and of thick cotton <note>original: "banbagia"</note> on the outside, a quarter-braccio <note>A "braccio" or "arm" was a common Florentine measure, roughly 23 inches; a quarter-braccio is about 6 inches.</note> thick. And if you make it of fustian <note>A thick, durable twilled cotton cloth.</note> varnished on the outside of the cotton, it will be good. And if you make it of cotton on the outside and inside with fish glue and <term>agranti</term> <note>Likely a resin or binding agent, possibly related to "aggrante" or "alcaniglia".</note> and varnished, and the middle of simple cotton, tightened with nails that go from one surface to the other, it will be good; which you shall dry in the press.

<note>Study for a "deadly machine" or cluster bomb</note>
These balls could also be filled with small pieces of sulfur, which would cause one to faint away.

This is the most deadly machine that exists: when the center ball falls, it sets fire to the other balls in a timed sequence <note>original: "a ttermi" [a termine]</note>; and the center ball bursts and scatters the others, which catch fire in the time it takes to say an *Ave Maria* <note>A common Renaissance way of measuring a short duration of time, roughly 10-15 seconds.</note>; and on the outside is a shell that covers everything.

Let the small firecrackers <note>original: "scopietti"</note> of these balls be made of paper and filled between one and the other with casting plaster mixed with cloth clippings <note>original: "cimatura di panni"</note>; and give them fire with a bellows-tube <note>original: "soffione"</note> which ends its flame in the center of the ball among the powder, which should scatter all the balls filled with firecrackers at a good interval from one another.

<margin>Small wheel filled with firecrackers for a foot soldier.</margin>

<note>Description of a compass or mechanical instrument</note>
**a b c** — METHOD FOR A COMPASS — by fixing point **a**, you will be able to set point **b** precisely with the screw, by turning the screw **c**.

# — FOLIO 59 (verso). —

<note>Transcription of Leonardo's mirror writing in the manuscript facsimile above</note>

<margin>A man’s harness made of ropes</margin>
<note>Label "m" appears near the top hook on the wall drawing</note>

The method for how one should scale a fortress by night; that is, if you have no <term>intelligence</term><note>original: "jntelligenza"; here meaning a secret contact or spy inside the walls</note> within to pull up the rope ladders. You shall climb first by placing these iron rungs, arm’s length by arm’s length, into the crevices in the manner that appears here above. And when you are at the top, secure the rope ladder as you see here. The iron <insert>marked</insert> **m** is wrapped in <term>tow</term><note>coarse, unspun flax or hemp fiber</note> so that it does not make a noise. And once it is secure, if it seems right to you to pull up other ladders, pull them; otherwise, quickly send up the combatants. The small hook that is attached to the rope harness has a ring above it, if you wish, in which stays a cord that pulls with a <term>jack</term><note>original: "martineto"; a mechanical lifting device or crank</note> to the iron above, to which you will once again attach the hook of the said harnesses.

These ladders are made by 2 men and are also useful for a tower where you might fear that the rope ladder could be detached by enemies. Let them be driven so far into the wall that 1/3 is embedded and 1/8 remains outside.

<margin>The pyramid-shaped irons should be 1/2 <term>braccio</term><note>An Italian unit of measurement, roughly 23 inches or 58 cm</note> long, and the clear space between them should be 1/2 braccio.</margin>

These stakes are buried in the moats of castles; they are made one and 1/3 braccio long—1/3 remains out and 2/3 is beneath. They are made of chestnut or oak, with the tips charred <note>Charring the wood hardened the points and prevented rot in the damp soil of a moat</note>.

# CROSSING A RIVER BY AN ARMY CORPS.

— Bags for crossing waters.

— One must still *weigh carefully* <note>original: "peser quand il faut peser" - a phrase emphasizing deliberate consideration</note> in what manner one ought to proceed in order to cross rivers at will. First, one must place a man upon two bags [skins] <note>likely goatskin bladders or "outres" used as primitive flotation devices</note>, fastened together; then, if you find the riverbed suitable, but the river is dangerous due to the rapidity of its current, act in the manner illustrated below.

— If the river presents a danger due to its current, one must form two lines of horses across the river, positioned at a distance of 6 fathoms <term>brasses: a measurement of roughly 6 feet or 1.8 meters, based on the reach of a man's arms</term> from one another. Let the horses be so close in their lines that they almost touch, and let the line of horses or the squadron be positioned with their heads turned toward the oncoming water; this is done solely to repress and break the fury and impetuosity of the water. Between the one squadron and the other, the soldiers—both armed and unarmed—are made to pass. The upper squadron [which crosses first] <insert>positioned upstream</insert> must have the largest horses, to better break the impetuosity of the river; the lower [the one that crosses last] <insert>positioned downstream</insert> is to support the soldiers if they should happen to fall, to sustain them during the crossing.

<summary>This passage describes tactical methods for an army to cross a fast-moving river using inflatable skins for individuals and double lines of cavalry to break the current for infantry.</summary>
<keywords>river crossing, military tactics, flotation bags, cavalry screen, water safety, army logistics</keywords>

# WAR AND HISTORY. — ON WEIGHTS.

### ON WEIGHTS <note>original: "De Ponderibus"</note>

I ask: if a weight of one pound, falling from two fathoms <note>original: "brasses" - a measurement of roughly 6 feet</note>, sinks into the ground by one palm <note>original: "palme" - a measurement of about 3-4 inches</note>, how far will it sink when falling from 40 fathoms? Or likewise, how far will a weight of 2 pounds sink when falling from 2 fathoms?

It is also asked: if the weight has a width of a certain quantity *a*, and if that quantity is doubled for the same weight and dropped from the same height, how much further will the lesser width sink than the greater, assuming the ground offers uniform resistance <margin>This passage, although it appears first at the top of the manuscript page, must have been written after the others; the ink is more recent. See manuscript A. fᵒ 1 verso, 47 verso, Amoretti, *Historical Memoirs*, p. 133.</margin>.

— Let pavises <note>large convex shields used to protect archers or infantry</note> be made to withstand the fury of arrows arriving in great quantities.

— How the Germans intermingle and interlace, pressing close together, their long pikes against the enemy, stooping down and placing one of the ends on the ground while holding the rest in their hands.

— If the water is so high that infantry and cavalry cannot pass, let the river be diminished into many streams, as did Cyrus, King of the Persians, at the taking of Babylon, upon the river Ganges <note>The author likely confuses the Gyndes or Euphrates with the Ganges here</note>, which at its greatest width <note>original: "parcours de flèche" - literally an arrow's flight</note> is 10,000 fathoms; and also Alexander on the same river, and Caesar on the river Sicoris <note>The Segre in Spain</note>.

— Should it happen that the river is so deep that it cannot be forded, the captain should have numerous channels made to take the water and then return it further down the river; in this way, the river comes to subside and will be crossed with ease. Thus did Alexander in India against King Porus at the crossing of the river Hydaspes; thus did Caesar in Gaul (and also in Spain) on the river Liger <note>The Loire</note>; having ordered the cavalry into two bodies, he had the soldiers pass through the middle; and likewise did Hannibal in the Po, using elephants.

# FOLIO 62 (recto).

<note>Manuscript facsimile of Leonardo da Vinci's notes and drawings regarding military river crossings.</note>

<note>Sketch of a mountain landscape with a river valley.</note>

<margin>
To cross a river
with a current
</margin>

<note>Study of soldiers holding arms to form a chain for crossing a rapid river.</note>

...if it should happen that the infantry have to cross a river that is dangerous due to its vehement <note>original: "vemehente," meaning forceful or violent</note> current, this is the secure method. Let the soldiers take one another under the arms <note>original: "lebraca," likely a variant of "braccia" (arms)</note> and let them form a line in the manner of a palisade <term>palancato: a defensive wooden fence or barrier</term>, linked together by their arms. And let these rows arrange themselves to walk along the thread of the water <note>meaning parallel to the direction of the current</note>, and let no one turn sideways against the flow. This is a safe method, and the reason is that the first man at the top is the one who sustains the first impetus of the water; if he were alone, the water would throw him down, but all the others below him support him and make of themselves a shield for him. Thus, by this means, they secure one another.

In effect, if the river flows from right to left, each man in the rows, in passing from the first bank to the second, receives the flow of the river upon his right shoulder, and from his companion on the left, he receives the support of that companion's right shoulder against the escape of the water.

---

<note>Printed editorial transcription of the manuscript text.</note>

— if it should happen that the infantry have to cross a river dangerous for its vehement current, this is the secure method. Let the soldiers take one another under the arms and let them form a line in the manner of a palisade, linked by the arms. And let these rows arrange themselves in their path along the thread of the water and let no one turn across the course of it. And this is a secure method; the reason is that the first one at the top is he who sustains the first impetus, and if he were alone the water would throw him down, but all the others below support him and make of themselves a shield for him, whereby for this reason one secures the other.

In effect, they all have—if the river falls from right to left—each of the rows, in passing from the first to the second bank, receives from the right shoulder the course of the river, and [from] his companion on the left, the right shoulder of the companion [against] the escape of the water.

<note>Technical vocabulary: infantry, river, palisade, arms, troop/line, impetus, shield, bank.</note>

<summary>Leonardo describes a tactical maneuver for infantry to safely cross a fast-moving river by linking arms in a chain formation parallel to the current. This method uses the collective weight of the group to stabilize the lead soldier against the water's force.</summary>

**WHAT IS FORCE**
— force, I say, is a spiritual power, incorporeal and invisible, which with brief life is caused
in those bodies which by accidental violence stand outside of their natural being and rest — spiritual I said because in this force
there is active life, incorporeal and invisible I say because the body where it is born does not grow in weight nor in form, of short life because
it always desires to overcome its cause, and that being conquered, it kills itself.

# FOR ASPHYXIATING THE BESIEGED.

— The Germans are accustomed to asphyxiating the lords of the castle [the people who are inside the fortified castles] with the smoke of feathers, sulfur, and realgar <note>Realgar is a highly toxic arsenic sulfide mineral used historically in pyrotechnics and as a poison.</note>, and they make said fumes last 7 and 8 hours. # — FOLIO 64 (recto). —

<note>Manuscript facsimile of Leonardo da Vinci's Folio 64 (recto), showing a design for a hydraulic weapon or flood-release mechanism. The top section contains Leonardo's original mirror writing and drawings; the bottom section contains a printed transcription of the same text.</note>

### Manuscript Facsimile (Mirror Script)

-> A method for releasing a rush of water against an army, or bridges and city walls <-

<margin>
To create
a rush of
water
</margin>

<note>Drawing of a timber dam or sluice gate mechanism with rotating shutters. Points are labeled 'M', 'a', and 'b'. The mechanism is designed so that the pressure of the water helps swing the gates open once the lock is released.</note>

If you wish to flood a field or break down walls without <term>bombards</term><note>Early forms of cannons or mortars used for throwing heavy stone shot.</note>, and you have the convenience of a river, do as illustrated above. That is: set up piles as high as the bank of a river and place them half a <term>braccio</term><note>An Italian unit of measurement, literally a "length of an arm," roughly 23 inches or 58 centimeters.</note> from one another, or more if you have wider planks. Then, place said planks between one pile and the next and let it fill. When it is full, lift the fastening **M**, and the upper part of the plank **a** will move forward, and the lower part **b** will move backward. In this way, said planks will remain edge-on, and the water is free to escape. Ensure that the <term>sluice gates</term><note>original: "cateratte"</note> are all opened at the sound of a <term>gunshot</term><note>original: "scopietto," a small early firearm or carbine.</note> or another signal, so that they are opened at the same time. Thus, the arrival of the water against the opposing object encountered will be overwhelmed by a greater blow and impetuous force. And if the river should be very steep, make one of these every half mile, and let each one be opened with a rope—all its joints together—so that it acts better at one time and remains safe from whoever would close it.

---

### Printed Transcription

— A method for releasing a rush of water against an army, bridges, and city walls —
— M a b —
— for [?] the flood [?] —
— If you wish to flood a field or break down walls without bombards, and you have the convenience of a river, do as illustrated above. That is: set up piles as high as the bank of a river and place them half a braccio from one another, or more if you have wider planks. Then, place said planks between one pile and the next and let it fill. When it is full, lift the fastening **M**, and the upper part of the plank **a** will move forward, and the lower part **b** will move backward. In this way, said planks will remain edge-on, and the water is free to escape. Ensure that the sluice gates are all opened at the sound of a gunshot or another signal, so that they are opened at the same time. Thus, the arrival of the water against the opposing object encountered will be overwhelmed by a greater blow and impetuous force. And if the river should be very steep, make one of these every half mile, and let each one be opened with a rope—all its joints together—so that it acts better at one time and remains safe from whoever would close it.

# WATER LEVELS. — EXCAVATION INSTRUMENTS FOR PLANTING.

->— a b m s t —<-

— This is another means of taking the level of waters. Therefore, let **a b** be a body of still water; next, place a wall at a distance from **b** of 100 <term>braccia</term><note>original: "brasses" (braccia). A Renaissance unit of length, roughly 23 inches or 58 cm.</note>, and however much distance there is from **s** to **t**, that will be the drop of the water.

->— m n f g —<-

— If you wish to make a hole underground with ease, have the instrument figured above; then, to make the hole, you shall turn the screw to the right hand with the lever **m n**, and the screw will sink in, creating its own nut-thread within the earth. When it has entered to your liking, stop the lever **m n**, and, doing the opposite to the left, you shall turn the levers **f g**. Furthermore, it will be better to turn in the same direction; and the screw will rise, and, ascending without turning, will carry away with it the soil that was above it.

->— c d —<-

— This instrument also is good for the aforementioned task. That is to say, the path <gloss>traversed</gloss> by the foot makes the path <gloss>for</gloss> the other part above, cutting the ground, from which <gloss>results</gloss> the hole. The lever **c d** wrenches the instrument out at the beginning, and then it is easily pulled outward, drawing the entire instrument out. This would be <gloss>used</gloss> for planting vines and other <gloss>fruit-bearing plants</gloss>.

# LEVELS

— m n <note>Reference to the first figure on the right of the original manuscript page.</note> —

— a s t y <note>Reference to the second figure at the top, read from right to left.</note> — The space... —

— r f <note>Reference to the figure on the top left.</note> —

— Level that is adjusted by a screw —

— If you wish to know how much higher one plane is than another, proceed as follows: Place your level between your eye and the object whose descent <note>original: "abaissement"; refers here to the difference in elevation or the drop in height</note> you wish to determine; place the illustrated staff at the lower position, and move it up and down until your eye **a**, and the two sights **s t**, are in a single thread with [on the same horizontal line as] the top of the black band marked on the card **r**. Mark the staff below, at point **f**, with a nail. Then, carry the staff to the opposite side, *in such a way that...* doing the same thing as before, so that your eye **y**, and likewise **t s**, are in one [on the same] line as the black of the same card, placed at the top of the staff, and mark below with the second nail. The first nail will be **m**, and the second **n**, and however much distance there is from **m** to **n**, that is how much lower one of the positions is than the other.

— m m [n] <note>Reference to the figure at the bottom of the page.</note> — Cord <note>original: "Corde"; likely referring to a leveling line or a measurement cord.</note> —

— This is the manner in which the level must be made: that is to say, [it should be] 2 <term>brasses</term> <note>A "brasse" (fathom) was a traditional unit of length based on the reach of a man's arms, roughly 1.6 to 1.9 meters.</note> long, and one inch thick on each side of the square. Let it be made of fir wood, so that it does not warp, and let it have a wide channel in the upper surface, one finger thick and of the same depth. Next, wet the cord, fill the channel with water, and lower first one end and then the other until the water is flush with the edges; then, go about cleaning [wipe away] the water that abounds [overflows] at the heads [ends] of the channel with your fingers until they remain dry; then, place two iron pieces at **m n**, as thick as a cord, and ensure that one is on the same horizontal as the other and the object being viewed.

# VARIOUS MACHINES. — WALLS OF PAVIA. — DIKES.

— About ½ a <term>braccia</term> <note>A Renaissance unit of measurement; in Florence, roughly 23 inches or 58 cm.</note> thick, 2 <term>braccia</term> long, with 4 handles. And let it be made of oak, and bound with iron hoops at the heads [ends] <insert>1</insert>.

— These piles must be between a third and a half of a <term>braccia</term> thick, and about 2 ½ <term>braccia</term> long; they should be made of oak or alder, that is <unclear>illegible</unclear>, and above all, let them be green <note>Freshly cut wood was preferred for underwater foundations as it resists rot better when permanently submerged than seasoned wood.</note>. I have seen the reconstruction of the foundations of some portion of the old walls of Pavia, founded on the banks of the Ticino <note>original: "Tessin"</note>. The piles that had grown old there were of oak, and black as charcoal; those made of alder had a red color like Brazilwood <note>A wood known for its deep red dye; the author is noting the remarkable preservation and color change of the timber underwater.</note>, were very heavy, hard as iron, and without any blemish. When you wish to drive the said piles, start their holes with an iron pile-driver.

— **M** — When you have created a palisade, pay close attention: if water begins to spring up between the said piles, place a pipe over it as seen in **M**, and then, throw in fresh lime until you level the heads of the piles, which should remain exposed by a third of a <term>braccia</term>; then, build upon them with large, square masonry blocks, and then with common ones.

— This wall, to provide resistance against riverbanks, must be 4 <term>braccia</term> thick; every 4 <term>braccia</term>, it requires a buttress <note>original: "éperon" (spur)</note> of 4 or up to 5 <term>braccia</term>, which project from this wall into the earth of the banks, and are 2 <term>braccia</term> thick. And let the wall be built with a slope <note>original: "escarpe"</note>, that is to say, for every 2 <term>braccia</term> of height, it should have one inch of <unclear>recession</unclear> for the slope.

— In places where you would not wish to build a full portico <note>A covered walkway supported by columns, typical of Renaissance courtyards.</note> around a courtyard—that is to say, where only one or two of the four facades have a portico—you should still design the other sides using the same order of columns. # FOLIO 69 (verso).

<header>DRIVING PILES¹. — POISONING SHIPS.</header>

### FOR THROWING POWDERED POISON ONTO GALLEYS.

— Let there be thrown among the enemy ships, using small <term>ballistae</term> <note>Ancient or medieval engines for hurling missiles, similar to giant crossbows.</note>, a mixture of <term>lime</term> <note>Calcium oxide, a caustic substance that causes severe irritation to the eyes and lungs.</note>, fine <term>orpiment</term> <note>A deep yellow arsenic sulfide mineral; highly toxic if inhaled or ingested.</note>, and powdered <term>verdigris</term> <note>A green pigment or crust formed on copper, brass, or bronze; it is poisonous when concentrated.</note>. All those who breathe in the said powder will be suffocated by their own breathing. But take care [pay attention] to have the wind in such a direction that it does not blow the powder back at you, or else have a piece of wet cloth over your nose and mouth so that the powder cannot pass through. It would also be effective to throw, from the <term>fighting tops</term> <note>original: "hunes"; platforms high up on the masts of a ship used by archers or for observation.</note> or from the ship itself, <term>cartridges</term> <note>original: "cartouches"; here referring to containers or casings made of cardboard.</note> covered in cardboard and filled with the aforementioned powder.

# FLIGHT BY FLAPPING WINGS.

->— M f a b c d¹. —<-

— **a** twists the wing, **b** turns it with the lever, **c** lowers it, **d** raises it from bottom to top, and the man, the pilot of this instrument, keeps his feet at **f** and **d**. The foot **f** lowers the wings and the foot **d** raises them. The pivot **M** must hang <note>original: "veut [doit] pendre"</note> outside of its perpendicular <note>outside of the vertical axis</note>, so that the wings, while descending, also lower themselves toward the man's feet; for it is this action that will make the bird move forward.

— You shall test this instrument over a lake, and you shall wear a long goatskin float <note>original: "outre" - a skin bag used for buoyancy</note> fastened at your waist, so that in falling, you do not happen to drown.

— It is also necessary that the lowering of the wings be done by the force of both feet at the same time; so that you may regulate your timing <note>original: "temporiser" - to slow or control the rhythm</note> and maintain your balance by lowering one wing faster than the other as needed, just as you see the kite <note>a type of bird of prey known for soaring</note> and other birds do.

And furthermore, the downward stroke of two feet is twice as strong as that of a single one; it is true that the movement is then twice as slow. As for rising, this is achieved by the force of a spring, or, if you wish, with the hand; or better yet by pulling your feet toward you, which is preferable because your hands are then more free².

---

<margin>1. **M** is at the top of the figure, the other letters at the bottom.</margin>
<margin>2. See: C. G. Gerli, *Drawings of Leonardo da Vinci*, plates XL, XLI and XLII. Folio reproduced on p. 31 of the *Writings of Leonardo da Vinci* by Charles Ravaisson-Mollien.</margin>

### [Facsimile of Folio 75v]

BASTION — So that the bastion is not burned, coat it with mud and grass instead of cloth clippings <note>original: "cimatura" - the shearings from woolen cloth, often used as stuffing or insulation</note>, so that the earth does not slip away.

— IN WHAT MANNER ONE OUGHT TO ASSAULT A BASTION MADE TO CLOSE OFF A PASSAGE. — Make portable pieces of bastions for a rush of men, which should be filled with hay and pointed in front so that the shots from the artillery can do no harm; and joined together, let them make a bastion of such size that they occupy all the openings of the artillery. And once the bridges are lowered, one will be able to fight the enemy with advantage.

<margin>
a b — for capsizing a vessel
</margin>

<margin>
one man — one man — a mast for capsizing other ships —
</margin>

— s t m a n f c d — There is a pole which is 4 <term>braccia</term> <note>A Florentine unit of measurement, roughly 23 inches or 58 cm</note> long and weighs 8 pounds in total. In its leaning, it takes as much projection over its plane as is half of its length. It is asked: how much of its weight does said pole give to point **m**, and how much to the 2 supports **c** and **d**? If you want to know the truth, take this path: divide the base of the triangle **m n s** in half, and as much as said half **a n** shall be, subtract that much from the base of the pole at the top **s t**, which will be one *braccio* weighing 2 pounds; and this weight remains upon the supports **c** and **d**, and 6 pounds remain upon **m**. Then, consider how far **c** is removed from the perpendicular of **s**, which is **n**, and you will find **c** is distant from **n** by 2 parts, and **d** by 3. Therefore, **c** has 2 parts of the aforementioned weight, and **d** has only one; whereby **c** has 16 ounces upon itself, and 8 remain upon **d**.

## FOR RAISING AND LOWERING — CARRIAGE — BELLS — MACHINE
## OF PRODIGIOUS FORCE

— This one yields a great profit <note>original: "gran profitto"; meaning mechanical advantage or efficiency</note>, that is to say, for raising and lowering. This occurs because each <term>screw</term> <note>original: "vis"</note> is in six doubles. And, in the rotation of the <term>nuts</term> <note>original: "écrou"</note> against the screws, each nut produces a reduction of one-sixth of a <term>braccio</term> <note>A Florentine unit of measurement, roughly 23 inches</note>, so that as there are 6 nuts, they produce one braccio of movement.

— Ensure that the weight you give to the carriage remains on the pivot of the wheel, above the pivot of the wheel below, at a <term>pinion</term> <note>original: "pignon"; a small gear</note> one-sixth thick. And the wheel is 2 and 1/2 braccia high, and the upper one is 2 and 2/3 braccia. Make the pinion with 8 <term>spindles</term> <note>original: "fuseaux"; the vertical rungs of a lantern gear</note>, and the wheel with 64 teeth.

— This is formidable <note>original: "terrible"; implying an awesome or overwhelming power</note>, and if you make the wheels and the pinions with the measurements shown opposite, one hundred pounds of force will pull one million, one hundred and forty-four thousand.

<summary>Leonardo details a vertical lifting mechanism using a system of screws and nuts to achieve high mechanical advantage. He calculates that a specific configuration of gears and pinions can multiply a force of one hundred pounds into over a million pounds of pulling power.</summary>
<keywords>mechanical advantage, gears, screws, lifting machines, force multiplication, braccia, pinions</keywords>

<term>Main spars (Maesstre dellalie)</term>: The primary structural supports or "master" ribs of a wing.
<term>Reinforced rods (Canne armate)</term>: Hollow reeds or canes strengthened internally or externally to increase their load-bearing capacity without adding significant weight.
<term>Cones (Coni)</term>: Mechanical wedges or tapered inserts used to force a specific curvature into the structural rods.

# ARTIFICIAL STONES — FLIGHT BY WING-STROKE.

->— A —<-

— A shall be a crate that can be opened and emptied, in which one can make molds of fine gravel and lime <note>A mixture essentially forming an early type of concrete</note> and let them dry on the ground, and then place them under the water, one on top of the other, to dam the impetuous current of the water.

# FLIGHT WITH FLAPPING WINGS

— This man exerts a force of 200 pounds with his head, and with his hands, he exerts a force of 200 pounds; and that is exactly what the man weighs. The wings *will go*... they will be moved in a cross-wise pattern, similar to the gait of a horse. This is why I maintain that this [system] is better than any [other]. <note>Leonardo often looked to animal locomotion—like the diagonal gait of a horse—to solve mechanical problems in flight.</note>

— Cord of the second joint; it passes to the second step [(pedal)]¹.

— Ladder for climbing up and down; let it be 12 fathoms high <term>brasse: an ancient unit of measurement based on the reach of a man's arms, roughly 6 feet</term>, let the wings span 40 fathoms, let their lift be 8 fathoms, let the body from stern [to] prow be 20 fathoms, 5 high, and let the external frame be made entirely of canes and cloth. <note>Leonardo specifies lightweight materials like cane and fabric to minimize weight while maintaining the massive scale required for lift.</note>

### STLOCLADLE <note>A term used by Leonardo for a specific type of fragmentation bomb or "fire-ball"</note>

<note>Drawing of a spherical explosive device (stlocladle) filled with small gun barrels (scoppietti).</note>

Stlocladles are a ball of one foot <note>approximately 30 cm</note> in size, which is filled and composed of hemp and fish glue. It is filled with the tails <note>breech ends</note> of small guns, and said tails should not exceed the length of a finger. Each tail is made of thin copper covered with sinew or glued paper, and all said tails have their bases <unclear>are</unclear> [?] perforated with a tiny hole. All of them rest against a copper ball, which is filled with various paths in the manner of a labyrinth and then filled with powder. These paths are full of transverse holes which connect with the holes of the small guns. Then, fire is applied in the manner of a bellows <note>or a blowpipe</note>, which fire shoots through 8 holes so that no person can pick it up and <unclear>toss it back</unclear> [?]. When the fire has reached the middle, the small guns immediately begin, one after the other, to spit out their deadly pellets with a terrifying noise. If you wish to use it on a galley <note>a Mediterranean warship</note>, make the small guns out of paper, and fill one and then the other with pitch mixed with powdered sulfur. This will perform three functions: first, it will do damage with the guns; second, it will attach a fire that cannot be extinguished and will burn the wood; and no person will be able to approach it because of the great stench.

### BUFFONICO <note>A "fright-device" or "buffoon-lance," intended more for psychological warfare and disruption than precision shooting</note>

<note>Drawing of a lance-mounted weapon (buffonico) with points 'a' and 'b' labeled.</note>

— a b —

The *buffonico* is an instrument placed on the tip of a lance; it is 2 cubits <note>original: "braca" - approximately 1.2 meters</note> long and 1/8 thick. It is made of iron plate and has a thin, pyramidal tube.

Above the extremity where the fire is to pass, first fill the large tube <note>original: "ianone," likely "canone"</note> well-packed and well-tamped, having beaten the powder through the mouth at **a** and **b**. Then make a small hole one-eighth [of a finger] long. Then put on the cover with the small tube which has a very thin hole. The powder should be fine and mixed with lead filings made with a rasp. Give it fire, and it will be of great terror and damage to the horses and to the enemies.

<summary>Leonardo describes the construction of a 'stlocladle', a sophisticated fragmentation bomb with a labyrinthine internal fuse, and the 'buffonico', a gunpowder-powered lance attachment designed to terrify enemy cavalry.</summary>

# LIFE-SAVING APPARATUS

->— Webbed fabric glove for swimming in the sea.<-

METHOD FOR SAVING ONESELF DURING A STORM OR A SHIPWRECK AT SEA. One must have a leather garment, which should be double-layered at the openings <note>original: "lèvres," literally "lips" or edges of the aperture</note> of the chest for the width of a finger, and likewise double-layered from the waist to the knee; furthermore, it must be made of leather that is secure against exhalation <note>meaning airtight or waterproof</note>. And if it should be necessary to jump into the sea, inflate <note>The original text uses "dégonfle" (deflate), but the context of survival suggests "gonfle" (inflate) was intended</note> the tails of your garment through the chest openings and jump into the sea; let yourself be guided by the waves if there is no shore nearby and you do not know the sea. Always keep the air cane <note>a breathing tube or snorkel</note> in your mouth, which leads into the garment; and if once or twice you need to take in common air <note>atmospheric air</note> and the foam prevents you, draw air from the garment into your mouth¹.

# BELLOWS AND WATER RESERVOIRS.

— Lead¹ — If you make the entry [the passage] of the water from one reservoir into the other such that it is of the same length as the bellows, it will blow very strongly.

— Lead² — Pole [Pivot] on which the cane [socket] of the bellows turns.

— o n³ — Vent [Opening] o, with a spring n that holds it open; and when the channel S T has passed, the opposite bottom makes it stay closed by force.

— R F M N — S T⁴ — These are a type of bellows without leather; they are of admirable utility and of very great durability. Their function [operation] is thus: The bellows is always, from the middle down, that is to say M N, full of water, and during the continual rotation of the bellows, N rises and reaches the vent [the opening] S T, which is made in the second outer casing, as it appears in the instrument below, and the hole o, which is in the reservoir N, comes to meet with the said channel S T; as much water as goes from N to M, just as much air enters through the hole o into the reservoir N, and just as much air leaves the reservoir M as N gives it water. And the air that is chased out of M by the water is that which makes the bellows blow. The said bellows must be of oak, because it resists water over time, and have on the interior a coat [layer] of turpentine and pitch; so that when there is no work, the upper part, which is out of the water, does not come to open <note>meaning the wood should not warp or crack when dry</note>. This bellows is turned with the counterweight of a man who walks upon it, by its ladder <note>likely a reference to a treadwheel mechanism</note>. It would also be of great utility to have it turned by the force of a waterfall. — The bottom of the bellows, below the channel S T, remains fixed, and the rest turns inside it, as a lid would... a box in its lid. Use salt water, so that it does not spoil inside the bellows⁵.

— R F M N — S T — These are types of bellows made without leather <term>sanza corame: bellows typically used flexible leather sides; Leonardo proposes a rigid wooden drum system</term>, and they are of admirable utility and very durable. Their function is as follows: the bellows is always half-full of water from the middle down, namely at M N. In the continuous turning of the bellows, N rises and reaches the vent S T, which is made in the second outer casing as appears in the instrument below. The hole *o* in chamber N then meets the said channel S T. As much water as flows from N to M, an equal amount of air enters through the hole *o* into chamber N; and as much air leaves chamber M as the water that N gives it. It is this air, chased out of M by the water, that causes the bellows to blow. These bellows should be made of oak so that they resist the water over time, and the interior should have a coat of turpentine and pitch <note>a waterproof resinous sealant</note> so that when it is not in use, the upper part which is out of the water does not crack open. This bellows is turned by the counterweight of a man who walks up its ladder <note>a treadmill or treadwheel integrated into the drum</note>; it would also be of great utility to make it rotate by the force of falling water.

— The base of the bellows below the channel S T stays still, and the rest turns inside it, like a box turning within its lid.
Take salt water so that it does not spoil <note>become stagnant or rot the wood</note> inside the bellows.

# ENGINES FOR WAR

— Circontronito [Thundering from all sides] <note>original: "Circontronito." A compound word suggesting a 360-degree thunderous blast</note>. —

— Circonfulgore [Radiating from all sides] <note>original: "Circonfulgore." Suggests a circular flash or lightning-like discharge</note>. —

— The *circunfulgore* is a naval machine. It was an invention of those from Majorca <note>original: "Maiolique." Leonardo often attributed specific inventions to regional experts</note>. One creates a circle of cannons <term>bombardes: early large-caliber cannons used to fire stone or iron balls</term>, in whatever number you please, provided it is not an odd number; for, in order for the shot to be powerful and so the ship does not recoil <note>original: "fuie," literally "flee" or "escape"</note>, it is necessary that one cannon supports the other and acts as an obstacle to it, and *always...* and to do this, one must ignite two cannons [placed] in opposite directions at the same time, so that if one wants to recoil to one side, the other opposes it.

— Vinea — Vinea — Foundation of a vinea —

— The *vinea* <term>vinea: literally "vineyard," a Roman-style mobile protective shed used in sieges to shield soldiers while they approached walls or leveled terrain</term> is a machine that clears the path and levels the embankments.

# JOUSTS. — HELICAL PROPULSER FOR AERONAUTICS¹.

— To joust against.....

— Support — These are in place of [replace] the elephants; with them, one can joust, and one can hold matches <note>slow-burning fuses used to ignite gunpowder</note> [?] to frighten the enemies' horses. One can also place musketeers <note>original: "escopettiers" — soldiers armed with early firearms</note> there who break through any troop.

— Let the outer extremity [the outer contour] of the screw [propeller] be made of iron wire, as thick as a rope, and let there be 8 braccia <note>an Italian unit of measurement, roughly 23 inches or 58 cm</note> from the circumference [the edge] to the center.

— I find that if this instrument made in the form of a screw is well made—that is, made of linen cloth, of which the pores have been stopped with starch—[and] is turned with speed, the said screw will create its own nut in the air and will rise high. Take the example of a wide, thin ruler moved violently through the air; you will see that your arm will be guided by the line of the edge of the said board.
Let the framework of the aforementioned be made of long, thick canes. One can make a small cardboard model of it, whose spindle [the axis] is a thin iron blade, twisted with force; upon being released, it causes the screw to turn.

# MECHANICAL WINGS.

### MECHANICAL WINGS.

->— The same as below¹.<-

->— How the one above should [function].<-

— If you wish to see the true test of the wings, make one out of cardboard reinforced with netting, with the primary spars² made of cane [reed], at least 20 braccia <note>An Italian unit of measurement, roughly 23 inches or 0.6 meters</note> in width and length, and fix it upon a heavy plank [?]³ weighing 200 pounds; it will produce, as illustrated above, a force ready [to act]. But if those arms, which were meant to fall in 4 beats, you make fall in 2, know that the man will leave his position and, moving violently, will reach a second position at the surface of the water.

# ACCOUNTS OF VARIOUS FLIGHTS (BAT AND EAGLE).

## ACCOUNTS OF VARIOUS FLIGHTS (BAT AND EAGLE).

— Weighs 2 ounces, opens [has a wingspan] of 1/2 brasse <note>The 'brasse' is an old unit of measurement, roughly equivalent to the reach of a man's outstretched arms, or about 5.3 feet.</note>.

— Weighs 240 ounces, opens to 3 brasses —

— I say that if the bat <insert>(pipistrelle?)</insert> weighs 2 ounces, and opens by 1/2 brasse, the eagle must, by this comparison [proportionally], open by 60 brasses, and no less; yet, we see by experience that it does not exceed the width of 3 brasses. And it would seem to many, who might not see or have not seen such animals, that one of the two could not fly, estimating that if the bat has its weight and width well proportioned, the eagle does not have enough, and that if [or else if] the eagle is well-suited with its own, the other has too much, an inconvenient [excess] and useless for its purpose [its flight]. But we see both carried with the greatest dexterity by their wings, especially the bat, which, with its rapid evolutions and the way it plays with the air, surpasses the rapid circuits and escapes of flies and gnats.

— The reason why the eagle supports itself with small wings just as the bat does with large ones is [found in] the comparison [of their respective proportions]:
When a single reed has within itself, from its thickness to its length, a proportion such as that which a bundle of similar reeds has, it will be as strong and as resistant as the said bundle is in itself. Indeed, if the bundle is made of 9 heads, and carries 9 ounces, and there are 9 ounces and there are 9 reeds bound together, a single one of the similar reeds of [of which there are] 9 heads will perhaps carry one ounce.

— Let there be, applied to the top of a reed, a weight <unclear>?</unclear>, you will see it bend to the ground; take a thousand of these reeds, tie them tightly together, fix them by the base, level them by the head, and load them; you will see that where, by the first reasoning, it should support about 3 1/2 pounds, it will support more than 40.
So that by this reasoning, the air which supports the bat—which weighs the two hundred and twentieth part of *the eagle*... of the weight of the eagle—[if it] had to be trodden and pressed by the structure of an eagle, it would have to be 60 times larger than its species¹.

---

1. See *The Writings of Leonardo da Vinci*, by Charles Ravaisson-Mollien, p. 12. <note>Ravaisson-Mollien was a 19th-century scholar instrumental in transcribing and translating Leonardo's manuscripts.</note>

# FOLIO 90 (verso).

## Manuscript Facsimile

<note>Study of a mechanical device for scuttling enemy ships (a ship-mounted pile-driver)</note>

A way to sink a ship. But first, it is necessary that they be entangled—that is, fastened together—in such a way that you, from your side, can detach at your will; so that when the ship goes to the bottom, it does not pull yours down with it. And it is done like this: pull a weight up high and then release it, and in falling it will give such a blow as is done to a <term>pile-driver</term><note>original: "palo a castello"; a heavy mechanical hammer used for driving stakes into the ground</note>. And in falling, it pulls back the head of a beam which is on a vertical pivot; and when the upper head of said wood comes back, the lower part goes forward and staves in the ship. But make sure that the wood is sharp, so that in rushing to the blow, the water does not offer resistance to it.

And above all, see to it that the chains <unclear>which</unclear> hold the ships fastened together can be cut at your will from your side, so that the adversary's ship, in sinking, does not pull you down with it.

How the voice of a "laughing echo" should be made, so that for every thing you say, you will be answered by many voices.

150 <term>braccia</term><note>A Florentine unit of measurement, roughly 23 inches or 58 centimeters</note> from one wall to the other; the voice that comes out of the horn is formed on the opposite wall, and from there the second reflects, and from the second to the first, like a ball that bounces between two walls, which diminishes its bounces, and in the same way the voices diminish.

## Printed Transcription

— A WAY TO SINK A SHIP. But first, it is necessary that they be entangled, that is, fastened together, in such a way that you from your side can detach at your will, so that when the ship goes to the bottom it does not pull yours with it. And it is done like this: pull a weight up high and then release it, and in falling it will give such a blow as is done to a pile-driver, and in falling it pulls back the head of a beam which is on a vertical pivot; and when the upper head of said wood comes back, the lower part goes forward and staves in the ship. But make sure that the wood is sharp, so that in rushing to the blow the water does not offer resistance to it.

— And above all, see to it that the chains [?] that hold the ships fastened together can be cut at your will from your side, so that the adversary's ship in sinking does not pull you down with it.

— Test at the mill how much you weigh by applying force with your shoulders against something and keep your feet upon the scale.

— The voice, having departed from the man and being struck against the wall, will flee upward if there is a retainer above said wall at a right angle; the upper face will send the voice back toward its source.

— How the voice of a "laughing echo" should be made, so that for every thing you say, you will be answered by many voices.

— 150 braccia from one wall to the other; the voice that comes out of the horn is formed on the opposite wall, and from there the second reflects, and from the second to the first, like a ball that bounces between two walls, which diminishes its bounces, and in the same way the voices diminish.

# FOLIO 1 (recto).

<note>This page contains a facsimile reproduction of Leonardo da Vinci's manuscript featuring mirror script and optical diagrams, followed by a printed diplomatic transcription in Italian.</note>

<note>The following is a translation of Leonardo's mirror-written notes on the nature of vision.</note>

->On the Eye<-

Why nature did not make the visual power equal throughout the visual faculty.

Nature did not make the visual power equal throughout the visual faculty, but gave to that faculty a power that is greater the closer it approaches its center. <note>Leonardo believed that the center of the eye was the point of highest resolution and strength, much like the modern understanding of the fovea.</note> This was done so as not to break the law given to all other powers, which are more effective the closer they are to their center. This is seen in the act of percussion <note>The force of an impact</note> of any body, and in the supports of the arms of a balance, where the weight diminishes its gravity as it moves closer to the center. It is seen in columns, walls, and pillars; it is seen in heat and in all other natural powers.

Why nature made the pupil convex, that is, raised like part of a ball.

Nature made the surface of the light <note>original: "lucie"; here referring to the pupil or the cornea through which light enters</note> placed in the eye with a convex shape so that surrounding things can imprint their images <note>original: "similitudini"; Leonardo used this term to describe the 'species' or visual representations of objects traveling through the air</note> with larger angles, which could not happen if the eye were flat.

---

->ON THE EYE<-

**WHY NATURE DID NOT MAKE THE VISUAL POWER EQUAL THROUGHOUT THE VISUAL FACULTY.**
— Nature did not make the visual power equal throughout the visual faculty, but gave to that faculty a power that is greater the closer it approaches its center. This was done so as not to break the law given to all other powers, which are more effective the closer they are to their center. This is seen in the act of percussion of any body, and in the supports of the arms of a balance, where the weight diminishes its gravity as it moves closer to the center. It is seen in columns, walls, and pillars; it is seen in heat and in all other natural powers.

**WHY NATURE MADE THE PUPIL CONVEX, THAT IS, RAISED LIKE PART OF A BALL.**
— Nature made the surface of the light placed in the eye with a convex shape so that surrounding things can imprint their images with larger angles, which could not happen if the eye were flat.

<sig>I</sig>

<term>Visual power (potentia visiva)</term>: The active force or ability of the eye to perceive images.
<term>Images (similitudini)</term>: The visual "likenesses" of objects that Leonardo believed traveled through the air to reach the eye.

<summary>Leonardo explains that visual acuity is strongest at the center of the eye, following a universal law of physics, and argues that the eye's convex shape is necessary to capture a wider field of view.</summary>
<keywords>optics, anatomy of the eye, visual power, convexity, geometry of vision, Leonardo da Vinci</keywords>

# [THE SPREADING OF RAYS FROM LUMINOUS BODIES]

-> [Figure: ] b c o  n a m — <-

## ON THE EYE

### WHY THE RAYS OF LUMINOUS BODIES BECOME LARGER THE FURTHER THEY ARE FROM THEIR SOURCE.

— The rays of luminous bodies grow larger as they move further from their origins. This is proven: Let **a** be the luminous body whose image <note>original: "simulacre"; Leonardo uses this to mean the visual representation or 'species' of an object</note> is imprinted in the pupil of the eye of the observer, and we shall say that such an impression is made in the pupil **c**, and the same image is also imprinted in the thickness of the upper lid <insert>[of the eye (the eyelid)]</insert> **b**, and also <note>original: "etiam"</note> in the lower lid **o**. By the upper and lower lids, the secondary images are reflected into the pupil of the eye **c**, but to the pupil receiving these three said images—which are divided by the images of the eyelids (in this case nearly closed)—it appears that the image <insert>[images]</insert> of the light source, imprinted in the thickness of the eyelids, are as if truly subdivided, and such divisions are pyramidal, because the intervals of the eyelids are also pyramidal. And because to the pupil receiving these 3 images, it seems that the 2 images which bounce back into it from the lids are joined from above and below to the middle image, which represents the luminous body, it seems to this pupil that image **b** is at **a n**, and image **o** is at **a m**, and it appears to it that both images are divided by the image of the light **a**. And because when the lips <insert>[the edges]</insert> of the eyelids are closed together, it is necessary that the moisture <term>aquosity: the watery substance or tear film</term> which continually keeps the lids soft in their friction against the eye, fills the angle *du* which is generated <insert>[formed]</insert> at the contact of the lids with the pupil of the eye, and [that] the surface of this moisture is concave, as is proven in the fourth [proposition] of the eighth [book] on waters, where it is said *always* (the contact that water has with its moist bank will always have a concave surface) (and if such a bank is dry, then the surface of the water bordering it will be convex). Therefore, such an angle being created by the contact the eyelid has with *the surface of* its pupil, the surface of the moisture filling such an angle will have a concave shape; and because every concave mirror shows the image of its object upside down within the pyramidal convergence of its rays, it follows definitively that the weights, or eyelids, of the eyes, reflected in such a cavity at the same time as the image of the light, will show these eyelids upside down. This is the cause why, the pupil being within the convergence of the pyramidal rays of the concave mirror, the pupil sees the radiating pyramids <insert>[formed of rays]</insert> of the intervals of the eyelids upside down; and this is the true cause of the rays of luminous bodies which, the more they widen, the more it appears they approach the eye. Now, such a demonstration must be divided into its parts to make it more intelligible, by first placing its concepts and other propositions necessary for such proof, etc.

<note>Leonardo is explaining the "starburst" effect seen when squinting at a light source. He correctly identifies that the tear film at the edge of the eyelid acts as a tiny liquid lens or mirror, though his explanation relies on his specific theories of "pyramidal" light propagation.</note>

<summary>Leonardo explains why light sources appear to have radiating "rays" when viewed through squinted eyes, attributing the effect to reflections and refractions caused by the moisture (tear film) on the edges of the eyelids acting as a concave mirror.</summary>
<keywords>optics, light rays, eyelids, tear film, concave mirror, pyramidal rays, vision, reflection</keywords>

-> **ON THE EYE** <-

**WHY THE RAYS OF LUMINOUS BODIES BECOME SO MUCH LARGER THE FURTHER THEY ARE FROM THEIR SOURCE.**

— The rays of luminous bodies grow so much larger as they move further from their origins — this is proven. Let **a** be the luminous body whose image <note>original: "simulacro"; Leonardo uses this to mean the visual representation or 'species' of an object</note> is imprinted in the pupil of the eye of the observer, and we shall say that such an impression is made in the pupil **c**. The same image is also imprinted in the thickness of the upper lid **b** and also <note>original: "hedetham" (etiam)</note> in the lower lid **o**. From the upper and lower lids, the secondary images are reflected into the pupil of the eye **c**. But to the pupil receiving these three said images—which are divided by the images of the eyelids (which in such a case are nearly closed)—it appears that the images of the light source, imprinted in the thickness of the eyelids, are truly subdivided. Such divisions are pyramidal <note>shaped like a cone or pyramid of light</note> because the intervals between the eyelids are also pyramidal. And because to the pupil receiving these three images, it seems that the two images which bounce back into it from the lids are joined above and below to the middle image representing the luminous body, it appears to this pupil that image **b** is at **a n**, and image **o** appears to be at **a m**, and that both images are divided from the image of the light **a**. 

And because when the lips <insert>the edges</insert> of the eyelids are closed together, it is necessary that the moisture <term>aquosity: the watery substance or tear film that lubricates the eye</term> which continually keeps the lids moistened and, in the rubbing of the eye, that this humidity fills the angle that is created in the contact that the lids make with the pupil of the eye. The surface of such moisture is concave, as is proven in the 4th [chapter] of the 8th [book] *On Waters*, where it says *always*: "the contact that water has with its moistened bank will always have a concave surface" (and if such a bank is dry, then the surface of the water bordering it will be convex). Therefore, finding such an angle created by the contact that the eyelid has with the surface of its pupil, the surface of the moisture filling such an angle will have a concave shape. 

And because every concave mirror shows the image of its object upside down within the pyramidal convergence of its rays, it follows that the weights <insert>or eyelids</insert> of the eyes, mirrored in such concavity together with the image of the light, will show those eyelids upside down. This is the cause why—the pupil being within the convergence of the pyramidal rays of the concave mirror—the pupil sees the radiant pyramids of the intervals of the eyelids upside down. And this is the true cause of the rays of luminous bodies, which dilate so much more the closer they seem to approach the eye. Now, this demonstration should be divided into its parts to make it better known, placing first its concepts and other propositions necessary for such proof, etc.

<summary>Leonardo explains why light sources appear to have "rays" or "streaks" when we squint, attributing the effect to reflections in the concave moisture (tears) trapped between the eyelid and the pupil.</summary>
<keywords>optics, vision, eyelids, reflection, concave mirrors, aquosity, light rays, anatomy of the eye</keywords>

# [HOW THE EYE SEES OBJECTS. — ENTRY OF RAYS INTO THE EYE. — SPECTACLES.]

-> [1st figure:] a o à ó — [2nd fig.:] r m p s n p q — [3rd fig.:] a n m b c d — [4th fig.:] f o r t p c a b d. <-

Do you wish to understand the manner in which the rays of luminous bodies are caused by the image <note>original: "simulacre"; the visual representation or "species" of an object</note> of these bodies, which are imprinted in the thickness of the lips of the eyes [the edges of the eyelids], which reflect into the pupil of these eyes? [Consider] the eye with the pupil; you do not see these lids, and you see the lights without rays.

## ON THE EYE

### WHETHER THE IMAGE [IMAGE] OR SIMULACRUM HAS A DETERMINED POSITION ABOVE THE EYE, OR NOT.

— The images of immobile objects have determined positions above the immobile eyes. This is proven: Let the object be **à b** [**à ó** (1st figure)], which sends the ray by the 7th [proposition]; it sends the ray to **[à] a**, by the shortest path, to the pupil **a o**; the opposite extremity of the object does the same [**ó**, by the ray] **o [ó] o**. Therefore, the image of the extremity **a [à]** is not imprinted in position **o** of the pupil, and **ó** is likewise not imprinted in **a**.

### WHETHER OBJECTS SEND THEIR IMAGES TO THE EYE WITH MEMBERS PROPORTIONED AS THEY ARE IN THEMSELVES.

— Objects do not send images to the eye with the parts proportioned as they are in that object; this is proven by the ninth [proposition], as well as how, among things of equal size, the most distant appears the smallest. Let the eye be **a** [(3rd figure)], and let its object be **b c d**. I say by the aforementioned 9th that **d [and] b**, parts of this object, will appear smaller than part **c**, because they are further from the eye than **c**, as is proven by the definition of the circle **a c**; **n m** is a sector of it, and [the distance to the center from each of the points] **b, d**, exceeds the distance from the periphery of the sector to the said eye.

### WHETHER THE SPECIES OF OBJECTS ARE TAKEN BY THE VISUAL VIRTUE AT THE SURFACE OF THE EYE, OR IF THEY PASS WITHIN.

— The glasses of spectacles <note>original: "lunettes"; referring to early eyeglasses</note> show us how the images of objects stop at the surface of these glasses, and from that surface penetrate, by bending [refracting] at the surface of the eye, a surface through which it is [thus] possible for the eye to see the shapes of the aforementioned objects. It is proven that this is possible because such a surface is a common boundary between the air and the eye, because it separates the aqueous humor <term>humeur albugineuse: the clear, watery fluid between the cornea and the lens</term> from the air, and separates the air from the aqueous humor. And if we wish to assert that the species <note>original: "espèces"; the formal qualities or visual data of an object</note> of said objects stop at the surface of the spectacles, one would say that in the spectacles of the elderly the thing will appear much larger than the real thing; and if this did not depend on the interposition of the glass between the eye and the object, then that object would show itself in its natural size; therefore, [the contrary being the case] it is a manifest sign *that the convergence of the species of any object, which is cut by the interposition of transparent bodies, will be imprinted on the surface of these bodies and will generate there a new convergence, leading the images of the objects to the eye.*

### HOW THE RECTITUDE OF THE CONVERGENCE OF SPECIES BENDS [REFRACTS] UPON ENTERING THE EYE.

— The straightness of the convergence of rays, when they penetrate the eye, bends [refracts], and this is the reason why at an equal distance the eye sees the object larger than the rules of the painters' perspective would dictate. And the cause is that the eye receives upon itself the intersection of the species **a b** at **o p** [4th figure], and the perspectivist, imagining that such rays are straight, cuts the rays at **r t**, and thus finds the things produced by his perspective much smaller than they are judged by the eye. And if, for the sake of argument, one said that the object **a b** would appear larger than it is, given that the thing coming to the eye by the lines **a o f** and **b p f** would appear in the space **c d** seen by the straight lines **f o c** and **f p d**, one would demonstrate that this is impossible; because if you wished to shoot an arrow with the power of the lateral rays **f o c**, you would believe you were striking with that arrow in position **c**, but it would strike in **a**.

<summary>This page examines the geometric optics of the eye, arguing that the eye perceives objects differently than linear perspective suggests due to the refraction of light at the eye's surface and through lenses. Leonardo demonstrates that the curvature of the eye and the use of spectacles alter the perceived size and position of objects.</summary>

->THE VISUAL FACULTY COMMON TO THE ENTIRE PUPIL. — THE INVERSION AND RIGHTING OF IMAGES.<-

[Figure 1:] f of k c h a n r v p o t m b q — [Figure 2:] d b a c — Crystalline sphere <note>The lens of the eye, which Leonardo believed was a perfect sphere located in the center of the eyeball.</note> placed in the middle of the eye. — Here the opinion is put forward that the pupil possesses the visual faculty <note>The power or ability to see.</note> in every part of its width, and this is indeed the case; without this, every demonstration collapses. — [Figure 3:] 2^a g d a n m o p l k h q r q s t v x y c. — Let an instrument be found that necessarily produces the same effect, and thus you will have found the true internal shape of the eyes. — [Figure 4:] a b c d — Every point of the pupil sees the whole object, and every point of the object sees the whole pupil.

### ON THE HUMAN EYE.

### HOW THE SPECIES <term>Species: In Renaissance optics, these are the "likenesses" or "images" shed by objects that travel through the air to the eye.</term> OF ANY BODY WHICH PASS THROUGH SOME OPENING <insert>air-hole, *spiraculo*</insert> TO THE EYE, ARE IMPRINTED UPSIDE DOWN IN ITS PUPIL, AND THE SENSE SEES THEM UPRIGHT.

— The pupil of the eye, which through the smallest round opening receives the species of bodies placed beyond that opening, *always* receives them upside down, and the visual faculty always sees them upright as they [actually] are. This arises because the said species *give themselves* <note>Pass through or transmit themselves.</note> through the center of the crystalline sphere placed in the middle of the eye, and beyond and within this center, they meet at a point, and then diverge to the opposite surface of this sphere, without deviating from their straight path; and on this surface, the species direct themselves according to the object that caused them, and from there [and there] they are taken by the impressionability <gloss>original: *inprensiua* — the receptive power of the eye</gloss> and sent to the common sense <note>The *sensus communis*, a theoretical part of the brain where all sensory data was thought to be processed and judged.</note>, where they are judged. It is proved that it is so: let **a n** [Figure 1] be the pupil of the eye **k h**, and let **p** be the small round opening made in the paper with the fine point of a stylus [punch] and let the object placed beyond this opening be **m b**; I say that the upper part of such an object cannot come to the upper part of the pupil of the eye by the straight line **m a**, because at **v** the passage is blocked for it by the interposition of the paper; but this upper extremity **m**, with a straight course, passes through the opening, beyond, to the lower part **n** of the pupil, or otherwise said of the crystalline sphere, and from there directs its course to the center of this sphere, then rises to the upper part of the opposite side, and from there runs to the common sense, as has been said.

### BELOW IS SET FORTH THE EXPERIMENT FROM WHICH THE CERTAINTY OF THIS NEW INVESTIGATION WAS BORN.

Let **g d** [Figure 3] be the eye of which the pupil **a p** sees, through the opening **q** (made in the paper **r s**) the object **t c**; I say that if you move the stylus **l q** from above to below the pupil, near this pupil along the line **k h**, it will appear outside the opening **q** that the movement of the stylus is [takes place in a direction] contrary to its true movement. The reason is that the stylus touching the line **a c**, it touches the highest line there is inside the opening **q**, and the lowest there is outside that opening; and when the stylus descends, it touches the line **n y**, that is to say the [second] highest in the opening, and the lowest outside the opening, and so continuing to lower the stylus in the opening, in front of the pupil, you mark the opposite outside of this opening, because if inside you descend through the fronts [ends] of the lines **a n m o p**, you raise [by that very act] outside at their fronts [ends] the lines **c y x v t**. Therefore, the stylus that touches the line **a c** occupies position **c**, and if you descend with this stylus to line **n**, you occupy position **y** outside the opening, and so on until the end of the movement.

### HOW AND IN WHAT MANNER THE PUPIL TAKES THE SIMULACRA <note>Images or representations.</note> OF OBJECTS WITHOUT THE INTERVENTION [INTERPOSITION] OF THE SAID AIR-HOLE.

— If in the second demonstration the pupil **a p** [Figure 3] receives at **p** the upper part of the simulacrum **t**, by means of [through the intervention of] the opening **q**, and if you remove the intervention of this opening, the simulacrum **t** will be imprinted at **a** and also at **p**, because every point of the pupil sees the whole simulacrum **t c**.

### [Facsimile Transcription]

#### on perspective

The pupil of the eye, which through the smallest round opening <term>spiraculo: literally a "breathing hole," used here to mean a pinhole or aperture</term> receives the species <term>species: the "likenesses" or "images" shed by objects that travel through the air to the eye</term> of bodies placed beyond that opening, always receives them upside down; and yet the visual faculty always sees them upright as they are. This arises because the said species pass through the center of the crystalline sphere <note>The lens of the eye, which Leonardo believed was a perfect sphere located in the center of the eyeball</note> placed in the middle of the eye; and after and within this center, they unite in a point and then dilate <note>spread out</note> onto the opposite surface of said sphere, without deviating from their straightness. On such a surface, the species are directed according to the object from which they are caused, and from there they are taken by the impressionable faculty and sent to the common sense <term>senso comune: the part of the brain where all sensory data was thought to be processed and judged</term> where they are judged. Let it be proved to be so. # [THE INVERSION AND RIGHTING OF IMAGES. — LENSES. — THE DIMINUTION OF IMAGES BY DISTANCE.]

[1st figure: ] a b c d e f l n v o p q r q s t i g h — [2nd figure: ] n a c d b e r t f h p k r g q l — [3rd figure: ] a b c d e n o f p — Through this experiment one will come to the knowledge of lenses <note>original: "lunettes," referring here to magnifying glasses or spectacles</note>, because when they are placed between the eye and the object, the images are formed there of the same size, or much larger, or much smaller than that object [just as occurs within the eye].

### THE HUMAN EYE

#### HOW UPRIGHT THINGS DO NOT APPEAR UPRIGHT TO THE VISUAL FACULTY UNLESS THEIR SPECIES PASS THROUGH TWO INTERSECTIONS.

— The object **k** arriving at **b** [1st figure], the surface of the cornea <note>original: "prunelle," the outer surface of the eye</note>, gives itself to the visual faculty <term>virtu visuelle: the power or "virtue" of sight</term> through 2 intersections, that is **n** and **s**, entering first from **b** to **d**, the pupil, and from **d** to **f**. It would pass through the intersection **n**, the center of the sphere of the cornea **c o l a b v**; but it first meets the crystalline sphere <note>the lens</note> before finishing its pyramid **c d n**. This pyramid **c d n**, upon its impact, is cut at **e f**, where the base of another pyramid is generated, that is **e f o**; and the sides of this pyramid intersect at **o**, and the image <term>simulacre: the visual representation or "likeness" of the object</term> **e f** passes to the opposite part of the vitreous sphere <note>the humor or fluid filling the eye</note>, and the right side **f** becomes the left at **q**, and the left side **e** becomes the right at **r**. Then, the 2nd intersection occurs at **s**, which is to say that the vitreous sphere casts its pyramid **v q r s**, and the right **r** passes through the intersection **s** and becomes the left at **i**, and the left **q** becomes the right at **g**. By this path, the eye, as an instrument, carries to the end of one of the optic nerves the upright thing as upright, and the left as left.

#### SECOND OPINION, WITH THE SAME 2 INTERSECTIONS.

— It is not denied that all the species that come to the surface of the cornea **a n b** [2nd figure] pass through the pupil **c d**, as has been proven; and further, it is granted that all the lines of these species which pass the center of the sphere starting at the said cornea are exchanged from right to left and left to right. That is to say, the right **a**, having passed **e**, the center of the sphere of the cornea, becomes the left at **t**, and **b** becomes the right at **r**, and grows significantly because the entire space **a b** comes into **r t**, and **r t** receives a size that appears similar to **a b**, as is proven in perspective. Then, it is not denied that the vitreous sphere **r t k h** renders it upright <note>Leonardo is debating if the image is "redressed" or flipped again</note> within the pyramid **k h r**, and, if you wish, inverts it after the intersection of the sides of this pyramid at points **g l**. Therefore, **a**, on the left, will become right at **t** after the intersection **e**, will descend as right to **k**, will pass through the second intersection **r**, and return to the left at point **g**.

#### WHY THINGS DIMINISHED BY THE PERSPECTIVE POINT APPEAR MUCH SMALLER THAN NATURAL ONES, EVEN THOUGH THEY MEASURE THE SAME SIZE AS THE DIMINISHED ONES.

— The large **a b** [2nd figure] is transformed into the small **r t**, and, with the same smallness, penetrates into **k h** and ends at **g l**, further diminished. This acts in the likeness of a concave mirror [3rd figure] **a b c d**, to which the object **e n** is opposed; one sees the reflected object there, which is increased in the entire space **b c**, and the second object **f p** does the same. But **e n** has its image upright in the mirror, while **f p** has its own upside down, and these images will be of equal size, their causes being equal. But before I affirm such a proposition, I will perform the experiment.

3. (3rd figure): Around the circumference of the figure, then from right to left.
