# [THE INVERSION AND RIGHTING OF IMAGES. — LENSES. — THE DIMINUTION OF IMAGES BY DISTANCE.]

[1st figure]: a b c d e f l n v o p q r q s t i g h — [2nd figure]: n a c d b e r t f h p k r g q l — [3rd figure]: a b c d e n o f p — By this proof, one will come to the knowledge of spectacles <note>original: "ochiali"; Leonardo is connecting the anatomy of the eye to the function of external lenses</note>, because when they are placed between the eye and the object, they make that object appear equal, or much larger, or smaller.

-> THE HUMAN EYE <-

**HOW RIGHT-HAND THINGS DO NOT APPEAR AS SUCH TO THE VISUAL FACULTY IF THEIR IMAGES DO NOT PASS THROUGH TWO INTERSECTIONS.**
The object **k** reaching the surface **b** of the light of the eye <note>original: "luce dellochio," referring to the cornea or the clear outer part of the eye</note> presents itself to the visual faculty <term>virtu visiua: the medieval/Renaissance concept of the "power" of sight located in the brain</term> through 2 intersections, namely **n** and **s**, entering first from **b** into the pupil **d**, and from **d** to **f** (and it would pass through the intersection **n**, the center of the sphere of light **c o l a b v**, but it first encounters the crystalline sphere <note>the lens</note> before its pyramid **c d n** finishes). At that impact, said pyramid **c d n** is cut at **e f**, where the base of another pyramid is generated, namely **e f o**, and the sides of this pyramid intersect at **o**, and the image <term>simulacro: a visual likeness or "species" of the object</term> **r s** passes to the opposite part of the vitreous sphere <note>the vitreous humor filling the eyeball</note>. The right side **f** becomes left at **q**, and the left **e** becomes right at **r**. Then the 2nd intersection occurs at **s**, meaning that the vitreous sphere casts its pyramid **v q r s**, and the right **r** passes through the intersection **s** and becomes left at **i**, and the left **q** becomes right at **g**. By this path, the instrument of the eye delivers to the front of one of the optic nerves the right-hand thing as right, and the left as left. —

**ACCORDING TO A SECOND OPINION WITH THE SAME 2 INTERSECTIONS.**
It is not denied that <insert>ch co que</insert> all the images <note>original: "spetie," the "species" or visual forms emitted by objects</note> that come to the surface of the light **a n b** pass through the pupil **c d**, as proven; and it is further granted that all the lines of these images which pass the center of the sphere beginning at said light do not swap from right to left and left to right—that is, that **a** on the right, having passed the center of the sphere of light, becomes left at **t**, and **b** becomes right at **r**, and increases greatly because the entire space **a b** comes into **r t**, and **r t** receives a size that appears similar to **a b**, as proven in perspective. — Then it is not denied that the vitreous sphere **r t k h** renders it upright within the pyramid **k h r**, and then reverses it after the intersection of the sides of that pyramid at points **g l**. Therefore, the left will become right at **t** after the first intersection **e**, and will descend as left as far as **k**, and will pass through the 2nd intersection **r**, and will return to being left at point **g**.

**WHY THINGS DIMINISHED BY THE PERSPECTIVE POINT APPEAR MUCH SMALLER THAN NATURAL ONES, EVEN THOUGH THEY MEASURE THE SAME SIZE AS THE SAID DIMINISHED ONES —**
The large **a b** refers to the small **r t**, and with the same smallness it penetrates into **k h** and ends in **g l**, still diminished. This is like a concave mirror **a b c d**, before which the object **e n** is placed; one sees that object mirrored and enlarged in the whole space **b c**. The same happens with the 2nd object **f p**, but the object **e n** has its image upright in the mirror, while **f p** has its image upside down. Such images will be of equal size if their causes are equal. But before I confirm such a proposition, I will perform an experiment. —

# FOLIO 3 (verso).

<note>Manuscript facsimile containing Leonardo da Vinci's mirror writing and optical diagrams</note>

->The human eye<-

->On conducting an experiment to show how the visual power employs the instrument of the eye<-

To conduct an experiment showing how the visual power <note>original: "virtu visiua" — the faculty or force of sight</note> receives the images <note>original: "spetie" — species; in Renaissance optics, these were the formal likenesses or "similitudes" emitted by objects</note> of objects from the eye, its instrument: a glass ball shall be made, five-eighths of a braccio <note>a Florentine unit of measurement, roughly 23 inches or 58 cm</note> in diameter. Then, let as much be cut away from one side so that the face may be placed into it as far as the ears. Then, at the bottom, let there be fixed a box-bottom of one-third of a braccio, which has a hole in the middle that is four times larger than the pupil of the eye, or thereabouts, for it does not matter. In addition to this, let a small, thin glass ball be fixed, one-sixth of a braccio in diameter. Having done this, fill everything with clear, lukewarm water, and put your face into this water and look into the ball; and note, and you will see that such an instrument will send the images of the objects <insert>s t</insert> to the eye just as the eye sends them to the visual power.

Here it is explained that the visual power is at the end of the optic nerves, of which <insert>h m</insert> is one. Therefore, we shall say that the visual power <insert>m</insert> cannot see an object <insert>a</insert> <note>Leonardo uses "stancho" here, likely meaning "distant" or "fixed" in this context</note> from that left side unless the ray of the image of such an object passes through the center of two spheres: namely, the sphere of light <insert>d k e</insert> <note>the cornea/aqueous humor</note> and through the sphere of the vitreous humor <insert>x y t v</insert>. Thus, the path of the ray will be <insert>a e r v z x</insert>. Therefore, the visual power <insert>m</insert> will see the object <insert>a</insert> represented to it at <insert>x</insert> on the left; and thus the instrument of the eye cannot return such an object to its same position except by means of two intersections which pass through the axis of the eye, as has been demonstrated.

The object <insert>a</insert> sends its likeness to the visual power through the line <insert>a r</insert> to the part <insert>r</insert> of the light <insert>c d f</insert>; then it enters through the pupil <insert>o</insert> and makes the intersection at <insert>o</insert>, and passes to the vitreous sphere at <insert>v</insert>, and penetrates that sphere with the part <insert>v q</insert>, and passes through the intersection <insert>n</insert>, and terminates in <insert>k</insert> at the front of the optic nerve <insert>k h l</insert>, from which it is then referred to the common sense <note>original: "senso comune" — the Aristotelian internal sense where all perceptions are integrated</note>. # [DILATION AND CONTRACTION OF THE PUPIL; THE REVERSAL OF IMAGES IN THE MIRROR].

[1st figure (1) h n a m g r q  pt q u — [2nd fig:] a b s c d — This figure should be made square. — [3rd fig. (2)] p p a b n m n o m — If the eyes together see a spherical object with a diameter smaller than the space interposed between the pupils of the eyes, they will see this spherical [object] beyond the diameter, and all the more so as it is closer to these eyes; consequently, this sphere will appear smaller than it is to the central lines of the visual power <note>original: "virtu visuelle" — the faculty of sight</note> of the eyes.

### ON THE HUMAN EYE

— If the cornea <note>original: "prunelle" — Leonardo often uses this to refer to the outer part of the eye or the iris</note> of the eye has its pupil which increases and decreases according to whether there is an excess or lack of brightness from what shines before it, it is necessary that every other object appears to grow or show itself larger or smaller to that pupil. And it is proven: Let h g [1st figure] be the cornea, n m its large pupil, which sees the object q u on the convexity of the cornea between r q; then let "a" be the *cornea* <insert>pupil</insert> diminished, and thus the object q u will show itself diminished on the convexity of the cornea, in the space p t.

### WHY THE MIRROR CHANGES, IN THE IMAGES OF OBJECTS, THE RIGHT SIDES TO THE LEFT, AND THE LEFT TO THE RIGHT.

The image <note>original: "simulacre" — a likeness or representation</note> of every object exchanges [a] in the mirror its right part at the meeting of the left of the object which is mirrored [reflected], and likewise the left at that of the right; it is proven that it is necessarily so, because every natural action is performed by nature in the shortest way and in the shortest time possible. Let a b [2nd figure] be a face that sends its image to the mirror c d; this face will have another face in this mirror turned toward it, which will have the left eye c at the meeting of the right eye a, and likewise the right eye d at the meeting of the left eye b. And if, for the sake of argument, one said that the right eye of the image *corresponds* by a *very short* line to the meeting of the right of the object, we would lead the lines from the right of the image to the right of the object, and likewise from the left to the left, lines which are a d and c d [b c], which are seen to be intersected; and it is proven that of all intersected lines, the right end always has its opposite end in the left side of the other. Now, such an effect is not produced by the shortest line, since the diameter <note>Leonardo uses "diameter" here to mean the diagonal</note> of a square [rectangle] is always longer than its side, and here a d is the diameter of the square [rectangle] a b c d, of which a c is one of the sides. Thus is concluded what was necessary for the proof of such an effect. And this effect in the mirror is that of someone who would look at you, that is to say, of someone having the left eye opposite your right, becoming by a miracle from left to right, just as letters do when they are printed, and as wax taking the impression of a carnelian <note>a reddish gemstone used for signet rings to stamp wax seals</note>.

### [THE VISUAL POWER COMMON TO THE ENTIRE PUPIL.]

---

->[2nd figure:] s t n m a b r cd g pq — [3rd fig.:] v r x an c h t g l mf¹ —<-

# THE HUMAN EYE

Whether it be true that every part of the pupil possesses the visual power <note>original: "vertu visuelle"; the capacity or faculty of sight</note>, and that such power is not reduced to a single point—as those who treat of perspective claim, asserting that all species <note>original: "espèces"; the visual forms or images of objects traveling through the air</note> of objects come to the eye in pyramids and are reduced to an angle in which the judgment of the thing seen is made—experience here shows the contrary.

Let one experiment thus: Let a hole be made with a large needle in a paper, roughly the size of a grain of millet, and let this paper be placed before the pupil of the eye at a distance of a third or a quarter of a cubit <note>original: "brasse"; a historical unit of length roughly equal to an arm's length</note>. Look through this hole *r* at the air *p q* [2nd figure], then interpose this needle or a similar straw between the pupil of your eye and the said hole in the paper; but ensure the needle is close to your eye, so that it touches the tips of your eyelashes; then, move the needle down, up, right, and left, in front of your pupil, and you will clearly see, in the air beyond the hole, the image of this needle making all the movements contrary to those you make with the needle between your eye and the aforementioned hole.

The cause of what is stated above consists in the fact that the visual power is spread throughout the entire pupil of the eye, and at every point of this pupil, the simulacra <note>original: "simulacres"; the visual representations or "ghosts" of objects</note> of objects placed before the eye are recognized; if it were not so, the [aforementioned] experiment would not take place. It is proved thus: let the circle *s t* [2nd figure] represent the pupil of the eye; let *a b c d* be the paper placed before the eye, distant from it by 1/3 of a cubit, in which a hole *r* the size of a grain of millet is made; let *n* be the thickness of the needle, placed as close as possible to the pupil of the eye, [moving] from *n* to *m* with a slow movement; you will then see the likeness of this needle move in the air, on the other side of the hole, from *q* to *p*, that is to say, in a contrary movement. This arises because, at the start of such a movement, the needle which is at *n* above, has its image pass through the hole *r* and occupies the air at the bottom part at *q*, and when the needle descends from *n* to *m*, its image in the air rises from *q* to *p*. And always the intersection of the straight lines of such species—or, if you prefer, shadows—of the needle, will be made at point *g*; thus every movement made in any direction beyond such a hole will be reversed. Now, if the visual power were not at *s*, you would not see the image of the needle at *q*, and if it were not at *t*, you would not see it at *p*; the same is true of every part of the pupil.

<margin>The adversary says that vision occurs in an angle, that is, at a single point, and that such a point will yield the same experimental result as the needle with the hole in the paper, and that it cannot be otherwise. Let there be, he says, the point *r* in the pupil *v x* [3rd figure], let *c h g l* be the paper in which the hole *t* is made, let *a* be the needle descending to *n*; one will also see its image move beyond the hole in a contrary movement, and it will go from *f* to rise to *m*. To that one, it is replied that he has not remembered the [question?] of the first, in which it was stated how all vision made by the eye in a uniform medium, and made by the straight line with the needle *a* placed before point *r*, will occupy point *m* via the straight line *r m*, and when it has descended from *a* to *n*, it will occupy the position *r f*, the point *f*. Therefore, we have demonstrated our proposition.</margin>

## [THE PUPIL IN RELATION TO THE BRAIN VENTRICLE CALLED THE *IMPRESSIVE* FACULTY. — DILATION AND CONTRACTION OF THE PUPIL.]

— On the great variation made by nocturnal animals from their large pupil during the night to their smaller pupil. — Proportion of the ventricle of impressions <note>original: "inprensiva"; referring to the *sensus communis* or the part of the brain where sensory data is received</note> located in the brain of animals relative to their pupil. — How an object appears larger when seen through a larger pupil.

# ON THE HUMAN EYE.

Next comes the eye of nocturnal animals, which see more by night than by day. And this stems in large part, as has been said previously, from the fact that there is a much greater difference between the increase and decrease of their pupil than there is for diurnal animals; for if the human pupil doubles its diameter at night—which is to say it increases to 4 times the area of the daytime pupil—the diameter of the pupil of the horned owl or tawny owl increases 10 times its daytime size, which in total means 100 times the area of the daytime pupil.

— Besides this, the ventricle located in the human brain, called the *impressive faculty* <note>original: "inprensiva"</note>, is more than 10 times the size of the entire human eye, of which the pupil—where sight is produced—is less than a thousandth part; whereas in the owl, the nocturnal pupil is much larger than the ventricle of its *impressive faculty* located in the brain. Therefore, regarding the proportion for man of the *impressive faculty* to his pupil, the *impressive faculty* is ten thousand times larger than the pupil, compared to the owl, in which they are almost equal. And this *impressive faculty* of man, compared to that of the owl, is like a large hall receiving light through a small hole, compared to a small room that is entirely open. For in the large hall, it is like night at midday, and in the small, open room, it is like day at midnight, provided the weather is not cloudy. And along with this, more powerful causes will be shown by means of the anatomy of the eyes and the *impressive faculty* of these two animated beings, man and the owl.

— An object will appear greater in light and in size when seen through a larger pupil. This can be tested in our own eyes: if you make a hole as small as can be in a piece of paper, bring it as close to the eye as possible, and look at a star through this hole, only a small part of the pupil can operate, seeing the star with a large space of sky around it; and it sees it so small that almost nothing could be smaller. And if you make the opening near the edge of said paper, you can, at the same time, see the same star with the other eye, and it will appear large to you. Thus, at the same time, you will see one star twice with two eyes, one of which is tiny and the other large. Furthermore, you will be able to see the entire body of the sun with little splendor <note>meaning brightness or glare</note>, because as much as the size decreases, the splendor decreases proportionally, as was proposed above. From this it follows that large pupils see little by day, as the overabundance of light hinders their vision.

It includes an optical experiment using a pinhole to demonstrate how pupil size influences the perceived magnitude and brightness of celestial bodies.</summary>

# DILATION AND CONTRACTION OF THE PUPIL. —
# NOCTURNAL ANIMALS.

Concerning the increase and decrease of the pupil of the eye, from day to night, and more so in nocturnal animals than in others of the day. — Concerning the eyes of nocturnal animals whose pupils grow significantly at night, more beyond comparison than [those of] diurnal ones. — Concerning the eye which sees at the same time dark things and bright things, that is to say, resplendent ones. — Why nocturnal animals see more by night than by day. — Concerning the placement of the humors in man, in relation to his brain.

## CONCERNING THE HUMAN EYE.

**THE PUPIL OF THE EYE CHANGES INTO AS MANY DIVERSE SIZES AS THERE ARE DIFFERENCES IN THE BRIGHTNESS AND DARKNESS OF THE OBJECTS WHICH PRESENT THEMSELVES BEFORE IT.**

In this case, nature has provided a remedy <insert>brought aid</insert> to the <term>visual faculty</term><note>original: "vertu visuelle"; the medieval and Renaissance concept of the power or "virtue" that enables sight</note>, when it has had to suffer from excessive light, by narrowing the pupil of the eye; and when it has had to suffer from various darknesses, by widening this pupil similarly to the mouth [the opening] of a purse. Nature acts here like someone who, having too much light in his dwelling, closes half a window, and more or less according to necessity; and when night comes, he opens the whole window to see the light better within the said dwelling.

Here nature employs <insert>establishes</insert> a continual equation <insert>a continual equilibrium</insert> by tempering and equalizing continually, by the increase of the pupil or its diminution, in proportion to the aforementioned darknesses or brightnesses which continually present themselves to it; you will see the experience of this in animals <insert>and nocturnal birds</insert>, such as cats, screech-owls, owls, and other similar ones, which at noon have a small pupil and in which at night it is very large. All animals of land, air, and water do the same, but more, beyond comparison, the nocturnal animals. If you wish to make the experiment for man, look fixedly at the pupil of his eye while holding a lit candle a little distance from him, and have him look at the light <insert>and move it</insert>, which you will bring closer to him little by little; you will see that this pupil will narrow as the light approaches it.

## WHETHER THE EYE SEES BRIGHT [and] DARK THINGS AT THE SAME TIME.

The <term>crystalline humor</term><note>original: "humeur cristalline"; what we now call the lens of the eye</note> <insert>condenses itself</insert>, which resides within the pupil, <insert>condenses itself</insert> at the encounter of the species <note>original: "espèces"; in Aristotelian optics, "species" are the forms or images of objects traveling through the air to the eye</note> of things that shine, and becomes rarefied at the encounter of dark things. And that this is true is manifested when the eye closes, because the reserved [preserved] species which were of bright things are seen as dark, and the dark ones represent themselves as bright; this occurs more in weak eyes than in powerful ones. Of this, I shall speak more fully in another place.

— Next comes the discourse on the eyes of nocturnal animals, which see better by night than by day. And this arises from the fact that the quantity [the volume] of the eyes is greater than their entire brain, especially [in] screech-owls, owls, <unclear>?</unclear>, little owls, horned owls, and similar [animals], which does not occur in man, who has a brain larger than any other terrestrial animal relative to his eyes; therefore, he sees little light after the day.

[REFLECTION OF THE SUN IN WATER, PERSPECTIVE, STARS.]

— The small size of the pupil is the reason why the image <note>original: "simulacre," referring to a reflected image or likeness</note> of the sun appears as a tiny thing on the surface of the water. — If the eye were as large as the sphere of water, this water, when seen by the sun, would be entirely a single image of that sun. — How, if the sphere of water, through a great distance, diminishes to the appearance of a star, the image of the sun would occupy it entirely. — How distance makes the stars, which are many times larger than the earth, appear extremely small. —

---

### ON THE HUMAN EYE.

THE IMAGE OF THE SUN IS UNIQUE IN THE ENTIRE SPHERE OF WATER WHICH SEES THE SUN AND IS SEEN BY THE SUN, BUT IT APPEARS DIVIDED INTO AS MANY PARTS AS THERE ARE EYES OF ANIMALS SEEING THE SURFACE OF THE WATER FROM VARIOUS POSITIONS.

— What is proposed here is proven, since whatever path the eyes of navigators take, carried by ships throughout the universe, they see the image of the sun at the same time in all the waters of their hemisphere, through all movements made, and from all aspects. — If...

IF THE EYE WERE AS LARGE AS THE SPHERE OF WATER, IT WOULD SEE THE IMAGE OF THE SUN OCCUPYING A LARGE PART OF THE OCEAN.

This is demonstrated, for if you move across a bridge from which you see the image of the sun in the waters of the river, and you advance by about 25 braccia <note>An ancient unit of measurement, roughly a "cubit" or the length of an arm; approximately 23 inches</note>, you will see the image of the sun advance by the same amount on the surface of said water. And thus, if one were to put together all the images seen during the movement in question, you would have made a single image, which would have the shape of a flaming beam. Now, imagine making a circle of which the beam is the diameter, and that this entire circle is full of images; without doubt, you would see a single image, and the diameter would be 25 braccia; now, you must understand that if a pupil had for its diameter the same 25 braccia, it would see, without moving, in the same water, an image of the sun which would measure 78 and 4/7 braccia.

IF, BY THE LONG DISTANCE AT WHICH THE EYE WOULD BE FROM THE SPHERE OF WATER, THE SPHERE OF WATER DIMINISHED TO THE SIZE OF A COMMON IMAGE OF THE SUN, AS IS SHOWN IN PERSPECTIVE, YOU WOULD SEE IN THE SPHERE OF THIS WATER WHICH IS SEEN BY THE SUN ONLY A SINGLE IMAGE OF THE SUN.

— It is proven in perspective how things distant from the eye, even though they are extremely large, show themselves as extremely small figures, a thing seen without much demonstration; one sees if you lift your eyes to the starry sky, you will see there a very great number of stars which appear extremely small, and, being many times larger than the earth, appear extremely small due to the long distance; and the light that you see in them not being their own power <note>not inherent to them</note>, but only an image of the sun which is mirrored [reflected] in them; for, by themselves, the stars have no light, but rather a surface like the sphere of water, fit to receive and return the light of the sun which is mirrored [reflected] in them.

<summary>The author explains that the perceived size of the sun's reflection depends on the size of the observer's pupil and their distance from the water. He concludes that stars do not emit their own light but are water-like spheres reflecting the sun.</summary>
<keywords>optics, reflection, astronomy, perspective, sun, stars, planetary light, braccia</keywords>

[DILATION AND CONTRACTION OF THE PUPIL. —
THE VISUAL FACULTY COMMON TO THE ENTIRE PUPIL.]

[1st figure.] t v x p h s r a n o p q. — [?]. — [Under the 2nd fig. :] [Opinion of the] adversary. If the whole of the pupil, according to the adversary, does not see because he believes—at night, does he believe it is to see a greater sum of things, or to know them better? No doubt he believes it is to see them larger, and consequently better than to see many of them; having only to judge one at a time, such an increase does not take place [?].

### ON THE HUMAN EYE

THE PUPIL OF THE EYE HAS THE VISUAL FACULTY <note>original: "vertu visuelle" — the power or ability to see</note> ENTIRELY WITHIN THE WHOLE [OF THIS PUPIL], AND ENTIRELY WITHIN EACH OF ITS PARTS. AN OBJECT PLACED BEFORE THE EYE, AND SMALLER THAN ITS PUPIL, DOES NOT OCCUPY, FOR THE EYE, [THE PLACE OF] ANY OTHER DISTANT OBJECT, AND, ALTHOUGH IT IS DENSE, IT ACTS AS A TRANSPARENT THING.

Here the adversary says that the visual faculty is reduced to a single point, and [that] from this it follows that any object placed before the pupil that is larger than that point will occupy <note>i.e., block or fill</note> the perception [(of the eye)]. I say that according to him, and if it were true that the visual faculty were reduced to [a] point, the convexity of the eye—which turns and, with its parts, faces a great portion of the universality of things placed before it—could not have such a curvature unless it were [in all its parts] equidistant to that point; nor should its surface have to be cut at equal distances from that point, so that each of them, with the same real proportions, corresponds, in the intersections of the angles, to the proportions of the resemblances [images] of the bodies corresponding [?] to that point.

To that man, one demonstrates the experiment, and then concludes the necessity of that experiment. And first, for the experiment: let one place before the pupil the thickness of a sewing needle of medium size; let it be as close to it as possible, and one will see that it will not prevent the perception of any object placed behind it at any distance. What I say here is entirely confirmed by experience, and necessity dictates it [and it cannot be otherwise], because if this visual faculty were reduced to a point, the smallest object placed in front of this visual faculty would occupy the perception of a large part of the sky; considering that if a large part of the sky sends the species <note>original: "espèces" — the visual forms or images emitted by objects in Aristotelian/Renaissance optics</note> of its stars to the pupil, an object placed near [the pupil], equal to half of its diameter, would occupy a *large part*—nearly half—of the sky. This is why nature, so that nothing should be lacking to the eyes of animals, has ensured that the pupil <note>original: "prunelle"</note> has the fewest possible number of obstructions *that may be possible*; whereas the [point-like] visual faculty would be a very great obstruction to them, since, as has been said, the smallest object placed before it would occupy a large part of space for it.

Experience further shows that canvas screens <margin>1. See, for the word *scacci* <note>likely referring to a grid or checkered pattern</note>, above: Manuscript B, folio 4 recto, 1st figure, 2nd paragraph.</margin> made of thick horsehair, placed before the eyes, do not occupy [hide] anything [placed] beyond them, and they occupy even less as they are brought closer to the eye; now, if the visual faculty were in a point, the closer the hairs approached it, the vaster would be the space they would have to occupy. Therefore, experience producing the opposite, it is true that the visual faculty is infused throughout the entire pupil, employs all its parts, sees beyond the said hair, surrounding it and seeing beyond the whole of its thickness; and necessarily the pyramids <note>term: pyramids — the cone-shaped "pyramids of light" or vision that Renaissance theorists believed connected the eye to the object</note> are formed near the said hairs.

<summary>This page argues against the theory that vision converges into a single mathematical point, demonstrating through experiments with needles and horsehair that the visual faculty exists across the entire surface of the pupil. This allows the eye to "see around" small nearby objects that would otherwise block the entire field of vision.</summary>

THE PUPIL OF THE EYE HAS THE VISUAL FACULTY <term>visual faculty: the innate power or "virtue" of the eye to perceive light and images</term> ENTIRELY IN THE WHOLE AND ENTIRELY IN EVERY ONE OF ITS PARTS. The adversary says here that the visual faculty is reduced to a single point, and from this it follows that every object placed before the pupil that is larger than that point will occupy <note>meaning: block from view</note> that which I have mentioned <unclear>?</unclear>. Perception says that after him <note>referring to the opponent's logic</note> it is clear that if the visual faculty were reduced to a point, the convexity of the eye—which with its parts turns toward a great portion of the universe placed before it—could not be of such curvature if it were not equidistant to that point; nor could its surface be cut at equal distances from that point so that each part, with the same real proportions, would correspond in the intersections of the angles with the proportions of the likenesses of the bodies responding to that point.

To this man, the experiment is demonstrated, and then the necessity of such an experiment is concluded. And first, for the experiment: let there be placed before the pupil the thickness of a medium-sized sewing needle, and let it be as close as possible; and it will be seen that the perception of no object placed at some distance behind such a pupil is impeded. This which I say is entirely in conformity with experience, and necessity dictates it because if such a visual faculty were reduced to a point, every tiny object placed before such a visual faculty would occupy the perception of a great part of the sky. Because if a great part of the sky sends the <term>species: the "likenesses" or formal images of objects that Leonardo believed traveled through the air to the eye</term> of its stars to the pupil, an object placed near it and equal to half of its diameter would occupy a great part—almost half—of that sky. Wherefore Nature, so that nothing is lacking to the eyes of animals, has made it so that this light has the <unclear>?</unclear> number of impediments that are possible, and the smallest possible, of which the visual faculty [being a single point] would be the greatest impediment; because, as said, every tiny object placed before it would cause a great obstruction.

<margin>
adversary — if the whole of the pupil, according to the adversary, does not see because it grows at night <unclear>?</unclear> does it grow to see a greater sum of things or to know them better? Without doubt it grows to see them larger, and consequently better; for to see many things, not having to judge more than one at a time, such growth would not occur.
</margin>

Again, experience shows that the grids of chessboards <note>likely referring to a sighting grid or "veil" used by artists for perspective</note> made of thick horsehair bristles placed before the eyes do not obstruct anything behind them; and they obstruct even less the closer they are brought to the eye. Whereas if the visual faculty were in a point, the closer such bristles were brought to it, the wider the space they would have to occupy. Therefore, the experiment proving the contrary, it is true that the visual faculty is infused throughout the entire pupil, and every part acts within itself and sees behind such a bristle, surrounding it and seeing beyond the thickness of its size; and by necessity, the <term>pyramids: the cone-shaped "pyramid of vision" formed by rays of light converging from an object to the eye</term> are formed near the aforementioned bristles.

# ON THE EYE

[REPORT ON THE RELATION OF THE VISUAL FACULTY TO THE SIZE OF THE PUPIL. — IMAGES DEPENDING ON THE SHAPE OF THE PUPIL.]

->[1st figure:] g a n o p b m r f — [2nd fig. :] f a g n o t v h s r t p —<-

# ON THE EYE

->EVERY CONCAVE PLACE WILL APPEAR DARKER IF SEEN FROM THE OUTSIDE THAN IF ONE IS INSIDE.<-

This arises because for the eye that is outside, in the light, the pupil contracts greatly, and for the one placed in a dark place, the pupil expands; and with a smaller pupil, the power <note>original: "puissance," referring to the intensity of the visual faculty</note> diminishes, and thus this power grows with the enlargement of its pupil. To a pupil of weak power, every small obscurity appears pitch-black, and if it grows in power, every great obscurity will appear illuminated to it.

Superabundant light harms the eye, and against this harm, the visual faculty <term>visual faculty: the innate power or "virtue" of the eye to perceive light and images</term> takes the same recourse as one who closes part of a window to diminish the overly brilliant light that the sun creates in his dwelling.

## HOW A LARGER PUPIL SEES A LARGER OBJECT.

(The larger the shape of the pupil of the eye, the larger the things seen will appear to it.) This is proven by the [fact] that the pupil is entirely disposed with the same power throughout the vision. Let us say that **r** [1st figure] is the pupil of the eye, which receives by pyramids <note>Leonardo uses "pyramids" to describe the cone of light rays traveling from an object to the eye</note> the object **g**, placed before it, and that this pyramid measures its width on the small rod <term>vergette: a small rod or line used as a geometric reference point in his diagrams</term> **a b**, in the section **o**. Next, the pupil will grow by the entire diameter **m f**; then, the object **g** will no longer form a pyramid, but its species <term>species: the "likenesses" or visual information shed by objects that travel through the air to the eye</term> will come to the pupil by parallel lines, and will intersect at the same rod **a b**, and thus the image <term>simulacre: a visual representation or "simulacrum" of the object formed within the eye</term> of object **g** will be increased according to the enlargement of the pupil.

## HOW THE PUPIL TAKES THE IMAGES OF THINGS PLACED BEFORE THE EYE ONLY THROUGH THE PUPIL, AND NOT THROUGH THE OBJECT.

— (The pupil of the eye receives the images of its objects by means of the surface of the pupil, and not from the object). This is proven in part by means of spectacles <note>original: "lunettes," referring to early eyeglasses or lenses</note>, through which the passing images of objects become larger or smaller, according to the greater or lesser curvature of the exterior surface of their glass; this is further proven by the quality of the interior and exterior angles made by the rays of the species that penetrate the surface of the eye—that is, the exterior angles **n o** [2nd figure], which must necessarily be equal to the two interior angles **t v**. And if the pupil, which is in itself flat, had to be penetrated by such rays of the species *between exterior angles*, so that the interior angles were equal to the exterior angles, then such angles could not be generated within the pupil of the eye, but [would be] as far from this pupil as the distance from the middle of the object to its opposite extremities—that is, as much as there is from **a** [to] **f**, and from **a** [to] **g**, so much would there be from the pupil **r** to **s** and to **t**. For if the pupil is flat, and with it the surrounding part occupied by the crystalline humor <term>crystalline humor: the lens of the eye, thought in the Renaissance to be the primary organ of sight</term>, it is necessary that these interior angles, and likewise the exterior ones, be right angles.

<vocab>visual faculty, pupil, image (simulacre), crystalline humor, pyramid, rod (vergette)</vocab>

## ON THE EYE

### WHY AN UPRIGHT OBJECT DOES NOT APPEAR REVERSED TO THE EYE.

The <term>species</term> <note>Leonardo uses "species" to refer to the visual images or "likenesses" of objects that travel through the air to the eye.</note> of objects, when they enter the eye, bend the straightness of their rays in the manner proven in perspective, when these species pass from the density of water to the rarity of air; but, to return to the proposition of the upright object which does not appear reversed in the eye, we see clearly through experience that the species which penetrate the <term>albuminous humor</term> <note>The aqueous humor, or the clear fluid between the cornea and the lens.</note> through the pupil of the eye meet in the sphere of the <term>crystalline humor</term> <note>The lens of the eye.</note>, regarding which there are two things [hypotheses] to consider: that is, either that the visual faculty is within it, or that it is at the extremity of the optic nerve, which takes these species and carries them back to the <term>common sense</term> <note>The "sensus communis," a theoretical part of the brain where all sensory input was thought to be processed.</note>, as occurs in the nerves of smell. And if such a faculty *is in the is in the* center of the crystalline humor, it receives the species at its surface; or they are carried back to it by the surface of the pupil, where the objects are reflected, or they are sent back to it by the surface of the <term>uvea</term> <note>The pigmented layer of the eye, including the iris.</note>, which terminates and coats the albuminous humor, which has darkness behind its transparency, just as the darkness of lead is placed behind the transparency of glass, so that things can be better reflected on the surface of that glass. But, if the visual faculty is at the bottom in the center of the crystalline sphere, then all things given to it by the surface of the pupil of the eye will appear to it in the true position in which they are, will not change from right to left, and will appear larger, as is proven in perspective. And if this crystalline sphere takes such species, reflected from the concavity of the uvea, it will take them upright, even though the uvea is a concave mirror; it will take them upright because the center of the crystalline sphere is concentric to the center of the sphere of the uvea. It is true that the species which pass to this uvea, coming from the outside of the eye, pass to the uvea through the center of the crystalline sphere, and having arrived at the uvea, they are inverted; and the same happens to those that pass to the uvea without passing through this humor. Therefore, we shall try, by assuming that the visual faculty resides at the extremity of the optic nerve, to say that from there one sees that, in the crystalline sphere, all things taken by it are righted, since those that were inverted in the uvea are taken by it by inverting them a second time, and thus the crystalline sphere makes upright (the species which were given to it inverted). To such a scholar of Optics, it will perhaps be said that the spherical surface of the crystalline, joined to the sphere of the albuminous, does not change its nature, and is as if the whole were albuminous; and for that reason, the albuminous sphere would not have this function as it would if surrounded by air. But here, one responds that this effect cannot take place, because a crystal ball placed in water performs the same function as in air.

<summary>Leonardo investigates the optical mechanics of the eye, proposing that the crystalline lens rights inverted images so they are perceived correctly by the brain. He suggests experiments using water-filled glass bulbs to simulate the eye's humors and test how light refracts and reflects within the ocular structure.</summary>

# — FOLIO 7 (verso). —

### Why the right-side object does not appear as the left in the eye

<note>Leonardo's mirror script transcribed left-to-right. This text contains an optical study exploring why images seen by the eye are not perceived as reversed, focusing on the refraction of light through the crystalline humor.</note>

The <term>species</term> <note>original: "spetie"; Leonardo uses this term to refer to the "likenesses" or visual images of objects that travel through the air to the eye.</note> of the objects of the eye, in the entry made by them into the eye, bend the straightness of their rays in the manner that is proven in perspective when these species pass from the density of water to the rarity of air. But to return to the purpose of the right-side thing which does not appear as the left in the eye, we see by manifest experience that the species which penetrate into the <term>albuminous humor</term> <note>original: "omore albusineo"; the aqueous humor, the clear fluid between the cornea and the lens.</note> through the pupil of the eye meet in the sphere of the <term>crystalline humor</term> <note>original: "omore cristallino"; the lens of the eye.</note>, in which two things are to be considered: that is, either that the visual virtue is in it, or that it is in the front of the <term>optic nerve</term> <note>original: "neruo ottitio".</note>, which front takes these species and refers them to the <term>common sense</term> <note>original: "senco comune"; the Aristotelian concept of the part of the brain where all senses are integrated.</note> as those nerves of smell do. And if such virtue is in the center of the crystalline humor, it takes the species with its surface and they are referred to it by the surface of the <term>light</term> <note>original: "luce"; here referring to the cornea or the opening of the eye.</note> where the objects are mirrored; or they are reflected to it by the surface of the <term>uvea</term> <note>original: "ugvea"; the pigmented layer of the eye.</note> which is the boundary and garment of the albuminous humor, which has darkness behind the transparency of the albuminous humor, just as behind the transparency of glass is placed the darkness of lead so that things can be better mirrored in the surface of such glass. But if the visual virtue is in the center of the crystalline sphere, then all the things that shall be given to it by the surface of the light of the eye will appear to it in their proper site where they are, and they will not change from right to left, and will appear larger as proven in perspective. And if such a crystalline sphere takes such species reflected from the concavity of the uvea, it will take them upright even though the uvea is a concave mirror; and it will take them upright because the center of the crystalline sphere is concentric with the center of the sphere of the uvea. But it is true that the species which pass to that uvea, which are outside the eye, pass to that uvea through the center of the crystalline sphere, and having reached the uvea they become reversed; and the same is done by those which pass to that uvea without passing through such humor. Therefore, we shall prove that such visual virtue is in the front of the optic nerve, and say that from there one sees in the crystalline sphere all the things taken by it to be righted; because those which were made reversed in the uvea, it [the crystalline sphere] takes them and reverses them once more, and thus such crystalline sphere provides them upright (the species which were given to it reversed) to that optic nerve. It will perhaps be said that the spherical surface of the crystalline, united with the sphere of the albuminous, does not change nature and is as if all were albuminous, and for this reason the albuminous sphere would not have that office which it would have if surrounded by air. But here one responds that such an effect cannot happen, because a ball of crystal placed in water performs the same office as in the air. —

## ON THE EYE

#### WHY THE RIGHT-SIDE OBJECT DOES NOT APPEAR AS THE LEFT IN THE EYE

The species of the objects of the eye, in the entry made by them into the eye, bend the straightness of their rays in the manner that is proven in perspective when these species pass from the density of water to the rarity of air. But to return to the purpose of the right-side thing which does not appear as the left in the eye, we see by manifest experience that the species which penetrate into the albuminous humor through the pupil of the eye meet in the sphere of the crystalline humor, in which two things are to be considered: that is, either that the visual virtue is in it, or that it is in the front of the optic nerve, which front takes these species and refers them to the common sense as those nerves of smell do. And if such virtue is in the center of the crystalline humor, it takes the species with its surface and they are referred to it by the surface of the light where the objects are mirrored; or they are reflected to it by the surface of the uvea which is the boundary and garment of the albuminous humor, which has darkness behind the transparency of the albuminous humor, just as behind the transparency of glass is placed the darkness of lead so that things can be better mirrored in the surface of such glass. But if the visual virtue is in the center of the crystalline sphere, then all the things that shall be given to it by the surface of the light of the eye will appear to it in their proper site where they are, and they will not change from right to left, and will appear larger as proven in perspective. And if such a crystalline sphere takes such species reflected from the concavity of the uvea, it will take them upright even though the uvea is a concave mirror; and it will take them upright because the center of the crystalline sphere is concentric with the center of the sphere of the uvea. But it is true that the species which pass to that uvea, which are outside the eye, pass to that uvea through the center of the crystalline sphere, and having reached the uvea they become reversed; and the same is done by those which pass to that uvea without passing through such humor. Therefore, we shall prove that such visual virtue is in the front of the optic nerve, and say that from there one sees in the crystalline sphere all the things taken by it to be righted; because those which were made reversed in the uvea, it takes them and reverses them once more, and thus such crystalline sphere provides them upright (the species which were given to it reversed) to that optic nerve. It will perhaps be said that the spherical surface of the crystalline, united with the sphere of the albuminous, does not change nature and is as if all were albuminous, and for this reason the albuminous sphere would not have that office which it would have if surrounded by air. But here one responds that such an effect cannot happen, because a ball of crystal placed in water performs the same office as in the air. —

93

<summary>Leonardo investigates the optical mechanism of the eye, theorizing that the crystalline lens acts to "right" images that have been inverted, ensuring we perceive the world without left-right reversal. He proposes experiments using water-filled glass bulbs to simulate the eye's humors and test refraction.</summary>

# [HOW THE EYE PERCEIVES IMAGES. — VARIOUS LINES OF VISION.]

-> [1st figure: ] k b h i o n q m d a p c o f g — [2nd fig.: ] q v o n m l k a b c d e f g h i n — [3rd fig.: ] n m o — [4th fig.: ] r s t n v x y m — <-

## ON THE HUMAN EYE.

IT IS DEMONSTRATED [EXPLAINED] WHY THE EYE SEES BEHIND ITSELF THINGS PLACED IN THE LATERAL SPACES.

The eye perceives, even if it does not have <term>discernment</term><note>The author distinguishes between "seeing" (the physical reception of light) and "knowing/discerning" (the brain's focused recognition of an object).</note> of it, the movement of two lights at the contact of the wall where the *nape—the middle of the nape*—of the viewer rests.

The reason for this is that the <term>pupil</term><note>The original uses "prunelle" and "pupille" somewhat interchangeably; here it refers to the crystalline lens or the receptive surface of the eye.</note> sees all the places from which it is seen, and [that] all the objects that see this pupil imprint their likeness upon it, because it is more prominent [protruding] than any other part of the eye; the opening or the hole of the pupil sees and is seen by all parts of this pupil; therefore, it can very well receive within itself what the pupil of the eye shows it. It is true that an object is less known [appears less distinct] when it is imprinted from a greater distance from the center of the pupil, where the extremity of the **median line** terminates [ends], which always travels in a straight line toward all objects of whose form one can have a certain [exact] and true knowledge. This line is straight, without any intersection, and is the master of the other lines, by which it is always moved, determining what the others see but do not recognize; this is the line **k g**, placed in the middle of all the other lines, which are as numerous as the <term>species</term><note>original: "espèces". In Renaissance optics, "species" were the formal images or "likenesses" shed by objects that travel through the air to the eye.</note> that come to the eye, point by point.

## IN WHAT MANNER THE SPECIES OF OBJECTS COME TO THE EYE.

The eye has within it a single line, placed in the middle of an infinity of other lines adhering to the one called the central line.

The eye has *a single—within it a single line*, which is called central, and all the species of objects that come to the eye via this line are perfectly seen, if too great a distance does not prevent it. Around this line, there are an infinity of others adhering to it; they possess a strength that is greater or lesser depending on whether they are closer to or more *distant from this central line*.

## THE FUNCTION OF THE CENTRAL LINES IN THE CONVERGENCE OF THE VISIBLE.

The convergence of the two central lines is always at a point where an angle is engendered [formed], with an opening [width] that is larger or smaller depending on whether the object is seen at a smaller or greater distance from the eye.

If the two central lines [(4th figure)] converge at object **x**, the interior adhering lines **s v** and **r y** will see object **t** occupying two places on the wall **n m**, that is to say at **v** [and] **y**; but if these central lines end at **t**, then object **x** will be seen by the two exterior adhering lines, that is to say **r x** and **s x**, because the right eye sees with the right adhering line and the left eye with the left adhering line.

<header>[INTERPOSITION BETWEEN THE EYE AND THE OBJECT. ILLUSION OF THE EYE.]</header>

[1st figure:] i h g a b f c d — [2nd fig.:] f g d e a b c — [3rd fig.:] a b s h i t c f d e g — [5th fig.:] a b c d f g e h i — [Under the 5th fig.:] Here again the sense is deceived, since the pupil a b sees, with part a, the <term>stylus</term><note>A pointed tool or pin used here as a physical obstruction in an optical experiment.</note> c occupying the field i; now, if this stylus were moved from c to d, the movement of the obstruction would go from i to h. # ON THE HUMAN EYE.

## WHY THE POINT OF THE STYLUS, BEING PLACED ACROSS THE PUPIL OF THE EYE, CASTS A LARGE SHADOW UPON THE OBJECT.

The point of the stylus, placed crosswise before the pupil of the eye, **a** (the diameter of whose thickness is much less than the diameter of the pupil), will occupy more or less space on other objects depending on whether it is closer to or further from the eye; this obstruction will darken, but not prevent, the passage of the <term>species</term><note>original: "espèces". In Renaissance science, these are the "likenesses" or formal qualities of an object that travel through the air to the eye.</note> of the aforementioned objects to the eye.

## WHICH PART OF THE FIELD IS SEEN BY THE EYES LOOKING THROUGH SOME VENT [[OPENING]].

Let there be two eyes which, through the opening d c [2nd figure], look at the field a c; I say that these two eyes will not see [together] anything of this field other than the space b. The rest of the right-hand space, a b, will be seen by the left eye g, and the remaining part of the left-hand space, b c, will be seen only by the right eye f.

## WHERE THE TWO EYES WILL NOT SEE THE FIELD ENTIRELY UNCOVERED, THROUGH A GIVEN OPENING.

The right eye a [3rd figure] sees the uncovered field e g, and sees all the rest e f covered by the wall s h; the eye b alone sees the field f d uncovered, and it sees the rest d g occupied by the wall i t. The triangular space c d e is seen neither by one eye nor the other, because eye a covers the extremity e with the edge of the vent h and eye b covers the extremity d with the edge of the vent i. Therefore, it is concluded that, although each of the two eyes sees a part of the uncovered field by itself, the other eye tints it [puts it in shadow] by carrying one of the sides of the wall over it. This is why one can conclude that with a single eye a thing appears less clear than with two; indeed, if one of the eyes is closed and sees darkness, the other is open and sees the light¹, light which mixes with the darkness in the <term>visual faculty</term><note>original: "vertu visuelle". The internal power or mechanism of sight.</note>, allowing neither simple light nor simple darkness to appear. It is no longer understood as anything but a mixture composed of darkness and light. Furthermore, one understands by this that the right eye, although it sees the left-hand thing on the left side *being on the left side*, believes it sees it with the left eye, and that the sense [of sight] does not perceive that it is being deceived. Likewise for the left eye, which sees the field on the right side; it seems to the sense again that it is deceived in this, that it has seen this field with the right eye, etc.

## [RAYS OF LUMINOUS BODIES CAUSED NOT BY THE OBJECTS, BUT BY THE PUPIL.]

[1st figure:] c b d a — [2nd fig.] o n — This eye sees the ray of the luminous body above that body.
— [Below the 2nd figure:] This second eye sees the luminous rays below the luminous body.
— [Below the 3rd figure:] This 3rd eye sees the upper and lower rays above and below the luminous body.
— [5th fig.:] c b d n a m — [6th and 7th fig.:] u [?] a b.

## ON THE EYE

### WHY THE RAYS OF LUMINOUS BODIES GROW AT THE SAME TIME AS THE SPACE INTERPOSED BETWEEN THEM AND THE EYE.

The lengths of the rays created by luminous bodies grow at the same time as the increase of the space that is interposed between these bodies and the eye. Here it is first necessary to define what the rays of luminous bodies are, and if they have their origin at the eye which looks at these bodies, or rather are born from these luminous bodies. Concluding that they are born from the eye, it is necessary to say why and in what manner, etc.

### WHY LUMINOUS BODIES SHOW THEIR EXTREMITIES [CONTOURS] FULL [COVERED] WITH STRAIGHT LUMINOUS RAYS.

The rays which show us the extremities of luminous bodies do not have their origin in these bodies, but in their <term>simulacrum</term><note>original: "simulacre". In Leonardo's optics, this refers to the image or "likeness" of an object transmitted to the eye.</note>, which is imprinted in the thickness of the <term>coverings</term> [eyelids] of the eyes that look at these bodies. One proves it first by persuasive means, which teaches us that the eye opened very wide does not show us such rays around the luminous body; and if the simulacrum of a star or other light passes to the eye through a very small hole made in paper placed before the eye, such luminous [bodies] are always without rays. But the true proof is shown by the ninth [proposition] of perspective; where it is said: (the angle of incidence is always equal to the angle of reflection); therefore, the rays which appear to extend from the luminous body at the contact of the eye that sees it, are born when the eye, almost closed, looks through the narrow slit interposed between the <term>lips</term> [edges of the eyelids] of the eyes at the luminous [body], whose simulacrum is mirrored [reflected] in the thickness of the lips [edges of the eyelids] which terminate the coverings [eyelids], and, after this impression, is reflected into the pupil of the eye. This pupil takes three simulacra of the same luminous [body], that is to say, two in the thicknesses of the lips that the coverings of the eye have [in the thickness of the edges of the eyelids], and one in the pupil, and *because they are very close*, these three [and the first two] simulacra, being very close to one another, appear to the eye to be in continuation and conjunction with the simulacrum of the pupil. 

And the proof that experience shows us, in confirmation of our proposition, manifests itself when, raising or lowering the face, one keeps the eye fixed and [partially] closed on the luminous body; the eye, when one raises the face, will lose all the lower rays of this luminous [body]. This arises because the simulacrum of the luminous body does not go to imprint itself in the thickness of the lower covering of the eye where the luminous body does not see it—it cannot imprint its simulacrum there—and because where the incident ray does not strike, it does not engender the reflected ray, which is why the pupil does not receive it. And thus it will happen when one lowers the face, because then the thickness of the upper covering does not see and is not seen by the luminous body, which is why, as has been said, the simulacrum cannot ~~produce~~ imprint itself there, and consequently the eye cannot see there what is not there; but it sees the simulacrum in the covering below, a covering which sees and is seen by the luminous body. Thus is proved what we conceived.

The adversary says that the ray bends [is inflected], because it arrives at the sense from the rare to the dense <note>A reference to the classical theory of refraction, where light bends when moving from a thin medium (air) to a dense one (the eye).</note>.

<summary>Leonardo explains that the "rays" seen around stars or candles are optical illusions caused by light reflecting off the edges of the eyelids into the pupil. He uses the law of reflection to argue that these rays are not part of the light source itself but are generated by the eye's anatomy.</summary>

...es] will always be without rays. But the true proof is shown by the ninth [proposition] of perspective, where it says: "the angle of incidence is always equal to the angle of reflection." Such a luminous body, whose simulacrum is reflected in the thickness of the lips that terminate these coverings, and after such an impression, reflects to the pupil of the eye. # FOLIO 10 (verso).

<note>The following is a translation of Leonardo's mirror-script handwriting, which explores the nature of light and the limitations of human vision regarding the edges of objects.</note>

**The images of objects infused into the opposing air are all in all of that air and all in every part of it. This is proved —**

**Conception of objects. — All that air sees the object placed opposite to its axis which is seen by the same object —**

This is proved by the 3rd [proposition] of this [treatise] which says (all visions made in the same quality of air are rectilinear — therefore, since it is possible to draw a straight line from the eye to every part of the air seen by that eye, that vision is rectilinear; and it is further proved by means of that which Aristotle says) <note>Aristotle, *Physics* or *De Anima*: Leonardo often cites the Aristotelian principle of nature acting via the shortest path.</note> every natural action is performed in the shortest way possible etc. Therefore, vision will be made by the shortest line, that is, a straight line.

<margin>
**ON THE IMAGES OF OBJECTS INFUSED THROUGH THE AIR**
</margin>

The images of objects <term>spetie</term> <note>From the Latin 'species'; in Renaissance optics, these were the 'likenesses' or formal qualities of an object that traveled through the air to the eye.</note> have their images infused in all the air seen by those objects: which images are all in all the said air and are all in every part of it.

<margin>
**HOW THE EYE DOES NOT RECOGNIZE THE BOUNDARY OF ANY BODY —**
</margin>

The eye will never be capable of [perceiving] the true boundary <term>termine</term> <note>The precise edge or mathematical limit where an object ends and the background begins.</note> possessed by the figures of any body standing out in a remote place — this is proved: let the pupil of the eye be **a b** and the edge of the body be **c**, and let **p** be the body placed before the eye of which the upper edge **c** of **p** is noted; let the field in which such an edge must be seen by that eye be **n m**. I say that the edge of such a body will not be known in what part of such a field it is terminated, and this is proved with the help of the 3rd [proposition] of this [treatise] which says: the visual faculty <term>virtu visiva</term> <note>The 'power of sight' which Leonardo argues is distributed across the whole pupil rather than being a single mathematical point.</note> is not in a point as the perspective painters would have it, but is all in all the pupil through which the images of objects penetrate inside the eye into a space larger than such a pupil; but the likenesses <term>simulacri</term> are more distinct the closer they are to the center of such faculty placed in said space, and so much less as they are more remote from that center. Therefore, if the faculty **a b** takes the edge of the object **c**, the central line of the visual faculty **r** sees **c** in the part of the field **f**, and the upper edge of this faculty, that is **s**, sees **c** in the field **h**, and the lowest part of the faculty sees **c** in the field **d**, and so it goes spreading throughout the field **d h**. And for this reason, such an edge is not known to the eye; but because the sense of the visual faculty is throughout all that faculty, it provides to the judgment <term>stimativa</term> <note>The 'estimative' faculty of the brain that processes sensory data.</note> a confused termination of that edge **c**, and more or less so as it is closer or further from that central line of the faculty [?] and more or less as **c** is more remote or closer to the eye —

**CONCEPTION OF THE OBJECTS. — ALL THAT AIR SEES THE OPPOSING OBJECT AXIS WHICH IS SEEN BY THE SAME OBJECT —**

*ON THE IMAGES OF OBJECTS INFUSED THROUGH THE AIR*
The images of objects have their images infused in all the air seen by those objects: which images are all in all the said air and are all in every part of it.

*HOW THE EYE DOES NOT RECOGNIZE THE BOUNDARY OF ANY BODY —*
The eye will never be capable of [perceiving] the true boundary that the figures of any body have when standing out in a remote place — this is proved: let the pupil of the eye be **a b** and the edge of the body be **c**, and let **p** be the body placed before the eye of which the upper edge **c** of **p** is noted; let the field in which such an edge must be seen by that eye be **n m**. I say that the edge of such a body will not be known in what part of such a field it is terminated, and this is proved with the help of the 3rd [proposition] of this [treatise] which says: the visual faculty is not in a point as the perspective painters would have it, but is all in all the pupil through which the images of objects penetrate inside the eye into a space larger than such a pupil; but the likenesses are more distinct the closer they are to the center of such faculty placed in said space, and so much less as they are more remote from that center. Therefore, if the faculty **a b** takes the edge of the object **c**, the central line of the visual faculty **r** sees **c** in the part of the field **f**, and the upper edge of this faculty, that is **s**, sees **c** in the field **h**, and the lowest part of the faculty sees **c** in the field **d**, and so it goes spreading throughout the field **d h**. And for this reason, such an edge is not known to the eye; but because the sense of the visual faculty is throughout all that faculty, it provides to the judgment a confused termination of that edge **c**, and more or less so as it is closer or further from that central line of the faculty [?] and more or less as **c** is more remote or closer to the eye —

<summary>Leonardo argues that the visual faculty is distributed across the entire pupil rather than a single point, leading to a natural blurring of object edges (sfumato) because different parts of the pupil see the edge against different parts of the background. He also asserts that visual information (species) fills the air in a rectilinear fashion, following the Aristotelian principle of the shortest path.</summary>
<keywords>optics, eye, vision, perspective, pupil, visual faculty, Aristotle, boundary, images, air, species, sfumato</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Leonardo's investigations into the physics of light and the physiology of the eye, specifically focusing on how "species" (images or visual information) propagate through the air and are received by the pupil.</meta>

# FOLIO 10 (verso).

<note>The following is a translation of Leonardo's mirror-script handwriting, which explores the nature of light and the limitations of human vision regarding the edges of objects.</note>

**The images of objects infused into the opposing air are all in all of that air and all in every part of it. This is proved —**

**Conception of objects. — All that air sees the object placed opposite to its axis which is seen by the same object —**

This is proved by the 3rd proposition of this treatise which says: all visions made in the same quality of air are rectilinear — therefore, since it is possible to draw a straight line from the eye to every part of the air seen by that eye, that vision is rectilinear; and it is further proved by means of that which Aristotle says: <note>original: "Aristotile dice"</note> every natural action is performed in the shortest way possible, etc. <note>Aristotle, Physics or De Anima: Leonardo often cites the Aristotelian principle of nature acting via the shortest path.</note> Therefore, vision will be made by the shortest line, that is, a straight line.

<margin>
**ON THE IMAGES OF OBJECTS INFUSED THROUGH THE AIR**
</margin>

The images of objects <term>species</term> <note>From the Latin 'species'; in Renaissance optics, these were the 'likenesses' or formal qualities of an object that traveled through the air to the eye.</note> have their images infused in all the air seen by those objects: which images are all in all the said air and are all in every part of it.

<margin>
**HOW THE EYE DOES NOT RECOGNIZE THE BOUNDARY OF ANY BODY —**
</margin>

The eye will never be capable of perceiving the true boundary <term>limit</term> <note>original: "termine"; the precise edge or mathematical limit where an object ends and the background begins.</note> of any body...

<summary>Leonardo explains his theory of "species," arguing that the visual information of an object fills the surrounding air entirely and travels in straight lines according to Aristotelian physics. He also begins to discuss why the human eye cannot perceive the mathematically perfect edges of objects.</summary>

<keywords>optics, species, rectilinear vision, Aristotle, perspective, boundaries of objects, Leonardo da Vinci</keywords>

1. Mr. Richter has so singularly insisted in: *The Journal of Fine Arts* <note>original: "Die Zeitschrift für bildende Kunst"</note>, on the errors of my transcription of the first passage of folio 1 recto, that I must show here that, while merely republishing this passage, he himself was not able to arrive at a perfect correction. Thus, he wrongly deviates from the transcription I gave of it (*The literary works of Leon. da V.*, Vol. I, no. 628), by reading: 2nd line of the manuscript, *o pero, o noce* [either pear or walnut], without the literal rectifying text carrying *opero, onoce* as it carries *ossorbo* [service-tree]; 4th line, literal text: (4.) *cressciere* [to grow] instead of: *cresciere* and *sechondo lumido* [according to the damp], instead of: *sechondo il se lumido*; 6th line, *bolito* [boiled], instead of: *bolito to*, and *sifreddi* [it cools], instead of: *sifredi*; 8th line, *poi* [then] [literal text: *po.*] instead of: *po*; finally, 6th line, by forgetting the words: *erascivga* [and it dries], after the word: *asciuttia* [dryness], although they are found in the translation "and dry it again". — In Italy, the painting chassis that precedes the text appeared in the inventory of the Arcouati donation as being an "incasto dacqua!" <note>water-inlay</note> What can be concluded from this, if not that it is perhaps fairer to look with indulgence upon the publications of unpublished texts such as those in question, rather than to overwhelm them with severity, especially when the possibility is given to easily arrive at absolute accuracy? In this regard, Mr. de Geymüller expressed in the *Chronicle of the Arts* <note>original: "Chronique des Arts"</note> of June 11, 1881, sentiments toward me for which I thank him, ideas on the various current and future works concerning Leonardo's writings, with which I very willingly associate myself and which have general approval.

2. Mr. Richter says in English (*The lit. works of L. da V.* (Vol. II, p. 171, note 318, and pl. XVII), regarding the explanatory figure I proposed in a note for the profile of folio 2 verso (Manuscript A): "The sketch as we see it can hardly have been intended for anything other than an experimental trial to ascertain relative proportions. We do not find that Leonardo made use of circular lines in other studies on the proportions of the human head. At the same time, we see that the proportions of this sketch are not in accord with the rules he usually observes." — 1st: Folio 63 recto of Manuscript A, plates VII to XI of the second volume of the *Liter. works, etc.*, provide examples of human faces divided geometrically. 2nd: Plate XVIII of the same work reproduces a well-known autograph page by Leonardo where one sees a man inscribed in a square and in a circle. 3rd: It is indisputable that the profile in question is inscribed in a circle, crossed by two circular arcs, and furthermore, bears certain marks on the circle circumscribed to the head, which do not seem to be due only to chance. Do these facts not sufficiently justify, until proven otherwise, the hypothesis I have put forward?

1. Mr. Richter, citing folio 40 verso (*The literary works of L. da V.*, vol. I, no. 543), says in a note: "It is unnecessary to give prominence to the points in which my reading differs of that of M. Ravaisson or to justify myself, since they are all of secondary importance, and can also be immediately verified from the photograph facsimile in his edition." This note, where the necessity of facsimiles is implicitly recognized, could lead one to believe in many reading errors on my part, although "all of secondary importance." There would only be one error there. Indeed, if Mr. Richter was right to read: *o alteza* and *una tola* (see above), and if one may hesitate to recognize: *chapitolo* or *chapitelo* (12th line), *stia* or *fia* (13th line), *riguardale* or *riguardalo* (16th line), *rotondo* or *retondo* (14th line), one only had to adopt my transcription for many other words, and not give another; indeed, the manuscript clearly bears, as I had transcribed (2nd line): *leffatto*, and not: *leffetto*; (3rd line): *aparisscha*, and not: *aparischa*; *proportione chespo chessi po*, and not: *proportine chessi po* (8th line): *ilmeno*, and not: *almeno*; (14th line): *abi*, and not: *aci* (16th line); *pola ombra*, to be interpreted: *poi la ombra*, and not: "poni la ombra"; 17th line, *buso*, and not: *baso*.

2. Mr. de Geymüller (*The literary works of Leon. da V.*, vol. II, p. 99) translates this passage thus: as if they were made in "hills," and adds in a note: "M. Ravaisson, in his edition of Ms A, gives a very different rendering of this passage, etc." But it should be noted in my defense, if I had translated poorly, that in citing my translation Mr. de G. forgot a question mark which was for me at least an excuse, printing: "vaulted [a cholli]" where I had printed: vaulted [? — acholli].

3. Mr. de Geymüller, same page, correctly notes the error reported above; but to a certain extent, he could not escape it himself, since he inserts in his literal text (19): "propositione Isolari chessone." — In the manuscript, the word *propositione* appears, judging by the handwriting, to have been traced immediately after the word *finestre*, like a title following a statement, and shortly before the words: *Quessto muro*; in any case, it was not done at the same time as the words *Isolari*, which do not begin, neither in handwriting nor in sense, a new chapter — See above, note 1 of folio 1 recto.

**Folio 2 recto (ENGLISH)** <note>original: "FRANÇAIS"; the errata refers to the translated portion of the edition</note>, 5th line, *instead of*: of these eyes [?] the eye — *read*: of these eyes [?] the eye; 12th line, *instead of*: to [to] — *read*: has [to].
**Folio 2 verso (ENGLISH)**, 20th line, *instead of*: the impressionability [inprensiva] — *read*: imprensiva <note>The term "imprensiva" is a technical term used by Leonardo to describe the "receptive" or "perceptive" power of the eye</note>.
**Folio 3 recto (ITALIAN)**, 5th line, *instead of*: ose, and of: esstre — *read*: cose and desstre <note>Correcting archaic Italian spellings for "things" and "right-hand"</note>. — **(ENGLISH)**, 25th line, *instead of*: do not pass — *read*: do not pass [pass]; 27th line, *instead of*: do not exchange — *read*: do not exchange [exchange]; 33rd line, *instead of*: does not make straight [? (does not straighten itself?) ] inside the pyramid k h r, and if you wish, reverses it [? (or, if you wish, does it not reverse itself?) ] — *read*: does not make straight [does not make the species straight, until] inside the pyramid k h r, and if you wish, reverses it [and then reverses them] [?].
**Folio 3 verso (ENGLISH)**, 5th line, *after*: of the eye, *add the note*: The other figures will be found further down; — 27th line, *instead of*: stancho [?] — *read*: left.
**Folio 4 recto (ITALIAN)**, 9th line, *instead of*: donde — *read*: donde <note>Likely a correction of a subtle transcription error in the Italian "from where"</note>.
**Folio 4 verso (ITALIAN)**, 6th line, *instead of*: mossra — *read*: mosstra; 24th line, *instead of*: esseperimento — *read*: essperimento <note>Correction to "experiment"</note>; 30th line, *instead of*: propsito — *read*: proposito. — **(ENGLISH)**, 45th line, *instead of*: the [? sought ?] — *read*: the ninth; 49th line, *instead of*: it will occupy — *read*: will occupy.
**Folio 5 recto (ENGLISH)**, 2nd line of the summary, 15th, 17th, 18th, 19th, 20th, 21st and 27th lines of the texts, *instead of*: inprensiva — *read*: imprensiva; 3rd line, *instead of*: the impression — *read*: the imprensiva; 18-19th lines, *instead of*: for man — *read*: is greater for man.
**Folio 5 verso (ITALIAN)**, 23rd line, *instead of*: barbaganni [?] — *read*: barbaganni <note>Italian for "barn owls"</note>; 22nd line, *instead of*: present themselves — *read*: present themselves, present themselves. — **(ENGLISH)**, 32nd line, *instead of*: condenses, which resides inside the pupil — *read*: which resides inside the pupil, condenses; 42nd line, *instead of*: owls, [?] owls — *read*: owls, screech owls.
**Folio 6 verso (ENGLISH)**, 21st line, *instead of*: correspond <note>plural</note> — *read*: correspond <note>singular</note>.
**Folio 7 recto (ENGLISH)**, 31st-32nd lines, *instead of*: of [by] the quality of the interior angles — *read*: of the angles of [by] the quality of the interior angles.
**Folio 7 verso (ENGLISH)**, 1st line, *instead of*: mop — *read*: m o p <note>Referring to labels on a geometric diagram</note>.
**Folio 8 recto (ENGLISH)**, 31st line, *instead of*: shows [what is happening] — *read*: shows itself — and add as a note: See: Venturi, *Essay*, etc., p. 23 (camera obscura <note>The "dark chamber" or early pinhole camera principle</note>), D.-M. Jordan, *The Notebook of L. da V.*, p. 74; Richter, *The literary works of L. da V.*, vol. II, p. 44, no. 71, and 70 note.
**Folio 9 recto (ENGLISH)**, at the bottom of the page, *instead of*: sense [of sight] — *read*: sense.
**Folio 10 verso (ENGLISH)**, 2nd line of the summary, *instead of*: indistinct <note>masculine</note> — *read*: indistinct <note>feminine</note>; 4th line, *instead of*: the <note>masculine</note> — *read*: the <note>feminine</note>.
